2027-07-03.title: Dukrono of St Thomas the Apostle
readings: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
Go from your country to the land I will show you
The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn
Oh, that I knew where I might find him
How beautiful are the feet of the messenger
Live as free people, as servants of God
In Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel
2027-07-03.alt: Dukrono (commemoration) of St Thomas the Apostle, Father in Faith of the Church in India: Holy Qurbono for the people. St Thomas Day. Also the name day of Most Rev. Joseph Mar Thomas.
2027-07-03.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
theo: On the evening of Easter Thomas was not with the others. When they told him, “We have seen the Lord,” he said: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” A week later Jesus came again and said to him: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” Thomas answered: “My Lord and my God!” It is the fullest confession of faith in the Gospels: the risen Jesus is Lord and God.

Jesus answered: “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” That blessing is for us. The faith of India was not built on seeing but on the word of the apostle who saw, touched and believed. According to the ancient tradition of our Church, Thomas came to Kerala around AD 52, preached, founded communities, and gave his life as a martyr at Mylapore around AD 72. We are Thomas Christians, Mar Thoma Nasranikal.

At the Last Supper it was Thomas who asked: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” And Jesus gave the great answer: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” The questioner became the witness; the one who wanted proof travelled the furthest of all the apostles to give it.

Abraham left his country for a land God would show him; Thomas left Galilee for India. Isaiah sings: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news.” Paul writes: “In Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.” Thomas is our father in faith. Today we thank God for him and ask for his courage to confess Jesus as Lord and God in our own land.
conn: Abraham's journey.
Genesis 12: leaving home at God's word; Thomas travels to the ends of the earth for Christ.
Beautiful feet.
Isaiah 52:7: the messenger on the mountains; Thomas on the mountain at Mylapore.
Father in faith.
1 Corinthians 4:15: a father through the gospel; Thomas, father of the Church in India.
Seeking God.
Job 23:3: “Oh, that I knew where I might find him!”; Thomas asks the way and finds it in Christ.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono we do what Thomas did: we see with the eyes of faith the risen Lord who shows us his wounds, and we say, as the priest elevates the Mysteries, “My Lord and my God.”
outline: Opening
The apostle of India.
Point 1 · Unless I see
Honest doubt brought to Jesus.
Point 2 · My Lord and my God
The highest confession of faith.
Point 3 · I am the way
Thomas's question and Christ's answer.
Point 4 · Blessed are those who have not seen
Our faith, received from Thomas.
Take-home line
“My Lord and my God!”
live: Make his confession yours
Say “My Lord and my God” at the elevation of the Holy Mysteries.
Visit a Thomas shrine
If possible, pray at a church linked with St Thomas, or pray for the whole Church in India.
Bring your doubts to Jesus
Bring an honest question to prayer instead of walking away from faith.
fathers: St Gregory the Great
The unbelief of Thomas has done more for our faith than the faith of the believing disciples; by touching he healed in us the wound of unbelief (Homilies on the Gospels 26).
St Ephrem the Syrian
Ephrem sings of the bones of the Apostle brought from India to Edessa by a merchant, and of Thomas who enlightened India (Nisibene Hymns 42).
magis: Catechism 644–645
The risen Jesus invites the disciples to touch him; Thomas confesses him Lord and God.
Catechism 448
The title “Lord” in the confession of Thomas expresses divine sovereignty.
Orientalium Ecclesiarum 1, 3
The Catholic Church holds in high esteem the institutions, rites and traditions of the Eastern Churches, which are of equal dignity.
saints: Sunday 4 July: VII Sunday after Pentecost. 6 July: St Maria Goretti. 11 July: St Benedict. 15 July (Thu): Commemoration of the Servant of God Archbishop Mar Ivanios.
2027-07-03.prayer: Lord Jesus, you showed your wounds to Thomas and led him from doubt to faith. Through his prayers keep us faithful to the faith he brought to India; make us witnesses in our land, and let our lives say with him: “My Lord and my God.” Amen.

2027-07-04.title: Seventh Sunday after Pentecost
readings: By your words you will be justified
The glory has departed from Israel
Their deeds do not permit them to return
Peace, peace, to the far and the near
The place was shaken; they spoke the word with boldness
He is our peace; the dividing wall broken down
A house divided against itself cannot stand
2027-07-04.alt: Season of Pentecost. Family Day: pray today for every family of the Church.
2027-07-04.verse: If a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.
theo: When Jesus casts out demons, some scribes say he does it by the ruler of demons. Jesus answers: “If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.” Satan divides; Christ unites. Wherever the Spirit is at work, he builds communion: in hearts, families, parishes and between Churches.

Jesus then gives a solemn warning: “Truly I tell you, people will be forgiven for their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit can never have forgiveness.” The Church teaches that this is not a sin too great for God's mercy, but the refusal to accept that mercy: calling the Spirit's work evil and so closing the door through which forgiveness comes. In the evening Gospel Jesus adds: “by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

St Paul tells the Ephesians that Christ “is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.” Jews and Gentiles, once far apart, are now “citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.” Isaiah had promised: “Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal them.”

The first Christians, threatened by the authorities, did not divide or despair. They prayed together: “Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness.” “When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness.” United prayer brings the Spirit; the Spirit brings courage.
conn: Atonement.
Leviticus 16: the Day of Atonement cleansed the people once a year; Christ's blood reconciles us once for all (Ephesians 2:13).
Glory departed.
1 Samuel 4:21–22: “Ichabod”, the glory has gone, when Israel was unfaithful; the glory returns in Christ, and dwells in the Church as God's temple (Ephesians 2:21–22).
A house divided.
Mark 3:25 and Ephesians 2:14: division is the devil's work; Christ breaks down the dividing wall.
Bold prayer.
Acts 4:31: the house shaken by the Spirit, the opposite of the divided house.
altar: “In Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.” At the Holy Qurbono the sign of peace is exchanged before the anaphora: we cannot offer the one sacrifice while divided from our brother.
outline: Opening
A house divided cannot stand.
Point 1 · Satan divides, Christ unites
The Spirit builds communion.
Point 2 · The sin against the Spirit
Refusing mercy; the power of our words.
Point 3 · He is our peace
The dividing wall broken down.
Point 4 · The place was shaken
United prayer, bold witness.
Take-home line
“He is our peace.”
live: Heal one division
Take one step toward reconciliation in your family or parish this week.
Guard your words
Avoid one careless or harsh word each day; “by your words you will be justified.”
Pray for Christian unity
Pray for the unity of the Churches of the Thomas tradition in Kerala.
fathers: St Augustine
The sin against the Holy Spirit is impenitence: a heart that refuses to the end the forgiveness the Spirit offers in the Church (Sermon 71).
St John Chrysostom
Christ did not only make peace between us and God, but between us and one another, removing the wall of enmity (Homilies on Ephesians 5).
magis: Catechism 1864
There are no limits to God's mercy, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept it by repenting rejects forgiveness and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 820–822
Christ bestows unity on his Church; the desire to recover the unity of all Christians is a gift of Christ and a call of the Spirit.
Unitatis Redintegratio 1
Division openly contradicts the will of Christ and is a scandal to the world.
saints: 6 July: St Maria Goretti. 11 July: St Benedict. Sunday 11 July: VIII Sunday after Pentecost. 15 July (Thu): Commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios.
2027-07-04.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are our peace; you broke down the dividing wall of hostility. Heal the divisions in our hearts, families, parishes and Churches. Guard our tongues, keep us open to the mercy of your Spirit, and fill us with boldness to speak your word. Amen.

2027-07-11.title: Eighth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: Let anyone with ears to hear listen
Oh, that I knew where I might find him
Obey my voice, and I will be your God
My servants shall sing for gladness of heart
A chosen race, a royal priesthood
The word of God is living and active
Those who hear the word and accept it bear fruit
2027-07-11.alt: Season of Pentecost. (The 2025–26 lectionary lists Mark 4 for both Gospels; check the 2026–27 lectionary.)
2027-07-11.verse: Indeed, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing until it divides soul from spirit, joints from marrow; it is able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
theo: “Indeed, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword… able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” God's word is not a dead letter; it cuts, heals, judges and gives life. When the Gospel is proclaimed in the Qurbono, Christ himself speaks. The question is not whether the word is powerful, but whether we listen.

In Mark's Gospel Jesus begins his teaching by the sea with one word: “Listen!” Then the sower goes out to sow. The seed is the word; the soil is the human heart. “And these are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.” And he ends: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” Listening is the first act of faith.

At the burning bush God speaks to Moses and reveals his name: “I AM WHO I AM… This is my name forever.” God is not an idea; he is the living One who speaks and sends: “I will be with you.” Jeremiah repeats God's one demand: “Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” To obey (in Latin ob-audire) is to listen deeply.

The Letter to the Hebrews joins the Word with mercy: “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy.” St Peter tells us who we have become by listening and believing: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people.”
conn: I AM.
Exodus 3:14: the divine name; Jesus speaks with the same authority: “Listen!”
Obey my voice.
Jeremiah 7:23: the covenant is listening; Mark 4:20: the good soil hears and accepts.
Seeking God.
Job 23:3: Job longs to find God; Hebrews 4:16: in Christ we may approach the throne with boldness.
A royal priesthood.
1 Peter 2:9: the people formed by the Word to declare God's wonders.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the Word is first proclaimed, then made flesh on the altar. The same Christ who speaks in the Gospel gives himself in the Mysteries; the hearing of the Word prepares the heart to receive the Bread.
outline: Opening
“Listen!”: the first word of the parable.
Point 1 · Living and active
The Word cuts, heals and judges.
Point 2 · Hearing and accepting
Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
Point 3 · I AM
The God who speaks and sends.
Point 4 · The throne of grace
A high priest who understands our weakness.
Take-home line
“Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
live: Ten minutes with the Word
Read the Sunday Gospel again each day this week, slowly, for ten minutes.
Listen to someone
Give one person your full attention this week, without interrupting.
Approach with boldness
Bring a weakness you are ashamed of to Christ in confession.
fathers: St Jerome
Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ (Commentary on Isaiah, Prologue).
St Ephrem the Syrian

Who can grasp all the richness of even one of your words, Lord? What we understand is much less than what we leave behind, like the thirsty who drink from a fountain (Commentary on the Diatessaron 1, 18).
magis: Catechism 131–133
The Church strongly exhorts all the faithful to learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ by frequent reading of the divine Scriptures.
Dei Verbum 21
In the sacred books the Father who is in heaven meets his children with great love and speaks with them.
Catechism 1546
The whole community of believers is, as such, priestly (1 Peter 2:9).
saints: 11 July: St Benedict. 15 July (Thu): Commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios (1953): Holy Qurbono for the people. 16 July: Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
2027-07-11.prayer: Lord God, I AM WHO I AM, your word is living and active. Open our ears to listen, our hearts to accept, and our lives to bear fruit thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Through Jesus, our merciful high priest, let us approach your throne of grace with boldness. Amen.

2027-07-15.title: Commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios
readings: Well done, good and trustworthy slave
Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there
Keep watch over the flock; it is more blessed to give
Remember your leaders; imitate their faith
2027-07-15.alt: Commemoration of Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios (died 15 July 1953), founder and first Metropolitan Archbishop of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church: Holy Qurbono for the people. His cause for canonisation is in progress; his tomb is at St Mary's Cathedral, Pattom, Thiruvananthapuram. The Panchangam also remembers Mar Kuriakose and Morth Yulithi (Sts Cyriacus and Julitta), and the anniversary of the episcopal ordination of Most Rev. Mathews Mar Polycarpos and Most Rev. Antony Mar Silvanos (2022).
2027-07-15.verse: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
theo: The Letter to the Hebrews says: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Today the Syro-Malankara Church remembers her father, Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. We remember him not to look back, but to imitate his faith.

Geevarghese, born in 1882 at Mavelikara, was a brilliant scholar and teacher. Drawn to prayer and to the monastic life, he founded the Bethany Ashram (Order of the Imitation of Christ) in 1919 and the Bethany Sisters in 1925. Longing for the unity of the Church, he searched for the communion of the Malankara Church with the See of Peter. On 20 September 1930, with Bishop Mar Theophilos and a few companions, he was received into full communion with the Catholic Church, keeping the venerable West Syriac liturgy. In 1932 he became the first Archbishop of Trivandrum.

Like Abraham and Moses, he left security behind. The reunion cost him churches, properties and friends; he began again in poverty, in small chapels and simple houses. Like the servant in the parable who traded with his talents, he did not bury what he had received: his learning, his liturgy, his love for the Malankara tradition became a gift to the universal Church. “Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things.”

Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus could be his: “Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son… remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” Today we thank God for him, pray for the unity of all Christians, and ask God, if it is his will, to glorify his servant.
conn: Moses' death.
Deuteronomy 34: Moses sees the promised land and dies; Mar Ivanios led his people into communion and died having seen the Church grow.
I will be with you.
Exodus 3:12: God sends Moses with this promise; the same promise sustained the reunion movement.
Honour the priests.
Sirach 7:29–30: love and honour the Lord's ministers.
The faithful servant.
Matthew 24:45: the servant set over the household to give them food at the proper time.
altar: Mar Ivanios loved the West Syriac Holy Qurbono and brought it whole into Catholic communion. Every time we celebrate it in Malayalam, we receive the fruit of his labours. Pray today for our Major Archbishop and bishops, his successors.
outline: Opening
Remember your leaders.
Point 1 · A seeker
Scholar, monk, founder of Bethany.
Point 2 · The cost of unity
1930: communion with Peter, keeping our tradition.
Point 3 · Talents traded
He did not bury what he received.
Point 4 · Imitate their faith
Love for the Church, prayer, unity.
Take-home line
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
live: Visit or pray
If possible, visit the tomb at Pattom; otherwise pray for the Church he founded.
Pray for unity
Pray daily this week for the unity of all the Churches of Kerala.
Trade your talents
Use one gift you have received for the Church instead of burying it.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch
Where the bishop appears, there let the people be, just as where Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8).
St Cyprian of Carthage
The Church is one, though she spreads far and wide; like the rays of the sun, many, yet one light (On the Unity of the Catholic Church 5).
magis: Orientalium Ecclesiarum 2–3
The Eastern Catholic Churches, holding the same faith, should keep their own rites and traditions whole and entire.
Ut Unum Sint 1
Christ calls all his disciples to unity; the commitment to ecumenism is a duty of the Church.
Catechism 1561
The ordained minister acts in the name of Christ the Head for the building up of the Church.
saints: 16 July: Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Sunday 18 July: IX Sunday after Pentecost.
2027-07-15.prayer: Lord Jesus, the same yesterday, today and forever, we thank you for Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who loved your Church and sought her unity at great cost. Keep our Malankara Church faithful to the faith he lived, bless our Major Archbishop and bishops, make all Christians one, and, if it be your will, glorify your servant. Amen.

2027-07-18.title: Ninth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: Wheat and weeds; mustard seed; yeast
Keep the statutes, for this is your wisdom
Do not associate with the proud
The earth lies polluted; they have broken the covenant
Paul arrives in Rome and takes courage
Those who humble themselves will be exalted
2027-07-18.alt: Season of Pentecost. Remind the faithful that the Fifteen Days' Fast (Shunoyo Nombu) begins on 1 August in preparation for the Assumption of Mary, Mother of God (15 August).
2027-07-18.verse: For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
theo: At a dinner Jesus watches the guests choosing the places of honour and says: “When you are invited, go and sit down at the lowest place, so that when your host comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher’; then you will be honoured in the presence of all who sit at the table with you. For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” Humility is not thinking little of ourselves; it is letting God decide our place.

In the evening Gospel Jesus tells three small parables of the kingdom. A man sows good seed, but while everyone sleeps an enemy sows weeds among the wheat. The servants want to pull them up at once. The master says: “No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them. Let both of them grow together until the harvest.” God is patient. The Church on earth is a field of wheat and weeds; judgment belongs to God at the harvest, not to us now.

The kingdom is also like a mustard seed, “the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches”; and like yeast that a woman mixed into three measures of flour until all of it was leavened. God works through small and hidden things: a family Rosary, a catechism class, one honest worker in an office.

Paul reaches Rome as a prisoner, but believers walk out to meet him, and “on seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage.” He reminds the Corinthians, who were taking one another to court, of what they had become: “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.” A humble and patient Church, aware of the grace she has received, will grow like the mustard seed.
conn: Wisdom in obedience.
Deuteronomy 4:6: keeping God's law will make the nations say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people.”
The proud.
Sirach 13 and Luke 14: pride seeks the high place; God lifts the lowly.
Trust.
Psalm 22:4: “In you our ancestors trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them”; the master's patience in the parable.
The broken covenant.
Isaiah 24:5: the earth defiled by sin; the weeds sown by the enemy.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Lord invites us to his table not because we are worthy but because he is merciful. We come as those who take the lowest place, and he says, “Friend, move up higher.”
outline: Opening
Who sits at the top table?
Point 1 · The lowest place
Humility lets God decide.
Point 2 · Wheat and weeds
God's patience; judgment is his.
Point 3 · Mustard seed and yeast
Small hidden beginnings, great growth.
Point 4 · Washed and sanctified
Remember the grace you received.
Take-home line
“Those who humble themselves will be exalted.”
live: Take the lower place
Let someone else go first this week: in a queue, a conversation, a decision.
Be patient with the weeds
Stop condemning one person you find difficult; leave judgment to God.
Prepare for Shunoyo
Plan how you will keep the Fifteen Days' Fast from 1 August.
fathers: St Augustine
Do not be in a hurry to separate; many who are weeds today become wheat tomorrow (Sermon 73A).
St John Chrysostom
The Lord forbids the uprooting of the weeds so that no one may be killed; he does not forbid restraining heretics, but forbids killing them (Homilies on Matthew 46).
magis: Catechism 2559
Humility is the foundation of prayer.
Catechism 827
The Church, embracing sinners in her bosom, is at once holy and always in need of purification.
Catechism 1269
The baptised are washed, sanctified and justified; they belong to Christ.
saints: 22 July: St Mary Magdalene. Sunday 25 July: X Sunday after Pentecost. 1 August: the Fifteen Days' Fast begins.
2027-07-18.prayer: Lord Jesus, you lifted up the humble and were patient with the field of wheat and weeds. Teach us to take the lowest place, to leave judgment to you, and to trust the small seeds of your kingdom. Wash, sanctify and justify us in your Spirit, and prepare us to keep the fast in honour of your Mother. Amen.

2027-07-25.title: Tenth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: They all ate and were filled
I am the Lord who heals you
The Lord restored the fortunes of Job
Happy are those who fear the Lord
Paul teaches about the kingdom of God
If you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord
2027-07-25.alt: Season of Pentecost. In the 2025–26 lectionary the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost was the Syro-Malankara Catholic Sunday School Day, with the collection and the “cover collection” sent to the eparchial curia for the faith formation of children. The Fifteen Days' Fast begins on Sunday 1 August.
2027-07-25.verse: Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
theo: The disciples ask: “Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” Jesus calls a child, puts the child among them and says: “Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes humble like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.” Children are not only the future of the Church; they show us now how to trust, to receive, to depend on the Father.

Jesus speaks with great seriousness about harm done to children: “If any of you put a stumbling block before one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for you if a great millstone were fastened around your neck and you were drowned in the depth of the sea… Take care that you do not despise one of these little ones; for, I tell you, in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father.” “It is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.” Protecting and forming children is a holy duty of every family and parish.

St Paul gives the heart of what we teach them: “if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For one believes with the heart and so is justified, and one confesses with the mouth and so is saved… Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.” Faith is believed in the heart and spoken with the lips. Sunday School exists so that children may learn both.

At Marah the water was bitter, and the people could not drink. God showed Moses a piece of wood; when it was thrown into the water, the water became sweet. Then God said: “I am the LORD who heals you.” The Fathers saw in that wood the Cross, which makes the bitter waters of life sweet. In Rome Paul, a prisoner, “welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness.” Teachers of the faith carry on his work.
conn: Bitter water made sweet.
Exodus 15:25: the wood thrown into the water; the Cross makes life's bitterness sweet.
Job restored.
Job 42:10: the Lord restored Job when he prayed for his friends.
The just man.
Psalm 112:7: “They are not afraid of evil tidings; their hearts are firm, secure in the LORD.”
Teaching to the end.
Acts 28:30–31: Paul teaches openly in Rome; catechists continue his mission.
altar: Children prepare for First Holy Communion by learning that the Bread of the altar is Jesus himself. Every Qurbono is a lesson in childlike faith: we receive what we could never earn.
outline: Opening
Who is the greatest?
Point 1 · Become like children
Trust, receive, depend on the Father.
Point 2 · Do not despise the little ones
Protecting children is holy.
Point 3 · Believe and confess
Romans 10: heart and lips.
Point 4 · The Lord who heals
Marah and the Cross; teachers of the faith.
Take-home line
“Unless you change and become like children…”
live: Thank a catechist
Thank your children's Sunday School teacher this week.
Pray with a child
Pray with a child in your family each evening this week.
Prepare for the fast
Decide how your family will keep the Fifteen Days' Fast.
fathers: St Hilary of Poitiers

Children follow their father, love their mother, do not know how to wish evil on their neighbour, do not care for wealth, are not proud: to be like them is to enter the kingdom (Commentary on Matthew 18, 1).
St Ambrose
The wood thrown into the bitter water is the Cross of Christ, which makes the bitter waters sweet (On the Mysteries 3, 14).
magis: Catechism 526
To become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the kingdom.
Catechism 2226
Education in the faith by the parents should begin in the child's earliest years.
Catechism 185–186
Whoever says “I believe” says “I pledge myself to what we believe”; the profession of faith with the lips.
saints: 28 July: St Alphonsa. 29 July: Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus. 31 July: St Ignatius of Loyola. 1 August: the Fifteen Days' Fast (Shunoyo Nombu) begins.
2027-07-25.prayer: Lord Jesus, you placed a child in the midst of your disciples. Make us humble and trusting like children; help us protect and form the little ones you love; bless our catechists and Sunday School teachers; and make the bitter waters of our lives sweet by your Cross. Amen.

2027-07-01.title: Thursday of the sixth week after Pentecost · Aaron the High Priest
readings: Every high priest is chosen from among mortals and takes the honour only when called by God, just as Aaron was
Zechariah the priest and Elizabeth, a descendant of Aaron; the whole assembly prays outside at the hour of incense
2027-07-01.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers today Aaron the High Priest (പ്രധാനാചാര്യനായ അഹറോൻ), the brother of Moses, the first to hold the priestly office of Israel. Today is also the first day of July, which the Syriac calendar calls Tammuz (തോമ്മൂസ്).
2027-07-01.verse: And one does not presume to take this honor, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
theo: Today is the first day of July, the Syriac month of Tammuz, and the Panchangam begins it by remembering a priest: Aaron, the brother of Moses and the first High Priest of Israel. He did not push himself forward. The Epistle says so plainly: “And one does not presume to take this honor, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was.” At Sinai the Lord said to Moses: “Then bring near to you your brother Aaron, and his sons with him, from among the Israelites, to serve me as priests.” The calling came first; the vestments, the oil and the altar followed. And the vestments themselves carried a lesson. On the shoulders of the High Priest were two stones engraved with the names of the sons of Israel: “Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord on his two shoulders for remembrance.” On the breastpiece over his heart were the same names, “for a continual remembrance before the Lord.” A priest in the Bible is never a man standing alone. He carries a whole people on his shoulders and on his heart.

Then the Epistle says something that may surprise us. The high priest “is able to deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is subject to weakness; and because of this he must offer sacrifice for his own sins as well as for those of the people.” Aaron's own story shows it. While Moses was on the mountain, the people gathered around Aaron and asked him to make gods for them, and he fashioned a golden calf (Exodus 32:1–4). When Moses questioned him, Aaron answered with excuses (Exodus 32:21–24). The Bible does not hide the failing of its first High Priest. Yet the same Aaron, when a plague broke out in the camp, took his censer at the word of Moses and ran into the middle of the assembly, and the text says: “He stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stopped.” A sinner standing between death and life with incense in his hand: that is the picture of a priest. God himself confirmed the choice when the leaders of the tribes laid their staffs before him, and “the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted. It put forth buds, produced blossoms, and bore ripe almonds.” At the end, on Mount Hor, Moses placed Aaron's vestments on his son Eleazar, so that the priesthood passed on (Numbers 20:25–28).

All of this was a shadow, and the Letter to the Hebrews shows where the light falls. Aaron had to offer sacrifice for his own sins before he could offer it for others. Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, “has been tested as we are, yet without sin,” so that we may “approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:15–16). The sacrifices of the old covenant had to be repeated again and again; of Christ the letter says that he “has no need to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins, and then for those of the people; this he did once for all when he offered himself” (Hebrews 7:27). The Church therefore does not think of her priests as men who add something to the one sacrifice of the Cross. They serve in the name and in the person of Christ, so that the one offering made once for all is made present on the altar for every generation (Catechism 1545, in substance). We thank God for our bishops, priests and deacons, and we ask ourselves how often we pray for them by name.

St Luke begins his Gospel inside this very priesthood. “In the days of King Herod of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly order of Abijah. His wife was a descendant of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.” Aaron's line, after more than a thousand years, has reached the threshold of the New Testament. Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous, advanced in years and without a child. Zechariah “was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and offer incense.” Then Luke adds a sentence that is easy to miss: “Now at the time of the incense offering, the whole assembly of the people was praying outside.” The priest is inside, the people are outside, and the smoke of the incense rises between them, as the psalmist had prayed: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). It is at that hour of prayer, in that meeting of priest and people, that the angel appears and the new age begins. The same shape is in every Holy Qurbono: the priest at the altar, the people in prayer, the incense rising, and heaven opening above them. As the month begins, let us pray that our priests may be faithful to the call by which God took them from among us, and let us not stay outside the church even when we sit inside it, but pray with them.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did I last pray for a priest by name, and when did I last thank one?
Point 1 · Called by God
Aaron did not take the honour for himself; the Lord brought him near, and Christ says the same to his Apostles.
Point 2 · A priest who knows weakness
The golden calf, and the censer between the dead and the living: God works through a sinner who stands for the people.
Point 3 · The one High Priest
Aaron offered for his own sins first; Jesus, tested yet without sin, offered himself once for all.
Point 4 · The incense and the people outside
Zechariah inside, the whole assembly praying outside: the prayer of the people rises with the priest's offering.
Take-home line
“He stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stopped.”
live: Pray for those who serve (Hebrews 5:1)
Name one priest or bishop who has served you and pray for him by name each day this week; thank him in person or by a message.
Carry names on your heart (Exodus 28:29)
Write down five names you want to carry before God, as Aaron carried the names of the tribes, and offer them in prayer at the next Holy Qurbono.
Let prayer rise like incense (Psalm 141:2)
Fix one hour each evening this week, when the lamp is lit at home, for a few quiet minutes of prayer with the family.
2027-07-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, great High Priest, tested as we are yet without sin, you offered yourself once for all and you ever live to make intercession for us. We thank you for Aaron, whom you called from among his people to stand before you with their names on his heart, and we ask that you keep our bishops, priests and deacons faithful to the call by which you took them from among us. Make them gentle with the ignorant and the wayward, since they too are subject to weakness. Let our prayer rise before you like incense, and let none of your people stay outside when your holy mysteries are celebrated. At the beginning of this new month bless our homes and our parish, and bring us at last to the sanctuary of heaven, where you live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the priest stands at the altar before God for the people, with the censer, the bread and the wine; he does not act in his own name but in the name of Christ, the one High Priest, whose single offering on the Cross is made present for us, and the incense that rises is the prayer of the whole assembly.
conn: Chosen from among the people.
Exodus 28:1 and Hebrews 5:4: Aaron is brought near by the Lord and does not take the honour himself; John 15:16: “You did not choose me but I chose you.” The call always comes first from God.
Carrying the people.

Exodus 28:12 and 28:29: the names of the tribes on the shoulders and over the heart of the High Priest; Psalm 133:2 pictures the anointing oil running down from the head of Aaron over his robes, a sign of blessing flowing down on a whole community living in unity.
Incense and prayer.

Exodus 30:7–8: fragrant incense offered by Aaron morning and evening; Luke 1:9–10: the people pray outside while Zechariah offers incense; Psalm 141:2 and Revelation 8:3–4: the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God.
fathers: St John Chrysostom

The priestly office is carried out on earth, but it ranks among heavenly things, for it was not a man or an angel but the Paraclete himself who established this ministry (On the Priesthood 3.4, in substance).
St Augustine

For you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian: the first is a duty that I accept, the second a grace that I receive; the priest is a servant of God's people and at the same time one of them (Sermon 340.1, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1539–1540

The Lord set the tribe of Levi apart for the liturgical service of Israel and consecrated Aaron and his sons by a special rite; yet that priesthood could not bring about salvation and had to repeat its sacrifices without end, awaiting the sacrifice of Christ that would sanctify once for all (in substance).
Catechism 1544–1545

Everything that the priesthood of the old covenant foreshadowed is fulfilled in Christ, the one mediator between God and humankind; his one priesthood is made present through the ministerial priesthood without diminishing the uniqueness of Christ's priesthood (in substance).
Lumen Gentium 10

The common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial priesthood of the ordained differ in essence and not only in degree, yet they are ordered one to the other; each in its own way shares in the one priesthood of Christ (in substance).

2027-07-02.title: Friday of the sixth week after Pentecost · First Friday
readings: The churches of Macedonia gave themselves first to the Lord: abundant joy and extreme poverty overflowing in generosity
“I have shown you many good works from the Father”: believe the works, that the Father is in me and I am in the Father
2027-07-02.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost. Today is the First Friday of the month. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam.
2027-07-02.verse: so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.
theo: Today is the First Friday of the month. Every Friday recalls the Cross, and many Catholic parishes give the first Friday of each month to special prayer, the Holy Qurbono and devotion to the Heart of Jesus, the heart that loved us to the end. Today's Epistle shows what such a heart looks like in those who follow him. St Paul writes to Corinth about the churches of Macedonia, the communities of Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, the first that he founded on European soil. They were small, poor, and already suffering. And Paul says of them: “for during a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.” Joy and poverty side by side, and out of them a flood of giving. They “voluntarily gave according to their means, and even beyond their means.” Usually it is the collector who has to beg. Here the givers do the begging: they were “begging us earnestly for the privilege of sharing in this ministry to the saints.”

Something more precious than money is named in the next verse: “they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us.” The gift of self comes first and the gift of money follows from it. A parish that has given itself to the Lord is never short of gifts; a parish that gives only money, without itself, soon finds that even the money is hard to find. Paul does not command. He appeals to their pride in what is best in them: “Now as you excel in everything, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in utmost eagerness, and in our love for you, so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.” A few verses later he gives the reason that stands behind all Christian giving: “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Jesus gave himself first. The First Friday keeps this before our eyes: the Heart that was pierced on a Friday gave everything.

The Gospel carries us to the Temple at Jerusalem, in winter, at the Feast of the Dedication (John 10:22). Jesus has said, “The Father and I are one,” and some of his hearers pick up stones. When John writes “the Jews” in such a scene he means those in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus on that occasion; we must remember that Jesus himself, his Mother, the Apostles and the first Christians were all Jews, and the Church teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597). Jesus answers with calm: “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these are you going to stone me?” The works are his credentials: the sick healed, the hungry fed, the sinner forgiven. Then he argues from their own Scripture: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?” If the Scripture could call those to whom the word of God came “gods”, can anyone say that “the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world is blaspheming because I said, ‘I am God's Son’?” The Fathers of the Church, especially in the East, drew from this the great truth that the Son of God became human so that we might share in his own life: “the Son of God became man so that we might become God,” wrote St Athanasius (On the Incarnation 54, in substance; Catechism 460).

Jesus ends with an invitation: “If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me. But if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” Believe the works. The same test is put to us. The Macedonians' joy in their poverty was such a work: a sign that Christ was alive in them. Few people in our days are argued into faith; many are drawn when they see a neighbour who gives more than he can afford and ask where that comes from. John says that they tried to arrest Jesus again “but he escaped from their hands.” His hour had not yet come. Later in the same discourse he says, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18), and on a Friday he did. Today we ask for a heart like his, and for works that point to him.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone looked at my works and not at my words, what would they say about the Father?
Point 1 · Joy and poverty overflowing
The churches of Macedonia give beyond their means and beg to be allowed to give.
Point 2 · They gave themselves first
The gift of self comes before the gift of money; Christ became poor for our sake.
Point 3 · Believe the works
The Father's works in Jesus; the Son of God became human so that we might share his life.
Take-home line
“they gave themselves first to the Lord”
live: Give yourself first (2 Corinthians 8:5)
Before giving anything this week, spend five minutes offering yourself to the Lord in prayer, and let the gift that follows come from that offering.
Give from your joy (2 Corinthians 8:2)
Choose one gift this week that costs you something, and give it with joy to a person or a cause in need.
Let your works speak (John 10:25)
Do one good work today that no one will notice, so that the Father may be seen in it.
2027-07-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, though you were rich, for our sake you became poor, so that by your poverty we might become rich. On this First Friday we look to your pierced Heart, which gave everything. Teach us to give ourselves first to you, and then whatever we have for the sake of your saints and your poor. Give us the joy of the churches of Macedonia, who found in their poverty a wealth of generosity. Let our works be so full of your love that those who see them may believe that you are in the Father and the Father is in you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono Christ gives himself first, his Body and his Blood, and we are invited to give ourselves with him: whatever we bring to the altar is joined to the one offering of the Cross, which began in the heart of the Son who gave everything.

2027-07-05.title: The Seventy-two Heralds · Monday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: The weapons of our warfare have divine power; authority given for building up and not for tearing down
The Lord sends out the seventy-two ahead of him in pairs: the harvest is plentiful, the laborers are few, “Peace to this house!”
2027-07-05.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the commemoration of the Seventy-two Heralds (എഴുപത്തിരണ്ട് അറിയിപ്പുകാർ), the disciples whom the Lord sent ahead of him in Luke 10:1. Yesterday was the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost, and on Saturday the Church kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha.
2027-07-05.verse: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
theo: On the Monday after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost the Panchangam turns to a group whose names we hardly know, the Seventy-two Heralds. St Luke writes: “After this the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go.” The word “others” tells us that these are not the Twelve, whom Luke has just shown being sent out in the previous chapter. As for the number, the manuscripts of the Gospel are divided between seventy and seventy-two, and the Malayalam Bible that we use has seventy-two, as does the Panchangam. Both numbers carry a meaning. The Twelve recall the twelve tribes of Israel; the seventy or seventy-two recall the nations of the earth, which the book of Genesis lists as seventy in its Hebrew text and seventy-two in the old Greek version, and also the seventy elders on whom Moses saw the spirit rest in the wilderness (Numbers 11:24–26). Many Christian writers, ancient and modern, therefore see in this second sending a sign that the Gospel is meant for all peoples. They are called heralds, announcers, because they go ahead: they prepare the towns for the Lord who is coming after them.

Their instructions begin with a surprise. Before saying “Go,” the Lord says “Pray”: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” The mission starts on our knees, and the Lord is the one who sends. Then comes a warning that is plain and without decoration: “See, I am sending you out like lambs into the midst of wolves.” They are to be defenceless and dependent: “Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals; and greet no one on the road.” The last words are not rudeness. On eastern roads a greeting could take hours of ceremony; the heralds have no time to lose. And they go in pairs. St Gregory the Great noticed that the Lord sends his disciples two by two because there are two commandments of love, of God and of neighbour, and love needs at least two (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance). Two people carry the message more truthfully than one, they hold each other up on the road, and their agreement is itself a proof.

Then the Lord describes how the Gospel spreads, and it is through homes. “Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house!’ And if anyone is there who shares in peace, your peace will rest on that person; but if not, it will return to you.” The first word of the herald is a blessing. “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking whatever they provide, for the laborer deserves to be paid. Do not move about from house to house.” They are to stay, to eat what is set before them and to learn the family's life; they are not to go about looking for a more comfortable house. It is a Kerala picture as much as a Galilean one: the family prayer in the evening, the priest's visit to bless the house, the neighbours who take a stranger in. And the message comes with healing: “cure the sick who are there, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’” Care and word go together. Even if a town refuses them, the message stands: “Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.” The refusal of some does not cancel the nearness of the kingdom.

The Epistle tells us what kind of weapons such messengers carry. St Paul has been ridiculed in Corinth: they say “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.” He answers: “Indeed, we live as human beings, but we do not wage war according to human standards; for the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power to destroy strongholds.” The heralds' weapons are the word, peace, prayer, patience and the care of the sick, and their aim is “to take every thought captive to obey Christ.” Their authority is “for building you up and not for tearing you down.” Our own Syriac tradition remembers heralds of this kind. Eusebius tells that after the Ascension Thomas sent Thaddaeus, whom he counts “one of the seventy,” to Edessa, where he healed and preached; the Syriac Churches honour him as Mar Addai (Church History 1.13, in substance). And on Saturday we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, the Apostle whom tradition says brought the Gospel to India. Every baptized person is also a herald today: Pope Francis wrote that we are no longer to say that we are disciples and missionaries, but always “missionary disciples.” Let us ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers, and let us begin by saying “Peace to this house” at our own door.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did I last say a blessing of peace on my own house, and when did I last pray for laborers for the harvest?
Point 1 · Sent ahead in pairs
The seventy-two go before the Lord to every town; the number points to all the nations; two by two, for love needs two.
Point 2 · Pray first
The harvest is plentiful and the laborers are few: the mission begins on our knees.
Point 3 · Peace to this house
The Gospel spreads through homes, a blessing first, then care of the sick and the word.
Point 4 · Weapons that are not human
Paul's weakness and the divine power of the word; authority to build up, never to tear down.
Take-home line
“The kingdom of God has come near to you.”
live: Pray for laborers (Luke 10:2)
Pray each day this week, the Our Father and one more prayer, that the Lord of the harvest may send laborers, priests, religious and lay missionaries, into his harvest.
Say “Peace to this house” (Luke 10:5)
When you come home this week, and when you visit a neighbour, begin by greeting the house with a word of blessing.
Go in pairs (Luke 10:1)
Invite a friend to visit with you one sick or lonely person from the parish this week, and bring a word of the Gospel with the visit.
2027-07-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Lord of the harvest, you appointed seventy-two disciples and sent them ahead of you in pairs to every town where you intended to go. Send laborers into your harvest, and make us laborers, lambs among wolves who trust in you alone. Teach us to bless every house we enter with your peace, to eat what is set before us and to care for the sick, and to say to everyone that the kingdom of God has come near. Give us the weapons that have divine power, the word of truth and the gentleness of patience, and let us use any authority only to build up. Through the prayers of the Seventy-two Heralds, of Mar Addai and of Mar Thoma Shleeha, make our Church a herald of your coming. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the end of the Holy Qurbono the people are sent out in peace, like the Seventy-two; what was received at the altar, the Word and the Body of the Lord, is carried into our homes and workplaces, and the peace that rests on us is to rest on every house we enter.
conn: Sent in pairs.
Mark 6:7: the Twelve are sent “two by two”; Acts 13:2–3: Barnabas and Saul are set apart and sent by the Holy Spirit; Luke 10:1: the seventy-two go in pairs to every place the Lord intends to visit.
The seventy and the nations.

Numbers 11:24–26: the spirit rests on seventy elders, and also on Eldad and Medad in the camp; Genesis 10: the table of the nations; Luke 10:17: the seventy return with joy, and the Lord tells them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
The herald and the harvest.

Isaiah 52:7: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news”; Matthew 9:37–38: the same saying about the harvest and the laborers; John 4:35–38: the fields are ripe for harvest and the sower and reaper rejoice together.
fathers: St Gregory the Great

The Lord sends the disciples two by two because there are two precepts of charity, to love God and to love our neighbour; and “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” cannot be said without sorrow, for there are many to hear and few to preach (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance).
Eusebius of Caesarea
After the Ascension Judas Thomas sent Thaddaeus, one of the seventy disciples of the Lord, to Edessa, where he healed the sick and preached the word of Christ (Church History 1.13, in substance).
magis: Catechism 849
The Church is sent by her founder to all nations; the missionary mandate is a command of her own essential universality, and she strives to preach the Gospel to all (in substance).
Ad Gentes 2
The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature, since she draws her origin from the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit according to the plan of God the Father (in substance).
Evangelii Gaudium 120

Every baptized person, whatever his or her role in the Church, is an agent of evangelization; we are no longer to say that we are disciples and missionaries, but rather that we are always missionary disciples (in substance).

2027-07-06.title: Tuesday of the seventh week after Pentecost · Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban · St Maria Goretti
readings: Remember your leaders and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever; we have an altar; a sacrifice of praise
The faithful and wise slave whom the master finds at work when he arrives
2027-07-06.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam prints today, in bold, the memory of Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban (പുലിക്കോട്ടിൽ ജോസഫ് റമ്പാന്റെ ഓർമ), and gives for it the readings for the memory of a bishop or priest. It also remembers St Maria Goretti (വി. മരിയ ഗൊരേത്തി). The Panchangam gives no further detail about the Ramban, and none is added here.
2027-07-06.verse: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
theo: Today the Panchangam keeps in bold letters the memory of Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban. We know him here only by the name and the title that are printed. A ramban, in the Syriac tradition, is a monk-priest, a priest who has given himself to a life of prayer and service; we do not add dates or deeds that the Panchangam does not give, and we entrust to God what only he knows fully. The Church has always known how to remember. The Holy Qurbono names the faithful departed, and in Kerala families keep the ormma, the remembrance day, with a Qurbono and a prayer for the one who has gone before. The Epistle gives the reason and the rule: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.” Remembering is not a sad habit; it is a school. We look at the end of a life and learn how to live. But note what the Letter says next, in the very next verse: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Leaders come and go; the faith we imitate is faith in the One who does not change.

From this foundation the Letter warns: “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings; for it is well for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by regulations about food, which have not benefited those who observe them.” Then comes a sentence that the Church has long heard as a word about the Holy Qurbono: “We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.” The sacrifices of the old sanctuary were offered for sin and burned outside the camp, and those who served in the tent could not eat of that sin offering. But the sacrifice of Christ is different: it is given to us as food. At every Qurbono we are fed from the altar of the new covenant. St Cyril of Jerusalem teaches that we pray there for the holy fathers, bishops and all who have fallen asleep among us, believing that it is of the greatest benefit to them while the holy sacrifice lies before us (Mystagogical Catecheses 5.9, in substance). This is why we can keep the memory of a Ramban with the Holy Qurbono: we remember him at the altar.

The Letter then takes us out of the gate. “Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” The Church has always seen in the monastic and priestly life one form of such going out, leaving the comfort of the camp for the sake of the Lord, but every Christian is called to walk that way. On this day the Panchangam also remembers a young witness to it, St Maria Goretti. She was a poor farm girl in Italy, one of a family who had lost their father and worked hard on the land. In July 1902, when she was eleven years old, a young man who lived in the same house tried to force her into sin. She refused, saying that it was a sin and that God did not want it. She was stabbed and died in hospital the next day, 6 July, after forgiving the man who attacked her. He later repented, and Maria's mother forgave him too. The Church honours her as a martyr who chose the Lord over her own safety, and as a patron of young people. Her last act was exactly what the Lord had done outside the gate: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).

The Epistle ends with what we can all do: “Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.” Praise and sharing: these are the offerings of ordinary Christians, day after day. The Gospel then asks what the servant is doing while the master is away: “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time? Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.” The Church has always heard this as a word for pastors, who feed the household with the word and the sacraments, but it also speaks to every father, mother, teacher and neighbour who has a household in their care. The wicked slave says in his heart, “My master is delayed,” and that thought is the beginning of the fall. Maria had eleven years; she was found faithful. A Ramban's life, whatever its length, is measured by the same question. Let us ask it of ourselves: if the Lord came this evening, what would he find us doing?
outline: Opening
Ask: whom do I remember with thanks for the faith that came to me, and what do I imitate in them?
Point 1 · Remember your leaders
Remembering as a school: consider the outcome of their lives, imitate their faith; the Ramban remembered by name only.
Point 2 · The same yesterday and today
Leaders pass, Christ remains; the altar from which we are fed, where we also remember the dead.
Point 3 · Outside the camp
Jesus suffered outside the gate; no lasting city; St Maria Goretti said no and forgave.
Point 4 · At work when the master comes
A sacrifice of praise and of sharing; the faithful and wise servant.
Take-home line
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
live: Remember with thanks (Hebrews 13:7)
Name three people who handed on the faith to you, among them a priest or monk, and pray for them at the next Holy Qurbono.
Offer a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 13:15)
Begin and end this day with a short prayer of thanksgiving, “the fruit of lips that confess his name.”
Forgive as the Lord forgave (Luke 23:34)
Choose one person who has hurt you and pray for them by name each evening this week.
2027-07-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the same yesterday and today and for ever. We thank you for those who spoke your word to us, and we commend to you your servant Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban, whose memory the Church keeps today; reward every priest and monk who served you faithfully. Let us consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith. Feed us at your altar, strengthen our hearts with your grace, and teach us to go out to you outside the camp, looking for the city that is to come. Through the prayers of St Maria Goretti, who refused what was wrong and forgave her enemy, make us brave in goodness and gentle in forgiveness. Find us at work, faithful and wise, when you come. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The Epistle says, “We have an altar,” and at the Holy Qurbono the Church stands at that altar to be fed with the Body and Blood of the Lord and to remember the faithful departed, including the priests and monks who once stood where the priest stands now.
conn: The same Lord.
Hebrews 13:8: “the same yesterday and today and forever”; Malachi 3:6: “For I the Lord do not change”; Hebrews 1:12 says the same of the Son.
Outside the camp.

Leviticus 16:27 describes the sin offering burned outside the camp; Hebrews 13:11–13 sees Jesus suffer outside the gate; Luke 23:34 gives his prayer for those who crucified him, which Maria Goretti repeated in her own way.
The sacrifice of praise.
Hosea 14:2 speaks of “the fruit of our lips”; Hebrews 13:15–16 joins praise and sharing; Matthew 24:45–46 names the faithful servant found at work.
fathers: St Augustine
His mother Monica, on her deathbed, asked only this of her sons: lay this body anywhere, and let it not trouble you; only remember me at the altar of the Lord (Confessions 9.11, in substance).
St Cyril of Jerusalem

At the holy sacrifice we pray for the holy fathers and bishops who have fallen asleep, and for all who have fallen asleep among us, believing that it is of the greatest benefit to them while the holy and most awesome sacrifice lies before us (Mystagogical Catecheses 5.9, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1371
The Eucharistic sacrifice is also offered for the faithful departed who have died in Christ but are not yet fully purified, so that they may enter into the light and peace of Christ (in substance).
Catechism 1032

From the beginning the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers for them, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice, so that, purified, they may attain the beatific vision of God (in substance).
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith; the martyr bears witness to Christ even to death, and the Church has always honoured such witness (in substance).
term: Ramban (റമ്പാൻ)

A title in the Syriac tradition for a monk-priest. It comes from the Syriac word rabban, “our teacher”. In the Malankara tradition it names a priest who has taken the monastic vows of a life of prayer and service.
kidsaint: Maria and the forgiving heart

Maria was a poor girl in Italy who helped her mother in the house and the fields, and who loved to pray. When she was only eleven, someone tried to make her do something wrong. Maria was very brave and said no, because she knew it would hurt God. She was badly hurt for this, and in hospital, before she died, she said that she forgave the person. Today the Church remembers her as a saint, a brave and forgiving friend of Jesus. Lesson: say no to what is wrong, and forgive those who hurt you, as Jesus did.

2027-07-07.title: Wednesday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: A divine jealousy: betrothed to one husband, to be presented to Christ; beware of another Jesus
“Let us go to Judea again”: Lazarus has fallen asleep, and Thomas says, “Let us also go, that we may die with him”
2027-07-07.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha was kept on Saturday, 3 July, and the Gospel today shows Thomas as a loyal and courageous friend.
2027-07-07.verse: Let us also go, that we may die with him.
theo: St Paul writes to the Corinthians with a feeling that he himself calls “a divine jealousy”: “I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The picture is a betrothal. In the Bible the love of God for his people is often told as a marriage (Hosea 2:19–20), and Paul sees himself as the friend of the bridegroom whose task is to bring the bride to him and to guard her faithfulness (John 3:29). His fear is not that the Corinthians will openly deny Christ but that they will be led astray little by little: “I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.” The serpent did not at first ask Eve to reject God; he asked a clever question. In the same way, Paul says, a stranger may come and proclaim “another Jesus than the one we proclaimed,” “a different spirit,” “a different gospel”, and the people “submit to it readily enough.” In our days voices about Jesus reach us from every side, from pulpits, screens and forwarded messages, and the question is the same: is this the Jesus whom the Apostles proclaimed, the Jesus of the Gospels and the Creed, who is the Son of God, died and rose? We ask it humbly, without contempt for anyone who sincerely seeks him; we ask it chiefly of ourselves, so that our own devotion remains simple and pure.

The Gospel begins when Jesus, having waited two days after hearing that Lazarus was ill, says to his disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.” The disciples are afraid: “Rabbi, the Jews were just now trying to stone you, and are you going there again?” (When John writes “the Jews” here he means some of the people and leaders of Judea who were hostile on that occasion; Jesus and his disciples were Jews themselves, and the Church does not blame the Jewish people as a whole for what happened to him: Nostra Aetate 4.) Jesus answers with a riddle about the day: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? Those who walk during the day do not stumble, because they see the light of this world. But those who walk at night stumble, because the light is not in them.” The hours of Jesus are measured by the Father's will. Whoever walks with him walks in daylight, even on a dangerous road, and cannot stumble; whoever walks without him walks in the dark, even on a smooth one. Then he says: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to awaken him.” The disciples take this for ordinary sleep and are relieved. “Then Jesus told them plainly, ‘Lazarus is dead.’”

Christians speak of the dead as those who have fallen asleep. The Greek word for a burial ground, koimeterion, from which we get “cemetery”, means a sleeping-place. St Augustine puts it in a phrase: to the Lord Lazarus was asleep, though to men he was dead, for the Lord could wake him as easily as one wakes a sleeper (Tractate on John 49, in substance). We do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And then the most unexpected voice speaks: “Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, ‘Let us also go, that we may die with him.’” Only four days ago, on Saturday, we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, the Apostle whom our tradition says carried the Gospel to India. Most people remember him for one doubt after the Resurrection, but here he speaks first and bravely. He does not understand what the Lord is about to do; he is gloomy, and he is ready to die. He goes. St Paul wished the Corinthians a sincere and pure devotion; Thomas shows what it looks like, a love that follows the Lord to Judea, to the tomb and to the end, even before it understands. The Lord says, “For your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Let us also go.
outline: Opening
Ask: where am I afraid to follow the Lord today, and what would it mean to say “Let us also go”?
Point 1 · One husband, a pure devotion
Paul's divine jealousy; the danger of another Jesus; keeping our devotion simple.
Point 2 · Walking in the day
Twelve hours of daylight: whoever walks with Jesus does not stumble; Lazarus is asleep.
Point 3 · Let us also go
Thomas the Twin, brave before he understands; the Dukrono we kept on Saturday.
Take-home line
“Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
live: Guard the pure devotion (2 Corinthians 11:3)
Test what you hear or read about Jesus this week against the Gospel and the Creed, and put aside what does not match.
Walk in the daylight (John 11:9)
Begin one task you have been putting off because of fear, saying a short prayer first: “Lord, I walk with you.”
Follow like Thomas (John 11:16)
Go this week to visit a grieving person or a sick one, even if you do not know what to say; your presence is a way of saying “Let us go.”
2027-07-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, bridegroom of your Church, you wish to present her to the Father without spot or wrinkle. Keep us in a sincere and pure devotion to you, and guard us from every other Jesus, every different spirit and every different gospel. Let us walk with you in the light of day, never stumbling, and never afraid to follow you even to Judea. Give us the courage of your Apostle Thomas, who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him,” and who carried your name to distant lands. Be with those who grieve, as you were with Martha and Mary, and awaken all who have fallen asleep in you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church, the bride, is united with her Bridegroom in the one Body, and she is given strength to walk with him to Judea, to the Cross and to the tomb, believing that those who sleep in him will be awakened.

2027-07-08.title: Thursday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: “Welcome him as you would welcome me”: Paul pleads for Onesimus and takes his debt on his own account
The disciples forget to bring bread: “Do you not remember the five loaves?” Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees
2027-07-08.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Panchangam prints the Epistle as “ഫിലെ 1:17–22”; this is read as the Letter to Philemon, verses 17 to 22, since that letter has a single chapter.
2027-07-08.verse: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
theo: The Letter to Philemon is the shortest of St Paul's letters and the most personal. It is a single page written from prison to a friend at Colossae, and its subject is a man named Onesimus, who had been in Philemon's household as a slave and had left it. Somehow Onesimus met Paul, and in that meeting he became a brother in Christ. Paul now sends him back with this letter. Today's verses are the heart of the appeal: “So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.” Paul does not command, though he could. He puts himself in the place of Onesimus: receive him as you would receive me. Then comes the sentence that Christian preachers have loved for two thousand years: “If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it.” In a few words Paul is doing what Christ did for us: he takes the debt of another onto his own account and signs for it with his own hand. The verse that comes just before today's reading says what Paul hopes Philemon will see: Onesimus is returning “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The Church has never read the letter as an approval of slavery; in time the Gospel it carries has undone it, and the Church teaches that the enslavement of human beings is a grave sin (Catechism 2414).

Paul ends with gentle words that show a whole way of life: “Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord! Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I am writing to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. One thing more: prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping through your prayers to be restored to you.” He trusts Philemon to go beyond what is asked, and he counts on the prayer of the house community, for the prayers of Philemon's family are the means by which Paul hopes to be released and to come to them. A guest room, a prayer and a forgiven debt: this is how the Gospel moves into a home. In Kerala, where a guest is treated as a blessing and a house is judged by the welcome it gives, the letter has a special ring. Welcome him as you would welcome me is a rule for the parish, for the family, and for every household that has to receive someone whom it would prefer not to see.

The Gospel looks at the disciples on the lake shore. They have crossed to the other side and “had forgotten to bring any bread.” The Lord, who has just met the Pharisees and Sadducees demanding a sign (Matthew 16:1–4), says: “Watch out, and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” The disciples only think of their empty baskets: “It is because we have brought no bread.” Jesus, perceiving this, says: “You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread? Do you still not perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?” The remedy for worry is memory: to count again what the Lord has already done. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Only then does he explain: “He had not told them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Yeast is a small thing that works in secret and spreads through the whole dough: “A little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough” (Galatians 5:9). Jesus names what can spread in a community, pride, hypocrisy, the demand for signs without faith. He is arguing within his own people, as the prophets did, and the warning is for each one of us, not for others. The yeast is not always bad: in the Antiochene tradition of our Church the bread of the Holy Qurbono is leavened, and the Lord himself says that the kingdom is like yeast. What counts is what spreads. Today we ask the Lord to keep the yeast of our hearts good, and to make us remember.
outline: Opening
Ask: what debt of another person could I take onto my own account today, and whom could I welcome as I would welcome Paul?
Point 1 · Welcome him as you would welcome me
Paul and Onesimus: a brother rather than a slave; the debt written on Paul's own account.
Point 2 · A guest room and a prayer
Trusting the house to do even more; the Gospel enters a home through welcome and prayer.
Point 3 · Do you not remember?
Little faith worries about bread; the remedy is to remember the loaves and the baskets.
Point 4 · The yeast
A little yeast works through the whole batch; beware of pride, hypocrisy and the demand for signs.
Take-home line
“Welcome him as you would welcome me.”
live: Welcome as you would welcome Christ (Philemon 17)
Receive one person this week whom you would find it easier to avoid, with the same courtesy that you would show to an honoured guest.
Take another's debt (Philemon 18)
Quietly pay or forgive a small debt, in money, time or an old grievance, as if it were charged to your own account.
Remember the loaves (Matthew 16:9)
Each evening this week write down three gifts that the Lord gave you that day, so that worry is answered by memory.
2027-07-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you took our debt onto your own account and paid it with your own hand on the Cross. Teach us to welcome one another as you have welcomed us, and to see in every person a brother or sister for whom you died. Make our homes places of welcome, with a guest room and an open door, and let the prayers of our families be heard. When we worry about our empty baskets, remind us of the loaves you have multiplied, and keep us from the yeast of pride, hypocrisy and little faith. Let the yeast of your kingdom work in us until the whole dough is leavened. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono we are welcomed by Christ as guests at his table, and, as he multiplied the loaves for the five thousand and the seven for the four thousand, he gives us his own Body in abundance: we remember what he has done, and we receive him.

2027-07-09.title: Friday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: God has shown mercy to all: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”
Jesus is hungry and finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit
2027-07-09.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-07-09.verse: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.
theo: Today's Epistle is the end of a long argument. In chapters 9 to 11 of his Letter to the Romans, St Paul wrestles with a sorrow that lay close to his heart: most of his own people, the Jews, had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah, while many Gentiles had. Had God's promise failed? Paul will not allow it: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means!
