I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.” And a few verses before today's passage he writes: “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” The Church has taken these words very seriously. The Second Vatican Council, in Nostra Aetate 4, recalled that the Jewish people remain most dear to God, who does not repent of the gifts he makes or of the calls he issues (in substance), and that the Church can never forget that she received the revelation of the Old Testament through them. Against this background we hear today's verses: “Just as you were once disobedient to God but have now received mercy because of their disobedience, so they have now been disobedient in order that, by the mercy shown to you, they too may now receive mercy.” Paul sees history as one great movement of mercy in which no one has a claim and no one may boast, and he ends the thought with a sentence that holds the whole of the gospel: “For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.”

Then Paul, who has been reasoning for three chapters, simply stops reasoning and begins to sing: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” St John Chrysostom, commenting on this passage, remarked that when Paul's argument reaches the mystery of God's plan he does not try to measure it; he adores (Homilies on Romans, in substance). The questions he asks, “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” and “Or who has given a gift to him, to receive a gift in return?”, remind us that God owes us nothing and that every good thing is a gift. Then comes the line the Church loves to pray: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.” From him, because he is the source of all that exists; through him, because he sustains and redeems it; to him, because he is the end for which everything was made. In these weeks of the monsoon, when the rain pours on the hills and the paddy fields drink and turn green again, it is easy to feel this. No one gave the rain a gift first. All of it comes from him, and all of it is meant to rise again in thanksgiving. The great prayers of the Holy Qurbono end exactly as Paul does, with glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the people's Amen.

The Gospel is short and strange. “On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether perhaps he would find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. He said to it, ‘May no one ever eat fruit from you again.’ And his disciples heard it.” St Mark places this story on either side of the cleansing of the Temple, and the two scenes are meant to be read together (Mark 11:15–17 and 11:20–24). The prophets often compared Israel to a fig tree from which God hoped for fruit (Hosea 9:10; Jeremiah 8:13), and Jesus here performs a prophetic sign, as the prophets did: an acted parable against religion that shows leaves and no fruit, splendid worship without justice, prayer and love. It is a warning for every believer, for each of us as much as for anyone, and it is no verdict on a people; Romans 11, which we heard first, forbids any Christian to think so. St Augustine, preaching on the fig tree, said that leaves without fruit are words without deeds (Sermon 89, in substance). Notice too that Jesus is hungry. He comes looking for us, hungry for our love, and the next morning the tree is found withered to its roots and he says to the disciples simply: “Have faith in God.” Let us ask ourselves today what fruit he would find in us, and let us give thanks that the God who is merciful to all keeps coming to us as one who hopes.
outline: Opening
Ask: if Jesus came to me hungry today, would he find fruit or only leaves?
Point 1 · Mercy for all
God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all; no one has a claim and no one may boast.
Point 2 · The depth of God
Paul reasons, then adores: from him and through him and to him are all things.
Point 3 · Leaves and fruit
The fig tree beside the Temple: prayer, justice and love are the fruit God looks for.
Take-home line
“For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.”
live: Sing the doxology (Romans 11:36)
Before each meal this week add one sentence of praise: “From you and through you and to you are all things. Glory to you for ever. Amen.”
Look for fruit (Mark 11:13)
Choose one part of your life that has only leaves, a prayer said without attention, a promise not kept, a quarrel not mended, and begin to bear fruit in it.
Remember the debt of mercy (Romans 11:30–31)
Pray today for the Jewish people, from whom we received the Scriptures, and for anyone you have looked down on.
2027-07-09.prayer: Lord God, from you and through you and to you are all things. We bless you for the depth of your riches and wisdom and knowledge, and for the mercy you have shown to all. Keep us from boasting, since everything we have is your gift; keep us from leaves without fruit, and teach us to bear the fruit of prayer, justice and love. Remember your ancient people, whose gifts and calling you have never taken back, and gather all peoples in your mercy. To you be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the great prayers rise into one long doxology, glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and the people answer Amen with Paul; and from the altar the Lord gives us the fruit that never fails.

2027-07-10.title: Saturday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus heals the only son of a desperate father
2027-07-10.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-07-10.verse: If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.
theo: St Paul asks a question that he has clearly asked himself with tears: “So I ask, have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means!” He is speaking of his own people, the Jews, most of whom had not yet recognised Jesus as the Messiah. Paul had once said that he could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his kindred (Romans 9:3), so this is no cold discussion. He answers that their stumbling is not the end of the story. “But through their stumbling salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.” God can bring good even out of a stumble, and the good that came to the nations is meant to draw Israel back with a holy longing. “Now if their stumbling means riches for the world, and if their defeat means riches for Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!” Paul is looking ahead to a day of fullness. The Catechism says that the glorious coming of the Messiah awaits the recognition of him by all Israel, and that the Church looks to that day with the hope of the whole world (Catechism 674, in substance). Meanwhile the Church must never speak of the Jewish people as rejected: the Jewish covenant has never been revoked (Catechism 839–840, in substance).

Paul then turns to us, the Gentiles: “Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry in order to make my own people jealous, and thus save some of them.” An apostle to the nations whose heart is still with his own people: this is the Paul we love. He adds, “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead!” When God's whole plan is complete it will feel like a resurrection. Then he gives two pictures: “If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.” In the Law a cake from the first of the dough was set aside for God (Numbers 15:17–21), and the whole baking was blessed by it. The patriarchs and the faith of Israel are that first portion and that root. In the verses that follow Paul will say that we Gentiles are wild branches grafted onto the tree, and that the root bears us and not we the root (Romans 11:17–24). Every Qurbono shows this. We sing the psalms of David, we cry Alleluia, a Hebrew word, we read Moses and the prophets before the Gospel, and our whole prayer breathes the air of the Scriptures of Israel. The Church of St Thomas in India has always lived on that root.

The Gospel brings us down from the mountain. “On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him.” The day before, on the mountain, Peter, James and John had seen the glory of Jesus; now, in the valley, there is a father in anguish. “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child. Suddenly a spirit seizes him, and all at once he shrieks.” Luke notes, as he does for the widow's son at Nain and for Jairus's daughter, that it is an only child. “I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” Jesus answers with a sigh that belongs to every teacher who has seen a lesson not understood: “You faithless and perverse generation, how much longer must I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” It is not a verdict on any one people; it is the sorrow of a master whose own disciples have not yet learned. Then, “While he was coming, the demon dashed him to the ground in convulsions. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.” The boy has been thrown down, but he is raised and given back; the Lord, who had come down the mountain, takes hold of him. St Mark's longer account records the father's cry, “I believe; help my unbelief!” and says that the boy lay like a corpse until Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up (Mark 9:24, 26–27). Stumbling is not falling. As the psalm says, “though we stumble, we shall not fall headlong, for the Lord holds us by the hand.” And Luke ends: “And all were astounded at the greatness of God.” In the valley, where the sick are, there the greatness of God is seen.
outline: Opening
Ask: where in my life, or in my family, have I stumbled and thought I had fallen?
Point 1 · Stumbling is not falling
Paul's question about his own people; God brings good even from a stumble, and holds his people by the hand.
Point 2 · The holy root
First fruits and root: the Church lives from the faith of Israel; no contempt, only gratitude.
Point 3 · Down from the mountain
The valley of the father and his only child: Jesus raises and gives back; the cry “I believe; help my unbelief!”
Take-home line
“If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.”
live: Give thanks for the root (Romans 11:16)
This week, when you hear a psalm or an Alleluia at Holy Qurbono, thank God for the people of Israel through whom the Scriptures came.
Bring him here (Luke 9:41)
Bring one person who is struggling, a sick relative, a worried friend, to Jesus in a specific prayer, and tell them you are praying.
Do not despair of a fall (Psalm 37:24)
If you have stumbled in a habit or a promise, go to confession and begin again; the Lord holds you by the hand.
2027-07-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came down from the mountain to the valley of the suffering and gave the child back to his father. We thank you for the root from which we have been fed, the faith of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the Scriptures of your people, and we ask you to hasten the day when all Israel will be saved and all the nations will be one in your love. When we stumble, hold us by the hand; when we cannot cast out our own evil, say to us, “Bring him here.” Heal the sick, comfort their parents, and make us glad to praise the greatness of God. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono we come down from the mountain of the Word to the table of the Lord; he takes the bread, as he took the boy by the hand, and gives us back, healed, to our Father.

2027-07-12.title: Monday of the eighth week after Pentecost
readings: Paul's ministry was a burden to no one; beware of those who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ
“Follow me, and I will make you fish for people”: the first four disciples leave their nets
2027-07-12.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration of its own is printed in the Panchangam today. St Benedict, the monk of Italy, is printed with the Sunday of 11 July, the day before.
2027-07-12.verse: And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.”
theo: Today's Epistle comes from the most painful pages of St Paul's letters, where he has to defend his own ministry before the people he had loved and served. Rival preachers had come to Corinth, boasting of their gifts, and some of them were being paid for their teaching. They looked down on Paul because he had worked with his hands (Acts 18:3) and had asked nothing from the Corinthians. Paul answers with a sharp irony: “Did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I proclaimed God's good news to you without payment?” He had accepted help from other churches, “I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you,” and he lists the friends from Macedonia who supplied his needs, the Philippians who had always helped him (Philippians 4:15–16). So, he says, “I did not burden anyone,” and “I will continue to refrain from burdening you in any way.” We must read him rightly. Paul does not teach that the Church should never support her ministers; elsewhere he says plainly that the Lord commanded those who proclaim the gospel to get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14). He is saying that he gave up this right at Corinth so that no one could say he preached for money. And he ends with the reason of the heart: “And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!”

Then Paul's tone turns grave: “For such boasters are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder! Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. So it is not strange if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. Their end will match their deeds.” The danger he names is not crude evil but a polished counterfeit, a message that sounds beautiful and a preacher who looks holy, but who seeks his own glory or gain. How does a simple believer tell the difference? The Lord himself gave the test: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16). St John adds: “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). The Church has always taught us to ask whether a teaching agrees with the faith handed down from the Apostles, which the bishops, in communion with the successor of Peter, are charged to guard, and whether the preacher bears the fruit of humility, love and service. This is not a call to suspicion of others; it is a call to be wise, for the simple believe everything, but the clever consider their steps (Proverbs 14:15). Paul himself is the pattern of the true apostle: he gives, he does not take; he works, he does not boast.

The Gospel shows us what the true call looks like at its beginning. “As he walked by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, ‘Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.’ Immediately they left their nets and followed him.” Then two more: “James son of Zebedee and his brother John, in the boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father, and followed him.” These men had no theology degree, no fine speech, no fame. They had boats, nets and a father, and they had a call. Anyone who has watched the fishermen of Kerala mend their nets on the beach after the monsoon knows how much a net means to a family. They left what they had in order to follow him, and he promised them no income, only a new kind of work: to draw people toward God. The false apostles take; the true Apostles leave. Yesterday the Panchangam remembered St Benedict, the monk of Italy who began his Rule with the single word “Listen” and taught his monks to put nothing before the love of Christ (Rule, Prologue and chapter 4, in substance). He too heard “Follow me” and left what he had. The same call goes out to each of us today, in the plain places where we work and mend our nets.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is my net, the thing I would find hardest to leave if Jesus said, “Follow me”?
Point 1 · Called by the lake
Four ordinary fishermen leave nets and boat at once; the call and the promise.
Point 2 · A burden to no one
Paul gives up his right to support at Corinth; his boast is love, not gain.
Point 3 · The disguise of light
Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light; test the spirits and know them by their fruits.
Take-home line
“Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.”
live: Leave one net (Matthew 4:20)
Name one thing you hold on to that keeps you from following Jesus more closely, and place it at his feet in prayer today.
Serve without a price (2 Corinthians 11:9)
Do one piece of service this week for which you ask nothing, and tell no one about it.
Test the spirits (1 John 4:1)
When a preacher, a message or a video claims to speak for God, ask whether it agrees with the Church's faith and bears the fruit of love and humility; ask your parish priest if you are unsure.
2027-07-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you walked beside the Sea of Galilee and called fishermen to follow you, and they left their nets at once. Call us also, and give us hearts that can leave what holds us back. Make us servants like Paul, a burden to no one, glad to give and not to take. Keep us from the disguises of light and from every preaching that seeks its own glory, and keep your Church in the faith of the Apostles. By the prayers of St Benedict and all your holy servants, teach us to listen and to put nothing before your love. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Lord still calls: Follow me. We leave our place in the pew, bring bread and wine, and he gives himself for us; the One who asked nothing of the Apostles but their nets, gives us his whole self.

2027-07-13.title: Tuesday of the eighth week after Pentecost · Mar Sheelas
readings: “We are the Lord's”: none of us lives or dies to himself or herself
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few: ask the Lord of the harvest
2027-07-13.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers Mar Sheelas (St Silas, companion of Paul) and keeps the name day of Most Rev. Antony Mar Silvanos.
2027-07-13.verse: If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
theo: The Epistle gives us one of the shortest and fullest summaries of the Christian life: “We do not live to ourselves, and we do not die to ourselves. If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.” Paul is writing to a church in which believers were judging one another over food and holy days. He answers not with a rule but with a belonging: we are the Lord's, and so is the brother or sister whom we are tempted to despise. “For to this end Christ died and lived again, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. Why do you pass judgment on your brother or sister? Or you, why do you despise your brother or sister? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God.” Then he quotes the prophet, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall give praise to God,” and concludes, “So then, each of us will be accountable to God.” The Church teaches that each person comes before the Lord at the moment of death and that our life is the time given for accepting his grace (Catechism 1021–1022, in substance). So today's reading is not a threat but a freedom: if we belong to the Lord, we need not be anxious about the judgments of others, and we have no right to pass them on others.

The Gospel shows how the Lord himself looks at people. “Then Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every sickness. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” St John Chrysostom, speaking of this verse, notes that the Lord is moved not by the crowd's strength but by its need, and that his compassion is the mark of the true shepherd (Homilies on Matthew, in substance). Then comes the saying that has sent so many to their vocation: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” St Gregory the Great, preaching on the same words in Luke's Gospel, said that we cannot speak of them without sorrow, for there are many who would listen to good things, but few to speak them (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance). The remedy Jesus gives is first of all prayer: ask the Lord of the harvest. And then, in the next chapter, the disciples who prayed are the ones sent out.

The Panchangam today remembers Mar Sheelas, St Silas, one of those laborers. We meet him in the Acts of the Apostles when the Church of Jerusalem resolved, after the first great council, to send two men to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: “Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leaders among the brothers.” They carried the letter that welcomed the Gentiles without burdening them, and they “were themselves prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the believers.” After the quarrel between Paul and Barnabas, “Paul chose Silas and set out, the believers commending him to the grace of the Lord.” At Philippi the two were beaten and thrown into prison, though both were Roman citizens, and at midnight, with their feet fastened in the stocks, “Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” That night the jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”, and they answered, “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He is usually identified with Silvanus, the form of the name found in the letters: Paul writes with “Silvanus and Timothy” to Thessalonica, and Peter says, “Through Silvanus, whom I consider a faithful brother, I have written this short letter to encourage you.” He served both Paul and Peter and carried the Church's peace from Jerusalem to the nations. Little else is known for certain, and later traditions about his end are not firm. Today we also remember Most Rev. Antony Mar Silvanos on his name day, and we pray that he may be a faithful brother and a servant of the Church's unity. Lord of the harvest, send out laborers.
outline: Opening
Ask: who do I belong to, and whom am I tempted to judge?
Point 1 · We are the Lord's
Living and dying to the Lord; the brother and sister are his too.
Point 2 · A shepherd's compassion
The crowds harassed and helpless; the harvest and the few laborers; first ask the Lord of the harvest.
Point 3 · Mar Sheelas
Silas the messenger of peace from Jerusalem to Antioch, prophet, companion of Paul and Peter, singing in prison.
Take-home line
“Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
live: Belong to the Lord (Romans 14:8)
Begin and end this day by saying aloud, “I am the Lord's, whether I live or die.”
Do not judge (Romans 14:10)
Choose one person you tend to despise or criticise, and pray for them by name every day this week.
Ask for laborers (Matthew 9:38)
Pray today for priests, religious and catechists, and for vocations from your own parish; and ask yourself what laborer's work you can do.
2027-07-13.prayer: Lord of the harvest, we are yours in life and in death, and so are all our brothers and sisters. Keep us from judging and despising one another, and give us the compassion with which you looked at the crowds. Through the prayers of Mar Sheelas, who carried the Church's peace and sang your praise in prison, send out laborers into your harvest, and make us ready to be among them. Bless Most Rev. Antony Mar Silvanos on his name day and all our bishops, that they may be faithful brothers and servants of unity. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono Christ, who died and lived again so that he might be Lord of the dead and the living, gives himself to us, and the shepherd with compassion for the crowds feeds the crowd; we leave the altar as his own, to be sent out to the harvest.
conn: Silas in the Acts.

Acts 15:22–32: Silas is sent with the letter from Jerusalem to Antioch and, being a prophet, strengthens the believers; Acts 15:40 and 16:25: Paul chooses him, and the two sing hymns at midnight in prison.
Silvanus in the letters.
1 Thessalonians 1:1 and 2 Corinthians 1:19 name Silvanus with Paul and Timothy, and 1 Peter 5:12 names him as the faithful brother through whom Peter wrote; he is generally identified with Silas.
Laborers for the harvest.
Luke 10:2 repeats Matthew 9:37–38 for the Seventy-two, whom the Panchangam remembered on 5 July.
fathers: St John Chrysostom
The Lord is moved not by the strength of the crowds but by their need; his compassion is the mark of the true shepherd (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
St Gregory the Great
We cannot say, The harvest is great but the laborers are few, without sorrow: there are many who would hear good things, but few to speak them (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance).
magis: Catechism 849
The Church, sent by her Lord to all nations, strives to preach the Gospel to all; the missionary mandate is a commission to the whole Church (in substance).
Catechism 1021–1022
Death ends the time open to accepting or rejecting the grace of Christ; each person is judged at death in a particular judgment, so that we live and die to the Lord (in substance).
Catechism 957
We keep the memory of the saints not only as examples but to strengthen the union of the whole Church in the Spirit, and so we ask their intercession (in substance).

2027-07-14.title: Wednesday of the eighth week after Pentecost
readings: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth: you are God's field, God's building
Two blind men cry, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” and Jesus says, “According to your faith let it be done to you”
2027-07-14.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. Tomorrow, Thursday 15 July, is the commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios.
2027-07-14.verse: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.
theo: The Church at Corinth had split into parties. “What I mean is that each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ’” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Today St Paul answers with a picture that every farmer in Kerala understands: “What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.” In these weeks the seedlings of paddy are being transplanted into the flooded fields and the coconut saplings are going into the wet earth. Anyone who has done that work knows that the planter and the person who waters each have a task, and that both together cannot make a single seed grow. Life comes from God, and the servants are only servants. Paul does not make light of their labor: “The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each.” The work is real, the reward is real, and the praise belongs to the Lord of the field.

Paul then gives two pictures of the Church: “For we are God's servants, working together; you are God's field, God's building.” A field and a building: a field that must be tended, patiently, season after season; a building that is raised stone upon stone. He goes on to say that he himself laid a foundation and another is building on it, and that “no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid; that foundation is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:10–11). The faith we received in India was planted and watered by many hands: the Apostle Thomas, according to tradition, who first sowed the Gospel on our shores; the mothers who taught prayers; the priests who kept the Qurbono alive in hard times. Tomorrow the Church of the Syro-Malankara tradition remembers one of those planters, Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. He founded the Bethany Ashram in 1919 and the Bethany Sisters in 1925, was received with Mar Theophilos and their companions into full communion with the Catholic Church on 20 September 1930, keeping the Syriac liturgy of the Malankara tradition, and in 1932 became the first Archbishop of Trivandrum. He planted in poverty and in tears, and the growth, in eparchies across India and beyond, has been God's. Tonight is a good evening to thank him, and to ask which part of the field has been given to us to plant or to water.

The Gospel brings us two men who could not see. “As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying loudly, ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’” They cannot see the road, but they see who he is, for “Son of David” is the title of the promised Messiah, and the prophet had said that “the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). They follow him all the way into a house, and there Jesus asks them one question: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” “Then he touched their eyes and said, ‘According to your faith let it be done to you.’ And their eyes were opened.” Faith here is not a payment that buys a miracle; it is an open hand. Then Jesus sternly orders them: “See that no one knows of this.” Probably he wished to avoid becoming a mere wonder-worker before his hour had come. But the two men “went away and spread the news about him throughout that district.” Their gratitude was too great to keep quiet. The cry of the blind men is the cry that rises in every Holy Qurbono: Lord, have mercy. And like the Corinthians whose eyes were dim with party spirit, we too need our eyes opened to see that all growth is God's gift, and that we are one field, one building, one body in the one Lord.
outline: Opening
Ask: who planted or watered the faith in me, and what part of the field has been given to me?
Point 1 · God gave the growth
Paul and Apollos are servants; the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing without God.
Point 2 · God's field, God's building
The Church is tended season after season, with Jesus Christ as the only foundation; the eve of the commemoration of Mar Ivanios.
Point 3 · According to your faith
Two blind men who see who Jesus is before they see his face; faith is an open hand; they cannot keep silent.
Take-home line
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”
live: Thank a planter (1 Corinthians 3:6)
Thank by name someone who planted or watered the faith in you, by a call, a prayer or a visit, and say a prayer for Archbishop Mar Ivanios tonight.
Do your part (1 Corinthians 3:8)
Choose one small piece of the Church's field, a class, a visit, a cleaning, a collection, and do it faithfully this week.
Say Lord, have mercy (Matthew 9:27)
Pray the cry of the blind men slowly three times each day: “Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us.”
2027-07-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the only foundation, and from you comes all growth. We thank you for those who planted and watered the faith in our land, and especially for Archbishop Mar Ivanios, whose memory we shall keep tomorrow. Make us faithful servants in your field, glad to plant and glad to water, and never proud of the harvest. Open our eyes, as you opened the eyes of the two blind men, to see you and to see one another as members of one building. Lord, have mercy on us. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church is built on the one foundation, Jesus Christ; we come as the blind men came into the house, crying for mercy, and the Lord touches our eyes and feeds us.

2027-07-16.title: Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Friday of the eighth week after Pentecost
readings: God sent his Son, born of a woman: no longer a slave but a child, and an heir
“Blessed is the womb that bore you!” “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
2027-07-16.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers today Our Lady of Mount Carmel (കർമലമാതാവ്). Elijah, who prayed on Mount Carmel, is remembered on 20 July.
2027-07-16.verse: But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
theo: Today the Church remembers Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the two readings the Panchangam gives us look at the Mother of the Lord from two sides. The Epistle looks at her from the side of God's plan: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.” This is the only place where St Paul mentions the mother of Jesus, and he does it without her name, in four words that hold the whole mystery: born of a woman. The Son of God did not come as an angel or a vision. He took flesh from a woman, and so truly that the Church, at the Council of Ephesus in 431, declared that she who bore him is to be called Mother of God, Theotokos. In our Syriac tradition the same truth is sung in the title Yoldath Aloho, she who gave birth to God (Catechism 495). St Cyril of Alexandria, who defended that title, asked how anyone who confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ is God could hesitate to call the Holy Virgin who bore him the Mother of God (Letter to the Monks of Egypt, in substance). And all this is for us: “And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’ So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.” The Son who was born of a woman makes us children of the Father.

The Gospel looks at Mary from the side of the heart. “While he was saying this, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, ‘Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!’” It is a simple woman's praise, the kind every mother in Kerala would understand: she blesses the mother because of the Son. And Jesus answers: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!” Some have heard this as if he were setting his mother aside, but the Church has always understood it the other way. The word “rather” does not take the blessing from Mary; it shows where her blessing comes from. Who ever heard the word of God and kept it as she did? “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). “Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Elizabeth had already told her, “blessed is she who believed” (Luke 1:45), and she herself had sung, “from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). St Augustine said that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance). The Second Vatican Council, quoting this very passage, says that the Blessed Virgin herself, in the course of her Son's preaching, received the words by which he declared blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, as she was faithfully doing (Lumen Gentium 58, in substance). So the woman in the crowd and Jesus do not disagree. Mary is the first and best of those who hear and keep.

Why Carmel? Mount Carmel is the green headland on the coast of the Holy Land near Haifa, and its name means garden or orchard. The prophets sang of its beauty (Isaiah 35:2). It is above all the mountain of the prophet Elijah, whom we shall remember on 20 July. After three years of drought, Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, “bowed himself down upon the earth and put his face between his knees,” and sent his servant to look toward the sea. “There is nothing.” Seven times he sent him. “At the seventh time he said, ‘Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand is rising out of the sea.’ ... In a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind; there was a heavy rain” (1 Kings 18:42–45). Anyone who has watched a Kerala sky in the first days of the monsoon, a small dark cloud at the edge of the sea growing into the rains, understands why the Christian imagination saw in that little cloud a sign of the Virgin Mary: from her, small and humble, came the One who is the rain of grace for a dry world. In the twelfth century hermits from the West settled on Mount Carmel, near the place remembered as the prophet's, and built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady. They became the Carmelite Order, and their patroness is Our Lady of Mount Carmel, whose feast is kept on 16 July.

The Carmelites spread her devotion in the sign of the scapular, two small pieces of brown cloth worn on the shoulders. According to a pious tradition, Our Lady gave it to St Simon Stock, an English Carmelite, on 16 July 1251; historians cannot confirm the details, but the devotion is old and has been blessed by the Church. The Church teaches that the scapular, like any sacramental, is a sign: of belonging to Mary, and of the wish to follow her, to hear the word of God and keep it. It cannot replace a life of faith, and it is the Son, not the cloth, who saves us. Here in Kerala, Carmel is a familiar name on churches, schools and convents, and the Carmelite family has served our land since 1831, when the first monastery of the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate was founded at Mannanam; one of its founders, St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, was canonised in 2014. And on the cross the Lord gave her to us: “Woman, here is your son.” “Here is your mother.” (John 19:26–27). Today, near the beginning of Karkidakam, when the rain is heaviest, let us ask the Mother of God to teach us the one blessedness her Son named: to hear the word of God and obey it.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone called me blessed, what would they have to see in my life?
Point 1 · Born of a woman
The Son of God took flesh from Mary; Theotokos, Yoldath Aloho; through him we are children and heirs.
Point 2 · Blessed are those who hear and keep
Not a rebuke but the secret of Mary's blessing: she heard the word and kept it.
Point 3 · Carmel, the garden and the little cloud
Elijah's prayer, the cloud no bigger than a hand, and the rain; Mary as the Mother from whom grace came to the world.
Point 4 · A sign that points to the Son
The brown scapular as a sign of belonging and a pledge to follow Mary; Carmelites in Kerala.
Take-home line
“Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!”
live: Hear and keep (Luke 11:28)
Read the Gospel of this Sunday (the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost) tonight and choose one sentence to keep through the week.
Renew the sign (Luke 2:19)

If you wear the scapular or a medal of Our Lady, renew what it stands for: to follow her in hearing and keeping the word. If you do not, say three Hail Marys at the end of the day and think of one word of the Gospel.
Look at the clouds (1 Kings 18:44)
In this month of rain, look up at the sky once each day and pray: “Mother of God, bring us your Son, the rain of grace.”
2027-07-16.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, born of a woman in the fullness of time, you gave us the Virgin Mary to be your Mother and ours. On this feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel we thank you for her faith: she heard your word and kept it, and she pondered it in her heart. Through her prayers make us children who cry Abba, Father, and disciples who hear and obey. As the prophet Elijah saw the little cloud rise from the sea and the rain come to the dry land, so let the grace you have given through her refresh your Church and our country. Bless all who wear her sign and all the Carmelite family, and lead us by the path of her faith to you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the Church remembers the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, before all the saints; and the Body that the Lord took from her is the Body we receive: the little cloud has become the rain of grace on the altar.
conn: Born of a woman.
Galatians 4:4 and Luke 1:31, 43: the Son of God took flesh from Mary, whom Elizabeth called “the mother of my Lord”; Luke 11:27 echoes this in the cry of the woman in the crowd.
Hear and keep.
Luke 1:38, 45; 2:19, 51: Mary's faith and obedience are what Jesus names as true blessedness in Luke 11:28; Luke 8:21 says the same of his mother and brothers.
The little cloud.
1 Kings 18:42–45: Elijah on Carmel; the Carmelite tradition has seen in the cloud rising from the sea a sign of Mary; the prophet is remembered on 20 July.
Mother at the cross.
John 19:26–27 and Acts 1:14: Mary is given to the disciple and is with the Apostles in prayer before Pentecost.
fathers: St Augustine
Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance).
St Cyril of Alexandria
If our Lord Jesus Christ is God, how can the Holy Virgin who bore him not be called Mother of God? (Letter to the Monks of Egypt, in substance).
magis: Catechism 495
Mary is acclaimed by Elizabeth as the mother of my Lord; the Church confesses her as truly Mother of God, Theotokos (in substance).
Catechism 148
The Virgin Mary most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith (in substance).
Lumen Gentium 58
In the course of her Son's preaching Mary received the words by which he declared blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, as she was faithfully doing (in substance).
Catechism 967–969
Mary is the model of faith and charity for the Church, and by her maternal love she cares for the brothers and sisters of her Son (in substance).

2027-07-17.title: Saturday of the eighth week after Pentecost · St Alexius of Rome
readings: Thanks be to God, who spreads through us in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing Christ
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”: good news to the poor, in the synagogue at Nazareth
2027-07-17.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. Tomorrow is the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Alexius of Rome (റോമിലെ വി. അലക്സിയോസ്), keeps the anniversary of the episcopal ordination of Most Rev. Thomas Mar Koorilos (1997), and keeps the name day of Most Rev. Yoohanon Mar Alexios. The Panchangam gives the readings of the weekday only.
2027-07-17.verse: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing;
theo: Paul writes today from a worried heart. He has come to Troas to proclaim the good news, and the Lord has opened a door for him, yet he cannot rest because his brother Titus is not there with news from Corinth. So he leaves the open door and goes on to Macedonia. Then, almost in the same breath, the worry turns into thanksgiving: “But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him.” The picture is of a victory procession in which incense is carried, so that the scent reaches the crowds long before they see the one who is passing. Paul does not claim to be the victor. He is part of the procession, and the fragrance is Christ's. Like every scent, it cannot choose whom it reaches: “For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life.” The same gospel is life to one who welcomes it and a sharp reproach to one who closes the door. Paul himself trembles at this: “Who is sufficient for these things?”

He answers by describing the kind of messenger God can use: “For we are not peddlers of God's word like so many; but in Christ we speak as persons of sincerity, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence.” A peddler waters down his goods to please the buyer. A person sent from God speaks as one who stands before God. In the Kerala monsoon, when rain has soaked the house and the cupboards smell of damp, an old household remedy is to burn a little frankincense or sambrani on a few embers. The smell fills the rooms, clings to clothes and stays in the hair. We carry with us the fragrance of whoever we have spent time with. The disciple who has stood in the presence of Christ in prayer and in the Holy Qurbono carries something of him into the market, the office and the kitchen without having to say a word.

The Gospel shows us the Lord himself in the synagogue of Nazareth, “as was his custom,” on the sabbath. The scroll of Isaiah is given to him, and he finds the place: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to let the oppressed go free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” The very word Christ means the Anointed One. The Spirit rests on him not for his own comfort but for the sake of the poor, the captive, the blind and the oppressed. Luke tells us that he then says: “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” The good news is not an idea about the future; it begins to happen when he opens his mouth. Paul's fragrance and the Lord's anointing are one thing seen from two sides: Christ is anointed, and the fragrance of that anointing is spread through those who belong to him.

Today the Panchangam also remembers St Alexius of Rome. The old Life of Alexius, whose historical details cannot be confirmed and which is best read as a story told by the Church to praise a way of life, tells of the only son of a wealthy Roman family who left his home and bride, lived for years as a beggar in a far-off city, and finally returned unrecognised to his father's house, where he lived out his days among the poor at the door. Whatever the details, the Church has loved this story because it makes Christ's own path visible: he who was rich became poor for our sake. Alexius's name is also borne today by Most Rev. Yoohanon Mar Alexios, whose name day the Panchangam keeps, and the Church remembers with thanks the anniversary of the episcopal ordination of Most Rev. Thomas Mar Koorilos in 1997. A bishop is anointed so that he may be a person “sent from God and standing in his presence.” We pray that these pastors, and all who serve us, may spread the fragrance of Christ.
outline: Opening
Ask: when people have been with me, what do they carry away: worry, or the fragrance of Christ?
Point 1 · The procession of Christ
Paul is not the victor; he carries the incense of the victory of Christ.
Point 2 · Sent from God, standing before him
A messenger is not a peddler; he speaks with sincerity from the presence of God.
Point 3 · The Anointed at Nazareth
The Spirit is given for the poor, the captive, the blind and the oppressed.
Point 4 · From riches to the door
St Alexius, according to the old Life, makes visible the Lord who became poor; pastors remembered today.
Take-home line
“Thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession.”
live: Carry the fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:14)
Before you leave home this morning, stand for one minute in prayer, and ask that whoever you meet today may meet the kindness of Christ in you.
Speak with sincerity (2 Corinthians 2:17)
Choose one conversation this week in which you have been tempted to soften the truth to please, and speak it gently and plainly.
Remember the pastors (Luke 4:18)
Pray today by name for your bishop and your parish priest, and for Thomas Mar Koorilos and Yoohanon Mar Alexios in particular, that they may bring good news to the poor.
2027-07-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, anointed by the Father with the Holy Spirit to bring good news to the poor, we thank you that in you we are always led in triumph. Let the fragrance of your knowledge spread through us in every place, in our homes, our work and our parish. Keep us sincere, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence, and make us gentle with the poor, the captive and the oppressed. Through the prayers of St Alexius, who for your sake became poor, and of all your saints, bless our bishops and priests, and bless Thomas Mar Koorilos and Yoohanon Mar Alexios whom we remember today. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the incense rises before the altar, a sign of prayer and of the fragrance of Christ's sacrifice; and the priest, anointed to serve, offers on our behalf the bread and wine that become the Body and Blood of the Lord.
conn: Incense and prayer.
Psalm 141:2: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you”; Ephesians 5:2: Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.”
The Anointed and the Spirit.
Isaiah 61:1–2, the passage the Lord reads at Nazareth; Acts 10:38: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he went about doing good.
He became poor for us.
2 Corinthians 8:9: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.”
fathers: St John Chrysostom

The fragrance of a perfume is felt by those near it even when the one who carries it says nothing; in this way the apostles, wherever they went, spread the knowledge of Christ simply by what they were (Homilies on Second Corinthians, in substance).
St Cyril of Alexandria
Christ is called the Anointed because as man he received the Spirit for our sake, so that the gift of the Spirit might pass from him to all of us who are his body (Commentary on Luke, in substance).
magis: Catechism 436
The word Christ comes from the Greek translation of the Hebrew Messiah, which means anointed; Jesus is the Christ because he is consecrated by the Spirit as priest, prophet and king (in substance).
Catechism 544
The kingdom belongs to the poor and the lowly, which means those who have accepted it with humble hearts; Jesus is sent to preach good news to the poor (in substance).
Catechism 2445
Love for the poor is incompatible with immoderate love of riches or their selfish use (in substance).

2027-07-19.title: Monday of the ninth week after Pentecost · Morth Makrina
readings: The mystery of lawlessness is already at work; the Lord Jesus will destroy it; the love of the truth that saves
The Pharisees ask for a sign from heaven: “no sign will be given to this generation”
2027-07-19.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers Morth Makrina (മൊർത്ത് മക്രീന, St Macrina the Younger, died 379), the sister of St Basil the Great and St Gregory of Nyssa. Morth is the Syriac title given to a holy woman, as Mar is given to a holy man.
2027-07-19.verse: Why does this generation ask for a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.
theo: Today's Epistle is among the hardest passages in all of Paul, and it helps to remember why he wrote it. Some in Thessalonica had been shaken by a rumour that the day of the Lord had already come, and Paul writes to steady them. He speaks of “the mystery of lawlessness”: “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but only until the one who now restrains it is removed. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will destroy with the breath of his mouth, annihilating him by the manifestation of his coming.” Christians have read this passage in many ways over the centuries, and the Church has never turned it into a timetable. What she takes from it is plain. Evil is real and works through deception, with “signs” and “wonders” that are false. But the Lord Jesus needs no great army to overcome it: the breath of his mouth is enough. And the reason why some are lost is not that God hides the truth but that they “refused to love the truth and so be saved.” The danger Paul names is a heart that has stopped loving what is true.

That is exactly the heart we meet in the Gospel. The Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, “asking him for a sign from heaven, to test him.” Only a few verses earlier, Mark has told us that Jesus fed four thousand people with seven loaves, with baskets left over. The signs were there. What they wanted was not a sign but a proof on their own terms, so that they could stay in charge of the question. Mark tells us something we do not often hear about the Lord: “And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, ‘Why does this generation ask for a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.’” It is not anger; it is the deep sigh of one who loves and is grieved by a closed door. Then he does a quiet and painful thing: “And he left them, and getting into the boat again, he went across to the other side.” The Lord does not force himself on those who test him. In the other Gospels he adds that the one sign given will be the sign of Jonah, his own death and rising. In the Holy Qurbono that sign is given to us again every Sunday.

On this day the Panchangam remembers Morth Makrina, whom the Church calls Macrina the Younger. Her brother, St Gregory of Nyssa, wrote her Life soon after she died in the year 379, and he tells us how a young woman of a Christian family in Cappadocia became the teacher of her whole family. After the death of her fiancé she chose to remain unmarried, and with her mother, Emmelia, she turned the family estate on the river Iris into a community in which women and men lived by prayer, psalm-singing and work, sharing their goods with the poor. She helped her brother Basil, who had come home proud of his learning in the schools, to turn towards a life with Christ; she raised her youngest brother, Peter, who became bishop of Sebaste; and Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, calls her his teacher. When he visited her in her last illness, he found her lying on a plank on the ground, and he heard her speak so clearly about the soul and the resurrection that he later wrote their conversation as a book. She died after a prayer of thanksgiving, signing herself with the cross.

Macrina never asked for a sign, and she never performed one that we would call a show. Her life was the sign: a quiet, steady, hidden holiness in which the whole family came to see Christ. That is what the Lord means when he refuses a sign to the testing crowd and offers himself to those who love the truth. In our own time many look for a sign in every new claim and every dramatic report of a vision, and forget the ordinary signs God has already given: the Gospel, the Holy Qurbono, the forgiveness of sins, and the faithful lives of people like Macrina. Let us ask for what she had: a heart that loves the truth and does not need to test the Lord, and a faith that shows itself in sharing the household's bread with the poor. As the monsoon rain wakes the fields each year without any announcement, so God's grace works quietly in a hidden life.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I believe because I love the truth, or do I keep asking for one more proof?
Point 1 · The mystery of lawlessness
Evil is real and deceives, but the breath of the Lord's mouth is enough to overcome it.
Point 2 · Love of the truth
The danger is not hidden truth but a heart that refuses to love it.
Point 3 · The sign refused
Jesus sighs and leaves; faith cannot be made to order.
Point 4 · Macrina, the quiet sign
A hidden life of prayer and sharing that taught a whole family.
Take-home line
“Why does this generation ask for a sign?”
live: Love the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:10)
Take one question of faith you have put off, and read the Gospel passage on it today, asking only what it really says.
Stop testing (Mark 8:11)
This week, do not ask God for proof before you do what you already know is right. Do it first, and trust.
Be a quiet sign (Matthew 5:16)
Do one hidden good deed at home this week, as Macrina did, without comment: a shared meal, a lamp lit, a visit paid.
2027-07-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sighed in your spirit over those who asked for a sign, and you give yourself to those who love the truth. Keep us from the deception of false wonders, and guard us from the evil one. Give us a heart that loves what is true and does not set conditions for you. Through the prayers of Morth Makrina, who taught her whole family by a hidden life of prayer, psalms and charity, make our homes places where your light is seen, and make us ready for the day of your coming. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The sign the Lord has given us is the sign of Jonah: his death and rising, which we proclaim at every Holy Qurbono; and there, without any show, the bread and wine become his Body and Blood for those who love the truth.
conn: Love the truth.
2 Thessalonians 2:10: “because they refused to love the truth and so be saved”; Psalm 25:5: “Lead me in your truth, and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation.”
The sign of Jonah.
Matthew 12:39: “An evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”
Do not harden your hearts.
Psalm 95:8–9: “do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness, when your ancestors tested me”; Hebrews 3:15 repeats the warning.
fathers: St Gregory of Nyssa
Writing of his sister Macrina, he says that for their youngest brother Peter she was father, teacher, guardian, mother and counsellor in every good (Life of Macrina, in substance).
St Gregory of Nyssa
In the dialogue he wrote after her death, Macrina teaches that the resurrection is the restoration of human nature to what it was in the beginning (On the Soul and the Resurrection, in substance).
magis: Catechism 548

Jesus accompanies his words with mighty works, wonders and signs, which show that the kingdom is present in him; but these signs do not remove the need for faith, and they are not given to those who ask for them out of curiosity or the desire for magic (in substance).
Catechism 675

Before Christ's second coming the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers; the deception of evil is an imposture that offers a solution to human problems at the price of apostasy from the truth (in substance).
Catechism 2013
All the faithful of whatever rank or state are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity (in substance).

2027-07-20.title: Elijah the Prophet · Tuesday of the ninth week after Pentecost
readings: These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ
“Elijah has come”: the question of the disciples as they came down from the mountain
2027-07-20.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Elijah the Prophet (ഏലിയാ നിബിയാ). Nibiya is the Syriac word for prophet. Elijah is one of the prophets of the Old Covenant whom the Panchangam remembers this month, with Aaron, Daniel and Ezekiel. The Panchangam gives the readings of the weekday only.
2027-07-20.verse: Elijah is indeed coming first to restore all things.
theo: Peter, James and John are coming down the mountain, and their heads are still full of what they have seen: the Lord shining like light, and with him Moses and Elijah, “who were talking with Jesus.” Jesus tells them to say nothing “until after the Son of Man had risen from the dead,” and they keep the matter to themselves, “questioning what this rising from the dead could mean.” Then comes the question that has been burning in them: “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” The scribes were reading the prophet Malachi: “Lo, I will send you the prophet Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. He will turn the hearts of parents to their children and the hearts of children to their parents.” They had just seen Elijah on the mountain. Why was he gone again? Jesus answers in two steps. First: “Elijah is indeed coming first to restore all things.” The promise stands. Then: “But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written about him.” Elijah has come in the person of John the Baptist, who, as the angel told Zechariah, would go before the Lord “with the spirit and power of Elijah.” And the way of the forerunner prepares the way of the Lord: they did to John whatever they pleased, and so the Son of Man “is to go through many sufferings and be treated with contempt.”

Who was Elijah, and why does the Church keep his memory in the season of Pentecost? He appears suddenly in the First Book of Kings, “the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead,” announcing a drought in the days of King Ahab. He is fed first by ravens, then by a poor widow of Zarephath, whose jar of meal “was not emptied, neither did the jug of oil fail, according to the word of the Lord.” On Mount Carmel he stands alone against the prophets of Baal and asks the people the question that he asks still: “How long will you go limping with two different opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” Fire falls and the people fall on their faces. Then Elijah climbs to the top of Carmel, bows with his face between his knees, and sends his servant to look at the sea, seven times. At the seventh time the servant says: “Look, a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand is rising out of the sea.” In July in Kerala, when the whole land waits for the rain and listens to it on the tiles, we know exactly what that cloud is. St James adds a word for ordinary believers: “Elijah was a human being like us, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain and the earth yielded its harvest.”

The same prophet then sits exhausted under a broom tree and begs to die: “It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my ancestors.” The great prophet is a person like us. And God does not answer with a speech. An angel touches him and says: “Get up and eat.” A second time: “Get up and eat, otherwise the journey will be too much for you.” “He got up, and ate and drank; then he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the mount of God.” There, God is not in the wind, nor the earthquake, nor the fire, but in “a sound of sheer silence.” The Fathers saw in the cake and the jar of water a sign of the bread that sustains the pilgrim, and the Church gives the Holy Qurbono to the dying as food for the last journey. The Second Book of Kings tells that Elijah went up in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire, and on the mountain of the Transfiguration he appears again, to listen to the Son.

Today's Epistle gives the key. Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone judge them in matters of food and drink, festivals, new moons or sabbaths: “These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” Paul is not despising the feasts of Israel, which the same Paul calls gifts that belong to Israel (Romans 9:4); he is telling Gentile believers not to let any human group make them anxious about what Christ has already fulfilled. The prophets, too, are a shadow, a light thrown ahead by the one who is coming. The voice at the Transfiguration says of Jesus: “Listen to him!” and then, “they saw no one with them any more, but only Jesus.” We honour Elijah, we pray with him, and we learn courage from him; but we follow the one to whom Moses and Elijah pointed, “the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows with a growth that is from God.” Let us ask the Lord to give us the courage of Elijah to choose, the humility of Elijah to rest and to eat what God provides, and the stillness of Elijah to hear a sound of sheer silence.
outline: Opening
Ask: where in my life am I still going limping between two opinions?
Point 1 · Elijah must come first
Malachi's promise; Elijah has come in John the Baptist, and the forerunner shares the Lord's fate.
Point 2 · Prayer and the little cloud
Carmel, the drought and the rain; Elijah is a human being like us.
Point 3 · Get up and eat
Despair under the broom tree; the bread of the journey; the sound of sheer silence.
Point 4 · Shadow and substance
The prophets point ahead; the substance belongs to Christ, the head of the body.
Take-home line
“they saw no one with them any more, but only Jesus”
live: Choose (1 Kings 18:21)
Name one habit or divided loyalty in your life, and make one clear decision this week to follow the Lord in it.
Pray for rain (James 5:17–18)
Pray today with persistence, as Elijah did, for something good that you are still waiting for, and for the farmers and families who depend on this monsoon.
Get up and eat (1 Kings 19:7)
If you are weary or discouraged, rest, eat, and then take up the journey; and if you can, receive the Holy Qurbono this week as food for the way.
2027-07-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you spoke with Moses and Elijah on the holy mountain, and the Father said of you, Listen to him. We thank you for the prophet Elijah, who stood alone for the living God, who prayed that the rain might come, and whom you strengthened with bread on the way. Give us the courage to choose you without dividing our hearts, the perseverance to pray when the heavens seem closed, and the humility to rise and eat when we are weary. Let us not be led by shadows, but hold fast to you, the head from whom the whole body grows with a growth that is from God. Through the prayers of the prophet Elijah, bless the farmers and the fields in this season of rain. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Elijah went in the strength of the food the angel gave him forty days to the mount of God; in the Holy Qurbono the Lord himself gives us the bread of life, the true food for the long journey, and the Church sends the Qurbono also to the dying as the bread of their last road.
conn: Elijah and John the Baptist.

Malachi 4:5–6 promises Elijah before the day of the Lord; Luke 1:17: John will go before the Lord “with the spirit and power of Elijah”; Matthew 17:10–13 records the same conversation after the Transfiguration.
The man of prayer.
James 5:17–18: Elijah “was a human being like us” and his prayer closed and opened the heavens; 1 Kings 18:42–45 is the little cloud rising from the sea.
Bread for the journey.
1 Kings 19:5–8: “Get up and eat”; John 6:51: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven”; the Church's viaticum is the Holy Qurbono given for the last journey.
fathers: St Ambrose

Elijah's long fast was the beginning of his ascent: by fasting and prayer he was lifted above earthly things, and the spirit that is strengthened by fasting is made ready to see God (On Elijah and Fasting, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

John is called Elijah, not because he is the same person but because he has the same spirit and task: both stood alone against the powerful, both called the people back to the Lord, and both lived by simplicity (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2582

Elijah, the father of the prophets, is the one in whom the prophetic tradition of Israel is gathered: he teaches the people to turn their hearts to the living God and shows what prayer is when the whole person stands before the Lord (in substance).
Catechism 696

Fire symbolises the transforming energy of the acts of the Holy Spirit; in Elijah's prayer on Mount Carmel, fire from heaven consumed the sacrifice, and the Spirit comes as fire on the Apostles at Pentecost (in substance).
Catechism 718
John the Baptist is the one sent to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah; in him the Spirit completes the work of the prophets (in substance).

2027-07-21.title: Daniel the Prophet · Wednesday of the ninth week after Pentecost
readings: We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak; the scriptures give steadfastness, encouragement and hope
The mustard seed and the yeast: the kingdom of heaven small, hidden and growing
2027-07-21.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Daniel the Prophet (ദാനിയേൽ നിബിയാ), one of the prophets of the Old Covenant whom it remembers this month, with Aaron, Elijah and Ezekiel. The Panchangam gives the readings of the weekday only.
2027-07-21.verse: I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.
theo: The Gospel gives us two very short parables, and both begin with something small. “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field; it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” The kitchens of Kerala know the mustard seed, tiny and black, which crackles in hot coconut oil. And then: “The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.” Three measures is a great quantity of flour, enough to feed a large household, and the yeast is hidden in it, working unseen through the night, as the batter rises in our own kitchens before the morning appam. Both parables say the same thing: God's kingdom does not enter the world with trumpets. It begins small and hidden, in a handful of fishermen, in a crucified carpenter, in a loaf of bread broken in an upper room, and from there it grows until it shelters the nations and leavens everything. Matthew then tells us why Jesus spoke in parables: “This was to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophet: ‘I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.’”

A prophet is the right companion for that verse, and today the Panchangam remembers Daniel. Daniel was a young Jew taken into exile in Babylon, trained for the king's service, who nevertheless “resolved that he would not defile himself with the royal rations of food and wine.” When King Nebuchadnezzar dreamed a dream that no wise man of Babylon could tell or explain, Daniel prayed, and then he blessed God: “He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and light dwells with him.” This is what Matthew means by proclaiming what has been hidden. In the dream Daniel saw a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, the pride of the empires of the earth, and “a stone was cut out, not by human hands,” and it struck the statue and broke it in pieces. “But the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” The Fathers saw in this stone Christ himself, small at his coming and unregarded, and yet the beginning of a kingdom that fills the earth. Daniel says plainly what the kingdom is: “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed.” In the next vision the king saw a mighty tree, so high that it could be seen to the ends of the earth, with “the birds of the air” nesting in its branches; and that was the tree of an empire's pride, which God cut down. The tree of Jesus' parable grows from the smallest seed, in humility, and is the one that does not fall.

Daniel's life shows what it means to live as a seed in the soil of a great empire. He prayed in the same way every day, “three times a day,” with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, even when the king's decree made this dangerous, and he would not hide his prayer. The Syriac tradition, which prays the hours seven times a day, has always seen in Daniel a teacher of the praying hours. He read the scriptures with attention: “I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years” of Jeremiah, and he turned to the Lord “by prayer and supplication with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.” Notice the way he prays: “we have sinned and done wrong.” He, the blameless one, takes the sins of his people on his own lips. That is exactly what today's Epistle describes: “We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Each of us must please our neighbor for the good purpose of building up the neighbor. For Christ did not please himself.” Daniel did not please himself; he bore the failings of his people before God.

Paul adds the reason why the Church reads the prophets: “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and by the encouragement of the scriptures we might have hope.” The scriptures teach us to be steadfast when the seed seems small and the yeast seems hidden. Daniel saw, in another vision, “one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven,” to whom was given “dominion and glory and kingship, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him,” a kingship that “shall never be destroyed.” Jesus took that figure to himself when he spoke of the Son of Man. So the small seed of the Gospel and the great kingdom of Daniel are one reality. Paul ends: “May the God of steadfastness and encouragement grant you to live in harmony with one another, in accordance with Christ Jesus, so that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The seed grows when it grows in harmony, with one voice.
outline: Opening
Ask: what small thing in my life do I think is too little to matter to God?
Point 1 · The seed and the yeast
The kingdom begins small and hidden, and grows until it shelters and leavens all.
Point 2 · Hidden things revealed
Daniel blesses the God who reveals deep and hidden things; Matthew's parables proclaim what was hidden.
Point 3 · The stone not cut by human hands
The kingdom that fills the earth; the tree of pride and the tree of the kingdom.
Point 4 · Steadfastness and one voice
Daniel's daily prayer and his prayer for his people; bearing one another's weakness, as Christ did.
Take-home line
“the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed”
live: Trust the small seed (Matthew 13:31)
Do one small good thing today that no one will notice, and trust God to make it grow.
Pray at the hours (Daniel 6:10)
Choose three times today, morning, noon and evening, for a short prayer, even a minute; let your home or your work be your upper room with an open window.
Bear with the weak (Romans 15:1)
This week, put up quietly with one failing of another person, and pray for that person by name, as Daniel prayed for his people.
2027-07-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the stone cut out without human hands, the seed that grows into the tree that shelters all, the yeast hidden in the flour of the world. We thank you for the prophet Daniel, who prayed in Babylon with his windows open toward Jerusalem, who bore the sins of his people on his lips, and who saw your kingdom coming. Teach us to trust the small beginnings of your grace, to pray at every hour, and to bear with one another as you did not please yourself. Keep us steadfast and encouraged by the scriptures, and let us with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the smallest portion of bread and a little wine become the Body and Blood of the Lord, the hidden seed of the kingdom; and the one voice of the whole Church sings the glory of the Father.
conn: Hidden things revealed.
Daniel 2:22: “He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and light dwells with him”; Psalm 78:2, quoted in Matthew 13:35: “I will open my mouth in a parable.”
The kingdom that fills the earth.
Daniel 2:34–35, 44: the stone cut out not by human hands becomes a great mountain; Daniel 7:13–14: the one like a human being receives an everlasting kingship.
The tree and the birds.
Daniel 4:10–12 describes the great tree with the birds of the air nesting in its branches; Matthew 13:32 uses the same image for the kingdom.
fathers: St Hippolytus of Rome

The stone cut out without human hands is Christ, who was born without the work of a man, and who breaks the kingdoms of the earth and becomes the mountain that fills the whole earth (Commentary on Daniel, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

By the mustard seed the Lord shows how his Gospel would grow: a few poor and unlearned men, scattered over the world, would fill it, like the small seed becoming a tree in which the birds find rest (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
magis: Catechism 541
Christ ushered in the kingdom of heaven on earth; the Church is the seed and beginning of that kingdom, and she grows slowly until the final consummation (in substance).
Catechism 546
Jesus' invitation to enter the kingdom comes in the form of parables, which call for a decision; the kingdom is revealed to those who hear with the heart (in substance).
Lumen Gentium 5
The Church receives the mission to proclaim and establish among all peoples the kingdom of Christ and of God, and she is on earth the seed and the beginning of that kingdom (in substance).

2027-07-22.title: St Mary Magdalene · Thursday of the ninth week after Pentecost
readings: If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: God has given us the ministry of reconciliation
Mary Magdalene at the tomb: “Mary!” “Rabbouni!” and “I have seen the Lord”
2027-07-22.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of St Mary Magdalene (വി. മഗ്ദലേന മറിയം). In the Roman calendar, since 2016, she is honoured with the title Apostle of the Apostles; the title is much older, and was given to her by teachers of the Church such as St Thomas Aquinas, because she was the first sent to announce the resurrection. The Panchangam gives the readings of the weekday only.
2027-07-22.verse: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”; and she told them that he had said these things to her.
theo: Who was Mary Magdalene? The Gospels tell us less than we would like, and what they tell us is enough. She came from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke names her among the women who followed Jesus and “provided for them out of their resources”: “Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.” She was a woman whom the Lord had delivered, and she did not go away afterwards. She was standing “near the cross of Jesus” with his mother and the other women; she saw where he was buried; and on the first day of the week she is the first to come to the tomb. We should say plainly what the Gospels do not say: they never say that she is the sinful woman of Luke chapter 7 or Mary of Bethany.
