An older tradition of the Western Church joined these women together, but the Church today keeps them distinct, and we read her as the Gospel gives her to us: a woman healed by the Lord, a faithful friend at the cross, and the first witness of the resurrection. Today's Epistle is the best commentary on her life: “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!”

Now follow her through the Gospel. “Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed.” In her first fear she runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, and they run to the tomb, see the linen wrappings, and return to their homes. But “Mary stood weeping outside the tomb.” The disciples have gone home, and she stays. She bends and looks in, and sees two angels in white who ask: “Woman, why are you weeping?” She answers: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” Then she turns and sees Jesus standing there, “but she did not know that it was Jesus.” He asks: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she says: “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” She speaks as a woman who has only one wish: to give the body of the Lord an honourable place.

Then comes the shortest and greatest sentence of the Gospel: “Jesus said to her, ‘Mary!’ She turned and said to him in Hebrew, ‘Rabbouni!’ (which means Teacher).” The risen Lord is not first known by sight or by argument. He is known when he calls her by name, as the Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name. And then he gives her a mission: “Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” She must not cling to the Lord as he was; a new relationship is beginning, in which he will be with his Church by the Spirit. And look at the words: “my brothers.” They were the men who fled, and he calls them brothers. “Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’; and she told them that he had said these things to her.” This is why the Church has called her the apostle of the apostles, the one who was sent to the Apostles.

Paul's words in the Epistle describe what she became: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting the message of reconciliation to us. So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us.” Mary Magdalene is the first ambassador of the risen Christ. She is sent to men who had abandoned the Lord, with a message of forgiveness: my brothers, my Father and your Father. In our tradition the morning prayer, Sapro, is the prayer of daybreak that remembers the resurrection, and in the dark of the monsoon mornings many Christians rise early to pray, as she came to the tomb while it was still dark. Let us ask her intercession: for the grace to stay when others go home, to seek the Lord with love even through tears, to listen for him to call us by name, and to go and tell others, with joy, “I have seen the Lord.”
outline: Opening
Ask: when I cannot find the Lord, do I go home, or do I stay and keep looking?
Point 1 · A woman delivered
Magdala, the seven demons, the cross and the burial; a faithful friend. She is not the sinful woman of Luke 7; the Gospel gives her as it is.
Point 2 · She stayed and wept
While it was still dark; the angels' question; seeking with tears and love.
Point 3 · “Mary!”
The Lord is known by being called by name; do not hold on, but go.
Point 4 · Apostle of the apostles
The ministry of reconciliation; sent to the brothers who had fled.
Take-home line
“I have seen the Lord”
live: Stay and seek (John 20:11)
When prayer feels dry, stay ten minutes longer in front of the cross or the tabernacle, telling the Lord everything, even your tears.
Listen for your name (John 20:16)
Take five minutes in silence and ask the Lord to call you by name; remember that in baptism he has already done so.
Go and tell (John 20:17–18)
Tell one person this week, simply, what the risen Lord has done for you; and reconcile with someone who has been distant from you.
2027-07-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you called Mary Magdalene by name in the garden and sent her to your brothers with the first word of the resurrection. We thank you for her faithfulness at the cross, her tears at the tomb and her joy in announcing that she had seen the Lord. Make us new creations in you. When we cannot find you, give us the love that stays and seeks. Call us by name, and when we hear your voice, send us as ambassadors of your reconciliation. Through the prayers of St Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, strengthen the faith of your Church and lead us to see you, face to face, in the light of your kingdom. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Lord who stood in the garden and called her by name comes to us under the form of bread and wine, and sends us out in peace with the same word: Go and tell.
conn: Faithful at the cross.
John 19:25: “standing near the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene”; Mark 15:47: she saw where he was laid.
Called by name.
John 10:3: the Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name and leads them out”; Isaiah 43:1: “I have called you by name, you are mine.”
A new creation.
Luke 8:2: “Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out”; Revelation 21:5: “See, I am making all things new.”
fathers: St Gregory the Great

She who stayed at the tomb to seek him found him, because she remained, and the love that seeks is the love that finds; the disciples had gone home and she kept on weeping and looking (Homilies on the Gospels 25, in substance).
St Thomas Aquinas

Because a woman had announced to the man the first word of death, so a woman is first to announce to the Apostles the word of life; thus she was made, as it were, the apostle of the apostles (Commentary on John, in substance).
magis: Catechism 641

Mary Magdalene and the holy women, who came to finish anointing the body, were the first to encounter the Risen One; thus the women were the first messengers of Christ's resurrection to the Apostles themselves (in substance).
Catechism 1442
Christ entrusted to his Apostles the ministry of reconciliation, and in the Church the sacrament of penance carries it forward (in substance).
Apostolorum Apostola

The decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship, 3 June 2016, raised the memorial of St Mary Magdalene in the Roman calendar to the rank of a feast, as the first witness of the Lord's resurrection and the apostle of the apostles (in substance).

2027-07-23.title: Ezekiel the Prophet · Friday of the ninth week after Pentecost
readings: He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son
“The one who endures to the end will be saved”: the beginning of the birth pangs and the good news to all nations
2027-07-23.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Ezekiel the Prophet (എസക്കിയേൽ നിബിയാ, the Panchangam's spelling), the last by date of the Old Testament saints whom it remembers this month, after Aaron, Elijah and Daniel. The Panchangam gives the readings of the weekday only.
2027-07-23.verse: But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
theo: Jesus is sitting on the Mount of Olives when the disciples come to him privately, saying: “Tell us, when will this be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?” He does not give them a timetable. He gives them a way to live: “Beware that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Messiah!’ and they will lead many astray. And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars; see that you are not alarmed; for this must take place, but the end is not yet.” Wars, famines and earthquakes are “but the beginning of the birth pangs”, which means that they are pains that lead to birth, not to death. Then comes the harder word about the disciples themselves: they will be hated, many will fall away, false prophets will arise, and “because of the increase of lawlessness, the love of many will grow cold.” In the floods that have come upon Kerala in recent years, we have seen both: fear, and also the warm love of neighbour for neighbour, the fishermen with their boats and the people who opened their churches and homes. Jesus says: “But the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the world, as a testimony to all the nations; and then the end will come.” The Church has never turned these words into a calendar. She hears in them a call to watchfulness, to endurance, and to mission.

Today the Panchangam remembers Ezekiel, a prophet for hard times. He was a priest, “Ezekiel son of Buzi,” who was carried into exile with the leaders of Judah, and in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, as he was “among the exiles by the river Chebar,” he writes, “the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.” He saw the glory of the Lord, not in the Temple in Jerusalem, but beside a canal in Babylon: the Lord had not been left behind in the ruined city, and he came to his people in exile. Ezekiel was told to eat a scroll, and he says: “Then I ate it; and in my mouth it was as sweet as honey.” The word of God is sweet even when it announces hard things. And he was made a sentinel: “Mortal, I have made you a sentinel for the house of Israel; whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.” The watchman on the wall is the picture of today's Gospel: beware, do not be led astray, stay awake. A watchman does not frighten people for the sake of it. He cries out so that they may live.

But Ezekiel is also the prophet of the new heart. To the exiles who thought that all was over, the Lord promised: “A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my spirit within you, and make you follow my statutes and be careful to observe my ordinances.” In the vision of the dry bones, the Lord asks: “Mortal, can these bones live?” and he commands the prophet to speak: “I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live.” The Church has long heard in this vision the promise of resurrection and of the gift of the Holy Spirit, which we remember in this season after Pentecost. At the end of the book, Ezekiel sees water flowing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east, growing into a river, so that “everything will live where the river goes.” In July in Kerala, when our rivers are full and the land is green, we know what a river can do for a dry land. The Fathers saw in this river baptism and the water that flowed from the side of Christ, and Saint John saw in the Book of Revelation “the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.”

Today's Epistle gives the ground of our endurance: “giving thanks to the Father, who has enabled you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.” The exiles in Babylon were transferred back to their land; we have been transferred into the kingdom of the Son by baptism. This is why we can endure to the end: our endurance does not rest on our own strength, but on what has already been done for us, the rescue, the transfer, the redemption. The Lord who spoke to the exiles by the river Chebar, who gave them a new heart and spoke of a river that heals, is the same Lord who tells us today: do not be alarmed. Let us ask him for the heart of flesh, for the watchfulness of the sentinel, and for the love that does not grow cold.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I hear bad news, do I become alarmed, or watchful?
Point 1 · Do not be led astray
Jesus gives no timetable; he gives a way to live in the birth pangs.
Point 2 · The sentinel
Ezekiel among the exiles by the river Chebar; sweet scroll and the watchman's duty to warn so that people may live.
Point 3 · A new heart and a river
The heart of flesh, the dry bones, the river that heals where it flows.
Point 4 · Rescued and transferred
Our endurance rests on what Christ has done; love that does not grow cold.
Take-home line
“the one who endures to the end will be saved”
live: Be watchful, not alarmed (Matthew 24:4, 6)
Before you share alarming news this week, check it, and pray; and do not let the news make you afraid.
Keep love warm (Matthew 24:12)
Do one act of generous love for a neighbour who is in need, especially if you are tempted to say that nobody cares any more.
Give thanks (Colossians 1:12)
Each evening this week, thank the Father for rescuing us from the power of darkness and bringing us into the kingdom of his Son.
2027-07-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sat on the Mount of Olives and taught your disciples to watch and to endure. We thank you for the prophet Ezekiel, who saw your glory among the exiles, who ate your word as sweet as honey, who was a sentinel for your people, and who promised a new heart and a river of life. Keep us from being led astray, and from alarm. Give us a heart of flesh, and let your love never grow cold in us. You have rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of your beloved Son; give us strength to endure to the end and to proclaim the good news to all the nations. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: From the side of Christ on the cross flowed blood and water, the river of life that Ezekiel saw coming from the temple; at the Holy Qurbono the Church drinks from that river, and the one who endures is fed with the Body and Blood of the Lord.
conn: The watchman.
Ezekiel 3:17 and 33:7: the prophet is made a sentinel for the house of Israel; Matthew 24:42: “Keep awake therefore, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.”
The new heart and the Spirit.

Ezekiel 36:26–27: “A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you”; Ezekiel 37:5: “I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live”; John 3:5 speaks of birth of water and Spirit.
The river of life.

Ezekiel 47:1, 9: water flows from below the threshold of the temple, and everything lives where the river goes; John 7:37–38: rivers of living water; Revelation 22:1–2: the river of the water of life.
fathers: St Gregory the Great

The watchman is set on a height so that he may see from afar; the one who is set over others to warn them must live above the common things of the earth, so that his words may help those who hear them (Homilies on Ezekiel, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

The Lord foretells wars and troubles so that the disciples may not be troubled when they come: he is giving them courage in advance, so that the trials may prove the strength of those who endure (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
magis: Catechism 715
Through the prophets, the Spirit prepares the people for the Messiah: God promises a new heart and a new spirit in the hearts of his people (in substance).
Catechism 673

Since the Ascension Christ's coming in glory has been imminent, even though it is not for us to know the times; this eschatological coming could be accomplished at any moment, and the Church waits and watches (in substance).
Catechism 162
Faith is a gift of God which he offers to us, but we can lose this priceless gift; to live, grow and persevere in the faith to the end, we must nourish it with the word of God (in substance).

2027-07-24.title: Saturday of the ninth week after Pentecost · St Sharbel
readings: With unveiled faces we are being transformed into the image of the Lord
The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head: follow me, and do not look back
2027-07-24.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Sharbel, the hermit of Lebanon (1828–1898), a saint of the Maronite Church, which like our own Church belongs to the West Syriac tradition.
2027-07-24.verse: all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another;
theo: St Paul puts two meetings with God side by side. When Moses came down from the mountain his face shone, and he covered it with a veil. Paul reads that veil as a sign: the glory on Moses' face was real, but it was passing, and it pointed ahead to a glory that does not fade. He writes as a son of Israel, with grief and love and no contempt; the Church still honours the Law and the Prophets as the word of God, and asks only to read them with Christ in view, for “only in Christ is it set aside.” Then comes the sentence at the heart of today's Epistle: “but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.” Turning is the whole work of the Christian life. Each morning we turn from our worries, our screens and our small resentments towards the face of the Lord, and as we turn, something is lifted from our eyes.

Paul goes on: “And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another; for this comes from the Lord, the Spirit.” This is a promise about prayer. We become like what we look at. A child who watches a screen all day begins to talk like the screen; a believer who looks every day at the face of Christ, in the Gospel, at the altar and in the poor, slowly begins to look like him. The change is not our own achievement. It “comes from the Lord, the Spirit,” who works quietly, from one degree of glory to the next, as a monsoon slowly turns a brown hillside green.

Today the Panchangam sets before us a man who spent his life looking at that face. Youssef Makhlouf was born in 1828 in the mountain village of Bekaa Kafra in Lebanon. At twenty-three he left home to become a monk at the monastery of St Maron at Annaya, and he took the name Sharbel, the name of an early Syriac martyr. He was ordained priest in 1859. In 1875, with the permission of his superiors, he went to the small hermitage of Sts Peter and Paul above the monastery, where he lived for twenty-three years in poverty, fasting, silence and prayer. According to his biographers he was stricken with a stroke while celebrating the Holy Qurbono in December 1898 and died on Christmas Eve; Pope Paul VI beatified him in 1965 and canonised him in 1977. His Church, the Maronite Church, shares with our own the Antiochene, West Syriac heritage, and its holy Qurbono is prayed in the same family of ancient rites. His feast is kept on 24 July because 24 December is the vigil of Christmas.

In the Gospel three would-be disciples meet the Lord on the road. To the first, who promises to follow wherever he goes, Jesus says that foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, “but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”: whoever follows him must be ready for a life whose only security is the Lord himself. To the second he says, “Follow me,” and when the man asks first to bury his father he answers, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” These are hard words, and they do not despise the fourth commandment; they say that when God calls, nothing may stand in front of him. To the third he says, “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Every farmer in the wet paddy knows that a ploughman who looks back cuts a crooked furrow. Not everyone is called to a hermitage, and the Church does not ask a father, a nurse or a teacher to leave home; but she asks every one of us to put a hand to the plow and not to look back, and to let the Lord come first in the house, the shop and the hospital ward.
outline: Opening
Ask: what do I look at most in a day, and what is it making me like?
Point 1 · The veil is taken away
Only in Christ is the veil removed; to turn to the Lord is the whole work of the Christian life.
Point 2 · Changed by looking
Beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, we are transformed from one degree of glory to the next.
Point 3 · St Sharbel, hermit of Annaya
Twenty-three years of silence and the Holy Qurbono: a life turned to the Lord.
Point 4 · Hand to the plow
The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; whoever follows him does not look back.
Take-home line
“Follow me.”
live: Turn to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:16)
Tomorrow morning, before you touch the phone, spend two minutes in silence before a crucifix or an icon and say: Lord, I turn to you.
Keep a quiet half hour (Mark 1:35)
This week set aside one half hour, early morning or late evening, with no screen and no talk, and give it to the Lord in the spirit of St Sharbel.
Do not look back (Luke 9:62)
Name one thing the Lord is asking of you that you keep postponing, and take its first step before Sunday.
2027-07-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the glory of the Father and the face in which we see him. Take away the veil that lies over our hearts, and turn our eyes to you every day. Through the prayers of St Sharbel, who sought you in silence and in the Holy Qurbono, teach us to love prayer, to follow you without looking back, and to be changed from one degree of glory to another by your Holy Spirit. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: St Sharbel prepared for the Holy Qurbono with long prayer and gave it the best hours of his day; at the altar the veil is lifted for all of us, for there the Lord who was hidden in Moses' cloud gives himself to be seen in faith, under the signs of bread and wine, as his Body and Blood.
conn: The veil of Moses.

2 Corinthians 3:13 looks back to Exodus 34:33–35: “When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil on his face”; he lifted it whenever he went in before the Lord, and Paul sees in this the pattern of turning to the Lord.
Seeing the face of God.

2 Corinthians 4:6: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”; the hermit's whole life is a gaze towards that face, and Matthew 5:8 promises that “the pure in heart” will see God.
Elisha at the plow.

Luke 9:61–62 recalls 1 Kings 19:19–21, where Elijah calls Elisha from the plow; Elisha asks to kiss his father and mother, and then follows; the Lord of the Gospel asks for an even more undivided following. The Panchangam remembers Elijah the Prophet on 20 July.
fathers: St Isaac of Nineveh

Love silence above everything, for it brings a fruit that the tongue cannot describe; at first we must force ourselves to love it, but afterwards a joy is born from it which draws us on (Ascetical Homilies, in substance).
St Augustine
You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Confessions 1.1, in substance).
magis: Catechism 920

Hermits, without always professing the three evangelical counsels, devote their life to the praise of God and the salvation of the world through a stricter separation from the world, the silence of solitude, and assiduous prayer and penance (in substance).
Catechism 2715
Contemplation is a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus: a farmer of Ars used to say before the tabernacle, “I look at him and he looks at me”; this gaze is a renunciation of self (in substance).
Catechism 2717
Contemplative prayer is silence, the symbol of the world to come, or silent love; in it words are not speeches but twigs that feed the fire of love (in substance).

2027-07-26.title: Monday of the tenth week after Pentecost
readings: Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret
“Jerusalem, Jerusalem”: Jesus longs to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings
2027-07-26.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. In other calendars of the Church the parents of the Virgin Mary, Sts Joachim and Anne, are remembered on 26 July.
2027-07-26.verse: For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, but worldly grief produces death.
theo: Today's Epistle is a letter of relief after a hard season. Paul had written to the Corinthians a sharp letter that caused them pain, and for a while he wondered whether he had done right. Then Titus came back with good news, and Paul could say, “I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.” In the middle of that joy he explains why the pain was worth it: “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, but worldly grief produces death.” There are two kinds of sorrow over sin. Worldly grief looks inward: it sulks, it makes excuses, it blames others, it sinks into shame and self-pity, and in the end it leaves a person more alone. Godly grief looks upward: it says, “I have sinned,” and gets up and goes to the one who forgives. Peter wept bitterly and came back to the Lord; the same night Judas was sorry too, but he looked at his sin and not at his Master, and despair finished what sin began. Paul lists what godly grief produced in Corinth: “what earnestness … what eagerness to clear yourselves … what longing, what zeal.” A good confession leaves us lighter, more alive and more eager to love.

In the Gospel some Pharisees come to Jesus with a warning: “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” They may be sincere friends. Jesus is not frightened. He calls Herod “that fox” and says that he will go on “casting out demons and performing cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I finish my work.” He is not on Herod's timetable but on his Father's, and the road runs to Jerusalem, “because it is impossible for a prophet to be killed outside of Jerusalem.” Luke has already told us that “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). Then the voice of the Lord changes from calm to tender: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” This is the lament of a son of Israel who loves the holy city. The Church teaches that what was done in his Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time or against the Jewish people today (Nostra Aetate 4); the Gospel shows how deeply the Lord loved the city to the end.

In Kerala we have all seen a hen when the monsoon rain comes down: she spreads her wings and the chicks run in, until only small beaks and feet show from beneath her. That is how God longs to gather us, and the sentence that grieves him is the last one: “you were not willing.” God is never unwilling; the only closed door is ours. Godly grief is simply the moment when we stop being unwilling and run under the wings. The passage ends with a promise: you will see him “when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’” At every Holy Qurbono we say it, and he comes.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I fall, do I run away from God or towards him?
Point 1 · Two kinds of sorrow
Worldly grief turns inward and leads to death; godly grief turns to God and leads to salvation.
Point 2 · The fox and the road
Jesus follows his Father's timetable to Jerusalem, unafraid of Herod.
Point 3 · The hen and her brood
God longs to gather us; the only barrier is “you were not willing.”
Take-home line
Let him gather you today.
live: Choose godly grief (2 Corinthians 7:10)
Think of one failing you have been brooding over and take it to the Sacrament of Reconciliation this week, instead of carrying it alone.
Run under his wings (Luke 13:34)
When you feel afraid or ashamed today, stop and pray one sentence: Lord, gather me.
2027-07-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you longed to gather the children of Jerusalem as a hen gathers her brood, and you long to gather us. Turn our sorrow for sin into the sorrow that leads to life, and make us willing to come to you. Give us the courage to follow you on the road you walked, unafraid of the fox, and let us live under the shelter of your wings. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church sings the welcome that Jerusalem sang: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the one who longs to gather his children under his wings gives himself to us as the bread of life.

2027-07-27.title: Tuesday of the tenth week after Pentecost
readings: We walk by faith, not by sight, and make it our aim to please the Lord
The barren fig tree: the gardener asks for one more year
2027-07-27.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Malayalam month of Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest rain, is under way.
2027-07-27.verse: for we walk by faith, not by sight.
theo: St Paul is writing about confidence, and the odd thing is that he is writing from a place where nothing can be seen. “So we are always confident; even though we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Anyone who has crossed a flooded paddy field at night along the narrow bund will know what he means. You cannot see the whole path; a small lamp shows the next step and the next, and you walk because you trust that the ground is there. Faith is that walk. Paul is not despising the body, which God made and will raise; he is saying that, as long as we live in it, we know the Lord by trust and not yet by sight, and that this is enough for courage. Because the end is the Lord, he gives life a single aim: “whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.” And he adds a sober reminder: “For all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.” We do not meet a stranger there. We meet the Christ who loved us and gave himself for us.

The Gospel puts a picture beside the aim to please him: a fig tree planted in a vineyard, which the owner has watched for three years and found without fruit. “Cut it down! Why should it be wasting the soil?” In our own compounds the picture is easy to see: a jackfruit or mango tree that gets the best of the soil and the rain and never bears. The tree is every one of us, and the soil that it wastes is the time, the gifts and the grace that God has given. Jesus told this parable immediately after speaking of repentance, when he said that unless people repent they will all perish (Luke 13:1–5). The fruit that he looks for is a changed life: the fruit of the Spirit, which is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

Then the gardener speaks, and the whole story turns on his voice: “Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it. If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.” The Church has long heard in these words the voice of Christ, who stands between us and judgment and asks for time. He does not ask the owner to ignore the barren tree; he promises to work: to dig around it, loosen the hard ground and feed it. And note what he feeds it with: the manure. God does not waste even the refuse of our lives, our failures and our humiliations; in his hands they become what makes us fruitful. The one more year is today, for “now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” In the lean, rainy weeks of Karkidakam our grandparents used to say that the tree you tend now feeds the house next year. Let us not waste the year that the Lord asks for us.
outline: Opening
Ask: if the owner of the vineyard came to my life today, what fruit would he find?
Point 1 · We walk by faith
A small lamp for the next step: trust in the Lord, whom we do not yet see.
Point 2 · Our aim to please him
Whether at home or away, we aim to please the Lord, before whose judgment seat we all stand.
Point 3 · One more year
The gardener asks for time, digs and feeds the tree; the time is now.
Take-home line
Let the Gardener work on you today.
live: Take the next step by faith (2 Corinthians 5:7)
Choose one decision you have delayed because you cannot see the whole road, and take its first step today in prayer.
Bear one fruit (Luke 13:9)
Name one fruit of the Spirit that is missing in you, patience or kindness for example, and practise it with one person today.
2027-07-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the Gardener who asks for one more year for each of us. Give us the faith to walk when we cannot see, and the aim to please you in all things. Dig around our hardness, feed us with your grace, and make us bear the fruit of love, so that when we stand before your judgment seat we may hear: Well done. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono faith sees what the eyes cannot: the bread and the wine are the Body and Blood of Christ, and the fruit of his sacrifice feeds us so that we may bear fruit that lasts.

2027-07-28.title: Wednesday of the tenth week after Pentecost · Morth Alphonsa
readings: “It is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me”
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain
2027-07-28.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam prints, in bold, Morth Alphonsa (St Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, 1910–1946), a Franciscan Clarist sister of Bharananganam in Kerala and a daughter of the Syro-Malabar Church. In the Syriac tradition a woman saint is called Morth, “my lady”.
2027-07-28.verse: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
theo: In three verses St Paul tells us where the centre of his life has moved. “For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.” He does not say that his person has been wiped out; he says that the centre has changed, that someone else has taken the first place. Every human being has a centre, and the question of the whole spiritual life is who or what stands there. Then Paul says something that no theory could say: “And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” Notice the small word me. The cross was not only for the world in general; it was for him, by name, and it is for each of us. Everything therefore is grace: “I do not nullify the grace of God.” We do not earn a place at the centre; Christ takes it, because he loves us.

In the Gospel Jesus says the same thing in the language of the field: “Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Every farmer in Kerala knows what happens to the seed that is sown in the wet earth of the monsoon. For some days nothing shows; the seed seems to have rotted and disappeared; then one morning the first green shoots come up, and later the field is full. Jesus says this first about himself: the Cross is the grain that falls into the earth, and the Resurrection is the harvest. Then he says it about his disciples: “Those who love their life lose it, and those who hate their life in this world will keep it for eternal life. Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.” This is not contempt for life, which is God's gift; it is a refusal to clutch at it. The disciple goes where Jesus goes, to the Cross, and through the Cross to the Father, who honours those who serve his Son.

Today the Panchangam prints the name of Morth Alphonsa in bold. Anna Muttathupadathu was born on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor near Kottayam, in a Syro-Malabar Christian family. Her mother died when she was only a few months old, and she grew up among her mother's relatives, who loved her. From her girlhood she wanted nothing except to belong wholly to Christ, and, according to the accounts of her life, when a marriage was being arranged for her she injured her foot so that the plan would be dropped; the Church does not hold this up as an example to copy, but it shows how single-hearted her love was. In 1927 she entered the Franciscan Clarist convent at Bharananganam and took the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception. Then came long years of illness, which she spent in prayer and patience; the sisters who nursed her remembered that she never complained, and that she smiled. She made her perpetual vows in 1936 and died on 28 July 1946, aged thirty-five. Pope John Paul II beatified her at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her on 12 October 2008, the first woman of Indian origin to be named a saint. Her tomb at Bharananganam draws thousands of pilgrims a year, many from other Churches and other faiths, and in these rainy days of Karkidakam they come to keep her feast.

Alphonsa did not go looking for suffering; it came to her, and she handed it to the Lord. That is the difference between the grain of wheat and waste: the grain falls into the earth for love. Lying on her sickbed she lived what Paul describes: Christ was living in her, and the life she lived she lived by faith in the Son of God who loved her and gave himself for her. The Church teaches that Christ, by his passion and death, has given a new meaning to suffering, so that it can unite us with his redemptive Passion (Catechism 1505). Her hidden life, which looked like a long waiting, has borne a harvest that she could not have imagined, and it speaks to all who are sick, to all who care for them, and to everyone whose plans have been broken. We honour her not by admiring her pain but by learning her trust, and we ask her, as one of the saints who have finished the journey, to pray for us (Catechism 956).
outline: Opening
Ask: who or what stands at the centre of my life?
Point 1 · Christ lives in me
Paul's life has a new centre: the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me.
Point 2 · The grain of wheat
The seed falls into the earth and dies, and bears much fruit; the Cross is the seed and the Resurrection the harvest.
Point 3 · Morth Alphonsa
From Kudamaloor to Bharananganam: a hidden life of prayer, illness and patience.
Point 4 · Suffering given in love
Pain united with the Passion of Christ is never wasted.
Take-home line
“If it dies, it bears much fruit.”
live: Put Christ at the centre (Galatians 2:20)
Begin each day this week with the prayer: Lord Jesus, live in me today.
Serve the sick (John 12:26)
Visit, ring or write to one person who is ill, in hospital or at home, and give them an hour of your time this week.
Offer a small pain (Colossians 1:24)
When a small pain or inconvenience comes today, offer it in one sentence of prayer for someone you name.
2027-07-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, grain of wheat fallen into the earth, you died and rose to bear fruit for the whole world. Through the prayers of Morth Alphonsa, who gave you her pain and her whole life, make us live no longer for ourselves but for you who loved us and gave yourself for us. Comfort all who are sick, strengthen those who care for them, and bring our hidden sacrifices to a harvest of joy. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono bread made from wheat and wine made from the vine are placed on the altar and become the Body and Blood of the Lord who fell into the earth and rose; St Alphonsa is remembered for her devotion to the Holy Eucharist, and at the altar every hidden pain offered in love is joined to his offering.
conn: For me, to live is Christ.
Philippians 1:21: “For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain”; the Epistle's “it is Christ who lives in me” says the same thing in another letter.
What you sow must die.
1 Corinthians 15:36: “What you sow does not come to life unless it dies”; Paul uses the Lord's picture of the seed for the resurrection of the body.
Serving and following.
John 12:26 is the Gospel of the servant; Romans 8:17 adds that we suffer with him “so that we may also be glorified with him”.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch
I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found the pure bread of Christ (Letter to the Romans 4, in substance).
St Augustine
The grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died is the Lord himself; he rose and bore much fruit, and we, the Church, are that harvest (Tractates on John 51, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1505
By his passion and death on the cross Christ has given a new meaning to suffering: it can henceforth configure us to him and unite us with his redemptive Passion (in substance).
Catechism 618

The Cross is the unique sacrifice of Christ, yet he wants to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who were its first beneficiaries; each one of us is called to take up his cross and follow him (in substance).
Catechism 956
The saints in heaven do not cease to intercede with the Father for us; their brotherly concern is of the greatest help to our weakness (in substance).

2027-07-29.title: Thursday of the tenth week after Pentecost · Martha, Mary and Lazarus of Bethany
readings: Let mutual love continue: do not neglect hospitality to strangers
Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, and Mary sits at his feet
2027-07-29.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam prints, in bold, Martha, Mary and Lazarus of Bethany (ബഥനിയിലെ മർത്തായും മറിയവും ലാസറും), the friends of Jesus whose home at Bethany received him. Luke does not name their village; John does, and the Church has long read the two Gospels together.
2027-07-29.verse: Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.
theo: The letter to the Hebrews ends with plain, practical love, and the first words are the oldest rule of the household: “Let mutual love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.” The writer is thinking of Abraham and Sarah at the oaks of Mamre, who ran out to three travellers in the noon heat, brought water and bread and a calf, and found that they had received God's own messengers. The letter goes on: remember those in prison as if you were in prison with them; let marriage be honoured by all; be content with what you have, “for he has said, ‘I will never leave you or forsake you.’” Then comes the confident cry of the one who has nothing and fears nothing: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can anyone do to me?” A home where love is steady, where the stranger is welcome and the poor are not forgotten, is a small Church. It is such a home that the Gospel puts before us today.

“Now as they went on their way, he entered a certain village, where a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home.” Luke says that Martha was the host, the one who opened the door, and we should not forget that before we hear her scolded. The Church has sometimes been unfair to Martha. She did what the Letter to the Hebrews asks: she welcomed a traveller, and she wanted the best for him. Her fault was not in serving; it was in being “worried and distracted by many things.” Her sister Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to what he was saying,” the place of a disciple at the feet of a teacher; Saul of Tarsus was brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel”. That Jesus accepts a woman in the disciple's place is itself a quiet revolution. When Martha asks him to send Mary to help, he does not rebuke her harshly; he calls her name twice, as one calls someone dear: “Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things; there is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

John fills in the rest of the picture. He names the village, Bethany, “the village of Mary and her sister Martha,” about two miles from Jerusalem, and he tells us in a single sentence how the Lord regarded this house: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” When Lazarus died, it was Martha who ran to meet the Lord on the road, and it was to Martha that he spoke the words that every funeral still repeats: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” And Martha answered with a confession as great as Peter's: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” Then Mary came and fell at his feet, Jesus began to weep, and Lazarus was called out of the tomb. At a supper in the same house some days later Martha was serving again, without complaint now, and Mary anointed his feet with costly perfume until “the house was filled with the fragrance.” The sisters who seem so different are two halves of one discipleship. Mary of Bethany should not be confused with Mary Magdalene, whom the Church remembered on 22 July.

The Church needs both houses of Bethany. Without Martha there would be no table, no school, no hospital, no one to open the door in the monsoon night; without Mary the table would have nothing to serve, for the one thing needed is to know who is sitting at it. Archbishop Mar Ivanios founded Bethany Ashram in 1919, and its name recalls the house at Bethany, a place where welcome and prayer belong together. In our own homes the lesson is easy to apply. In Kerala no visitor comes to the door without being offered water at least, and in the rains a traveller sheltering on the veranda is a guest of God. But when the guest is Jesus himself, hospitality begins with listening. At the Holy Qurbono the two halves of Bethany meet: first we sit at his feet to hear the Word, and then we are brought to his table, where he serves us himself with his own Body and Blood.
outline: Opening
Ask: when the Lord comes to my house, am I busy for him or with him?
Point 1 · The welcome
Hebrews 13: love, hospitality to strangers, content with what we have.
Point 2 · The one thing needed
Mary at the Lord's feet; Martha called by name, not scolded.
Point 3 · The friends of Jesus
Bethany: Martha's faith, Mary's tears and perfume, Lazarus raised.
Point 4 · Work and prayer together
Bethany Ashram and our own homes: welcome and prayer belong together.
Take-home line
“Mary has chosen the better part.”
live: Welcome someone (Hebrews 13:2)
Invite someone who is alone, a neighbour, a new family or a visitor to the parish, for tea or a meal this week.
Sit at his feet (Luke 10:39)
Before the first task tomorrow, read the Gospel of the day for five minutes in silence and listen to what the Lord says to you.
Serve without grumbling (John 12:2)
Do one task at home today, with no complaint and a prayer, as done for the Lord.
2027-07-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, friend of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, you were welcomed into their home at Bethany and you wept at their grief. Come into our homes. Make us welcoming to every stranger, attentive to your word, and faithful in service. Teach us the one thing that is needed, that we may sit at your feet and rise to serve, and bring us at last to the house where there is no more death. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the two halves of Bethany meet: we sit first at the Lord's feet to listen to the Word, as Mary did, and then we are brought to his table, where he serves us himself with his own Body and Blood, and sends us out to serve.
conn: Abraham's welcome.
Hebrews 13:2 recalls Genesis 18, where Abraham says to the three travellers at Mamre: “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant.”
At the feet of the teacher.
Luke 10:39: Mary “sat at the Lord's feet”; Acts 22:3 shows Paul as “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel”, the posture of a disciple.
The confession of Martha.
John 11:27: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world”: the active sister makes the great confession of faith, as Peter does at Caesarea Philippi.
fathers: St Augustine

Martha's task is good, but Mary's is better, for Martha's work will pass away with this life, while what Mary has chosen will not be taken from her; yet we are all both Martha and Mary, until we come to the home where we shall only rejoice in the Lord (Sermon 104, in substance).
St Benedict of Nursia
Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ, for he himself will say: I was a stranger and you took me in (Rule 53, in substance).
magis: Catechism 994
Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life”; Christ himself will raise up on the last day those who have believed in him (in substance).
Catechism 2447
The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily needs; to welcome the stranger is among them (in substance).
Catechism 2745
Prayer and Christian life are inseparable, for they concern the same love and the same renunciation, which proceeds from love (in substance).

2027-07-30.title: Friday of the tenth week after Pentecost
readings: You are children of the light and of the day: let us keep awake and be sober
At daybreak Jesus goes to a deserted place, and then goes on to proclaim the kingdom to other cities
2027-07-30.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-07-30.verse: for you are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.
theo: Paul begins this passage by saying that he has no need to write about “the times and the seasons.” The Thessalonians were anxious about when the Lord would return, and some seem to have been neglecting their daily work (compare 2 Thessalonians 3:11). Paul does not give a date. He gives a picture that every household knows: “you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” A thief sends no notice; no one who is ready for him is troubled when he comes. The people who are caught are those who say, “There is peace and security,” and have settled down comfortably on their own foundations, as though nothing could shake the house. We have seen in Kerala how fast a calm monsoon morning can turn into a flood. Security that depends on our own arrangements is thin. The security of the believer is of another kind, and Paul states it as a fact about who we are: “But you, beloved, are not in darkness, for that day to surprise you like a thief; for you are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.”

From that identity Paul draws a single instruction: “So then let us not fall asleep as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.” To keep awake is not to live in fear or to be forever scanning the sky. It means to be alert in the Lord, the opposite of the sleep of routine, in which days pass one after another and nothing is asked and nothing is given. To be sober is to keep a clear head, not dulled by the noise of news, by money or by pleasure. Paul goes on a few verses further to give the reason for the confidence: God “has destined us not for wrath but for obtaining salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep we may live with him.” The Day is not a trap but a meeting with the One who died for us. The early morning, with the first bell of the church, the first fishing boats going out and the first tea stalls opening, is the most natural picture of the Christian life: we live as people who are up before the light because we are expecting someone.

In the Gospel the first one awake is the Lord himself. The evening before, the whole town of Capernaum had crowded around the door with its sick; and now, “at daybreak he departed and went into a deserted place.” The Gospel of Mark tells us what he did there: he prayed (Mark 1:35). When the crowds find him and “wanted to prevent him from leaving them,” he answers, “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.” It would have been easy to stay where he was loved and needed. But he lives by his mission, not by popularity, and his mission comes from prayer: before he speaks to the people he speaks to the Father. Christians who keep awake are those who begin the day as he did and then go where they are sent, to the next town, the next ward, the next neighbour. “So he continued proclaiming the message in the synagogues of Judea.” The kingdom is not kept in one village; it goes on.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I awake in the Lord, or asleep in routine?
Point 1 · Children of light
We belong to the day; no thief of the night can surprise those who are ready.
Point 2 · Awake and sober
Alertness and a clear head, in confidence that God has destined us for salvation.
Point 3 · The Lord at daybreak
He prays in a deserted place, and then goes on to the other cities, for he was sent.
Take-home line
“Let us keep awake and be sober.”
live: Rise before the noise (Luke 4:42)
Get up ten minutes earlier tomorrow, before the phone and the news, and give those minutes to prayer.
Keep a clear head (1 Thessalonians 5:6)
Choose one thing that dulls you, too much news or screen time, and put it aside for one day this week.
2027-07-30.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you rose at daybreak and went to a deserted place to pray, and you went on to the other cities because you were sent. Keep us awake and sober, children of light and of the day. Let no thief of the night find us asleep, and send us where you wish, so that whether we are awake or asleep we may live with you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church keeps vigil for the Lord's coming: we proclaim his death, we confess his resurrection, and we wait in hope for his coming again, awake and sober, as children of the day.

2027-07-31.title: Saturday of the tenth week after Pentecost · St Ignatius of Loyola
readings: Do everything for the glory of God; be imitators of me, as I am of Christ
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple: first count the cost
2027-07-31.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), the founder of the Society of Jesus, a saint of the Latin Church, whose companion St Francis Xavier brought the Gospel to the coast of India.
2027-07-31.verse: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
theo: St Paul has been answering a question about meat that had been offered to idols, and at the end he lifts the whole discussion to a height: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” Nothing is too small for this. The meal, the work, the journey, the hours of the day that no one sees can be offered to God and made into praise. Paul then adds a rule for the common life: “Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved.” He seeks the good of others, in the hope that they will be saved. And the model is not himself but the Lord: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” An imitator is not a copy but a pupil, one who has watched someone close to Christ and has learned how to walk.

The Gospel is harder. Large crowds are travelling with Jesus, and he turns and speaks to them without softening anything: “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.” The word “hate” is the strong speech of the East, which the Lord himself explains elsewhere: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). He asks for the first place, not for the destruction of the family; the love of father and mother is a commandment, but no love may stand in the way of Christ. Then he gives two small stories: the builder who “does not first sit down and estimate the cost” and is laughed at when he cannot finish the tower, and the king who counts his ten thousand against twenty thousand and sends for the terms of peace. The Lord is not driving the crowd away; he wants them to choose with open eyes. Following him is neither a mood nor a bargain. “None of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.”

Both readings come alive in St Ignatius of Loyola. Íñigo López was born in 1491 in the Basque country of Spain, the youngest of a large noble family, and trained to be a soldier. In 1521 a cannonball broke his leg at the siege of Pamplona. During the long weeks of recovery he asked for adventure stories, and in the castle there were only a life of Christ and the lives of the saints. He noticed that when he dreamed of fame he felt empty afterwards, but when he thought of doing for God what the saints had done he stayed content. That was the beginning of his conversion. At Manresa he prayed and wrote the notes that became the Spiritual Exercises, he went as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, and in Paris he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber. On the hill of Montmartre in 1534 they made their vows together. Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, and Ignatius, elected its first Superior General, spent his last years in Rome writing letters and its constitutions. He died on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622 together with Francis Xavier. His motto, taken from today's Epistle, is Ad maiorem Dei gloriam: to the greater glory of God.

The Exercises begin with the sentence that sums up what Paul says: human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God, and by this means to save their souls. Everything else is for the sake of that end. Ignatius taught people to find God in all things, to look back each evening on the day in a short prayer called the examen, and to weigh in prayer the choices of their lives; this is how he put into practice Jesus' call to estimate the cost before building. His friend Xavier reached Goa in 1542 and travelled the coast of India. He went among the fishing villages in the south, including the shore of Travancore, and he is known to have prayed at Mylapore, where the tradition of the Thomas Christians places the tomb of the Apostle Thomas, so the first Jesuit of India honoured the same Apostle whom we remembered on 3 July. Many of our own children and grandchildren have studied in schools and colleges that Jesuits founded in Kerala. The lesson of Ignatius is for every one of us, in every state of life: ask what the Lord wants, count the cost, and then give the work, the meal and the ordinary day to the greater glory of God.
outline: Opening
Ask: for whose glory do I do the ordinary things of my day?
Point 1 · Everything for the glory of God
Eating, drinking, working: nothing is too small to be offered to God.
Point 2 · Count the cost
The tower and the king: Jesus asks the crowd to choose with open eyes.
Point 3 · St Ignatius of Loyola
From the cannonball at Pamplona to the Society of Jesus: a soldier who found a greater cause.
Point 4 · Imitators of Christ
Carry the cross and follow him; Francis Xavier in India.
Take-home line
Ad maiorem Dei gloriam: to the greater glory of God.
live: Offer the ordinary (1 Corinthians 10:31)
Before one meal and one task today, say: To the greater glory of God.
Make the examen (Luke 14:28)
Tonight, spend five minutes looking back over the day: give thanks, ask pardon, and name one thing to do better tomorrow.
Count the cost (Luke 14:28)
Think about one good work you have started, and ask honestly whether you have what it needs to finish it; if not, ask the Lord for it.
2027-07-31.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you called St Ignatius from the battlefield to follow you, and you made him a servant of your greater glory. Teach us to do everything, eating and drinking and all our work, for the glory of God. Help us to count the cost and to carry the cross, that we may be your true disciples and imitators of you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: St Ignatius celebrated the Mass with deep reverence, and often with tears; at the Holy Qurbono the whole life of the believer is brought to the altar and offered to the glory of the Father, together with the offering of the Son.
conn: Whatever you do.

Colossians 3:17: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him”; Paul says in two letters that the whole of life is a liturgy.
The cross every day.
Luke 9:23: “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me”; Luke 14:27 repeats the demand before a great crowd.
What does it profit?

Matthew 16:26: “For what will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life?” According to tradition St Ignatius kept repeating this verse to Francis Xavier in Paris, and it changed his life.
fathers: St Gregory the Great

We are told to hate our kin by refusing to follow them when they would turn us away from God, and yet to love them as our neighbours; in this way we hate and love at the same time (Homilies on the Gospels 37, in substance).
St Ignatius of Loyola
Human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save their souls (Spiritual Exercises 23, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2427

Human work proceeds from persons made in the image of God, and by enduring the hardship of work in union with Jesus man collaborates in a certain way with the Son of God in his redemptive work (in substance).
Catechism 2232
Family ties are important but not absolute: as the child grows towards maturity, his vocation from God is to be respected, and the call of Christ comes first (in substance).
Catechism 2013
All Christians, in any state or walk of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity (in substance).

quick: Thomas moved from doubt to the greatest confession: “My Lord and my God!”
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
Thomas, according to our tradition, brought the Gospel to India: he is our father in faith.
2027-07-03.action: Say “My Lord and my God” at the elevation during Holy Qurbono.
2027-07-03.question: Do I bring my doubts to Jesus, or walk away with them?
2027-07-03.special: Dukrono of St Thomas the Apostle (Saturday): Holy Qurbono for the people.
illus: An illustration

Seven and a half churches are linked by tradition with St Thomas in Kerala: Kodungallur, Palayur, Kottakkavu, Kokkamangalam, Niranam, Nilackal, Kollam and Thiruvithamcode. For almost two thousand years families have handed on the faith from parents to children. We are the fruit of one apostle's courage.

family.explain: Thomas said he would only believe if he could touch Jesus' wounds. When Jesus came, Thomas said: “My Lord and my God!” Later he came to India and told our ancestors about Jesus.
family.intention: We thank God for St Thomas and pray for the Church in India.
family.ask: Ask: “What questions do we have about God? Let's ask Jesus together.”

kidsaint: St Thomas the Apostle

Thomas was brave: when Jesus went toward danger he said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16). He had doubts, but when he met the risen Jesus he believed with all his heart, and according to tradition he travelled all the way to India. Lesson: honest questions can lead to strong faith.
term: Dukrono
Syriac for “remembrance, commemoration”: the feast of a saint, especially the anniversary of death or the translation of relics. The Dukrono of St Thomas is kept on 3 July.
termMore: The ancient name of the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, who trace their faith to the preaching of St Thomas. The Syro-Malankara and Syro-Malabar Churches are both heirs of this tradition.

quick: “A house divided against itself cannot stand”: Satan divides, Christ unites.
The sin against the Spirit is refusing God's mercy; guard your words.
“He is our peace”: Christ breaks down every dividing wall.
2027-07-04.action: Take one concrete step toward reconciliation in your family or parish this week.
2027-07-04.question: Where am I contributing to division, and where can I build peace?
illus: An illustration

In many Kerala villages two branches of one ancient Thomas Christian family worship in different churches across the same road. When they pray together at a funeral or a wedding, people say: this is how it should always be. Christ came to break down dividing walls.

family.explain: Jesus says a house where people fight against each other cannot stand. Families are strong when they forgive and stay together.
family.intention: We pray for peace and unity in our family.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone in our family we need to make peace with?”

kidsaint: St Maria Goretti (6 July)

An Italian girl of eleven who was attacked and mortally wounded by a young man named Alessandro. Before she died she forgave him. Years later he repented, and was present when she was declared a saint. Lesson: forgiveness can change even a hard heart.
term: Sin against the Holy Spirit
The “unforgivable” sin of Mark 3:29: not a sin too big for God's mercy, but the deliberate, final refusal of that mercy, which closes the heart to forgiveness (CCC 1864).
termMore: In the Syro-Malankara Qurbono the peace (Shlomo) is passed from the altar through the congregation before the anaphora, as a sign of reconciliation before offering the sacrifice (Matthew 5:23–24).

quick: “The word of God is living and active”: Christ speaks when the Gospel is proclaimed.
Good soil hears the word, accepts it, and bears fruit a hundredfold.
Jesus is a high priest who understands our weakness: approach with boldness.
2027-07-11.action: Read the Sunday Gospel again for ten minutes each day this week.
2027-07-11.question: Do I really listen when God's word is read?
2027-07-11.special: Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. Thursday 15 July: Commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios, Holy Qurbono for the people.
illus: An illustration

In many Kerala homes the Bible is placed on a stand with a lamp beside it, honoured like a guest. Honouring the Book is good; opening it every day is better. The word works only in the heart that listens.

family.explain: God's word is alive! When we read the Bible, God speaks to our hearts like a friend.
family.intention: We pray to listen to God's word every day.
family.ask: Ask: “What did God say to us in today's Gospel?”

catechism: Scripture in the life of the Church.
The common priesthood of the faithful.
kidsaint: St Benedict (11 July)
A young man who left the noisy city to pray in a cave, and later founded monasteries where monks prayed and worked. His Rule begins with the word “Listen.” Lesson: to hear God, we need quiet hearts.
term: Evangelion
In the Syro-Malankara Qurbono the Gospel (Evangelion) is proclaimed by the priest with candles and incense, and the people stand, because Christ himself speaks.
termMore: All the baptised share in Christ's priesthood (1 Peter 2:9): they offer their lives, prayers and work as spiritual sacrifices. This common priesthood differs in essence, not only in degree, from the ministerial priesthood of bishops and priests (Lumen Gentium 10).

quick: “Remember your leaders… imitate their faith.”
Mar Ivanios sought the unity of the Church and entered communion with Peter in 1930, keeping our liturgy.
Like the faithful servant, he traded the talents he received.
2027-07-15.action: Pray each day this week for the unity of the Churches in Kerala.
2027-07-15.question: What would I be ready to give up for the truth and unity of the Church?
2027-07-15.special: Commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios (Thursday): Holy Qurbono for the people. Pilgrimage to St Mary's Cathedral, Pattom.
illus: An illustration

After the reunion of 1930 Mar Ivanios and his companions had no cathedral and no properties. They celebrated the Qurbono in sheds and borrowed rooms. Today the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church has eparchies across India and in the diaspora. The seed sown in poverty grew.

family.explain: We remember good leaders who taught us about God, like Mar Ivanios, who gave up a lot so that our Church could be united with the Pope.
family.intention: We pray for our Church and for the unity of all Christians.
family.ask: Ask: “Who taught us about God? Let's thank God for them.”

kidsaint: Archbishop Mar Ivanios

A clever teacher who loved to pray and started a community called Bethany. He wanted all Christians to be one family with the Pope, and in 1930 he joined the Catholic Church even though he lost his churches and money. Lesson: love Jesus and his Church more than comfort.
term: Reunion Movement
The movement led by Mar Ivanios through which, in 1930, part of the Malankara Church entered full communion with the Catholic Church while keeping its West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy and traditions.
termMore: The Order of the Imitation of Christ (Bethany Ashram), founded by Mar Ivanios in 1919, and the Sisters of the Imitation of Christ (Bethany Madhom), founded in 1925: religious communities of the Syro-Malankara Church devoted to prayer, education and mission.

quick: “Those who humble themselves will be exalted”: let God choose our place.
Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest: God is patient.
The kingdom grows from small hidden things, like mustard seed and yeast.
2027-07-18.action: Let someone else go first each day this week.
2027-07-18.question: Where am I seeking the highest place?
2027-07-18.special: Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. Announce the Fifteen Days' Fast (Shunoyo Nombu) from 1 August.
illus: An illustration

A Kerala farmer who pulls the young weeds from a paddy field too early tears out the rice seedlings with them. He waits until both are grown and the difference is clear. God is the wise farmer of our hearts and of his Church.

family.explain: Jesus says not to rush for the best seat. Be humble, and God will lift you up.
family.intention: We pray for humble hearts.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we let others go first this week?”

kidsaint: St Mary Magdalene (22 July)

Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus who stayed near the cross when others ran away. On Easter morning she was the first to see the risen Jesus, and he sent her to tell the apostles. Lesson: Jesus loves humble, faithful hearts.
term: Shunoyo Nombu
The Fifteen Days' Fast (1–15 August) kept by the Syro-Malankara Church before the feast of the Shunoyo, the Assumption (Dormition) of the Mother of God into heaven.
termMore: Matthew 13 gathers seven parables: the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast, the treasure, the pearl and the net. Together they show that the kingdom begins small and hidden, grows by God's power, and is completed at the harvest.

quick: “Unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom.”
Do not despise the little ones; their angels see the Father's face.
“If you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord… you will be saved.”
2027-07-25.action: Thank your children's Sunday School teacher this week.
2027-07-25.question: In what way do I need to become more like a child before God?
2027-07-25.special: Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. (In 2025–26: Sunday School Day; collection and cover collection for children's faith formation. Check your eparchy's circular.) The Fifteen Days' Fast begins next Sunday, 1 August.
illus: An illustration

In Kerala parishes thousands of young people give up their Sunday mornings to teach catechism to children for no pay. One former student, now a doctor, said: “I forgot my school teachers' names, but I never forgot the teacher who taught me to pray.”

family.explain: Jesus put a child in the middle of the grown-ups and said: be like this child! Children trust God like a little one trusts mum and dad.
family.intention: We pray for all children and for those who teach them the faith.
family.ask: Ask: “What can grown-ups learn from children about trusting God?”

catechism: Parents as first teachers of the faith.
kidsaint: St Alphonsa (28 July)

A sister from Bharananganam in Kerala who was often sick and suffered a lot, but offered everything to Jesus with a smile. She loved children and prayed for everyone. She was the first woman from India to be declared a saint (2008). Lesson: we can offer our pains to Jesus with love.
term: Sunday School

The parish faith-formation programme in which children and teenagers learn the Bible, prayers, the sacraments and the teachings of the Church each Sunday. The Syro-Malankara Catholic Sunday School observes a day of prayer and support every year.
termMore: Jesus says the angels of the little ones “continually see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18:10). The Church teaches that from infancy to death human life is surrounded by the watchful care and intercession of angels (CCC 336).

quick: The Epistle says that no one takes the honour of the priesthood for himself: he is called by God, just as Aaron was.
The high priest can deal gently with sinners because he too is subject to weakness; Jesus, tested yet without sin, is the great High Priest who offered himself once for all.
In the Gospel Zechariah offers incense while the whole assembly prays outside; Elizabeth is a descendant of Aaron.
2027-07-01.action: Pray today by name for one priest or bishop, and thank God for the call by which he was taken from among us.
2027-07-01.question: Do I pray with my priest when I am in church, or do I stay outside while I sit inside?

family.explain: A priest is a person God chooses to be a special helper for his people. Aaron was the first High Priest, the brother of Moses. He wore beautiful clothes with twelve shining stones on his chest, and on each stone was the name of one family of Israel, so that wherever he went he carried the people with him. Zechariah, in our Gospel, was a priest who came from the family of Aaron. While he offered incense, the people were outside praying. Priests and people pray together, and Jesus is the greatest High Priest of all.
family.intention: We pray for our priests and bishops, and for the sacristans, altar servers and choir who help us to pray.
family.ask: Ask: “Which priest taught you something about Jesus? Let us say a prayer for him now.”

illus: An illustration

In a hill parish in Idukki the old sacristan had lit the charcoal for the censer every Sunday for forty years. During the monsoon the charcoal was damp and often refused to light, and on such mornings he would crouch at the back of the sacristy with a bundle of dry coconut husk, blowing patiently. A young deacon once asked him why he took such trouble, since the priest could surely begin the Qurbono without incense. The old man replied that the incense was not his and not the priest's either; it was the prayer of everyone outside the sanctuary rising to God, and his only work was to keep the fire alive so that the people's prayer would have somewhere to go. Years later that deacon, now a priest, said that whenever he swung the censer he remembered the old man crouching with the damp charcoal, and prayed for the people whose prayers it carried.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, great High Priest, you carry your people before the Father. Teach us to pray with our priests and to pray for them, and let our prayer rise before you like incense. Amen.
share: No one presumes to take this honour, but takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was (Hebrews 5:4). Who first showed me the meaning of a call from God?
He stood between the dead and the living (Numbers 16:48). Where am I asked to stand between a troubled person and God, by prayer or by presence?
The whole assembly of the people was praying outside (Luke 1:10). Do I take part in the prayer of the Church, or do I watch it?
pm.resp: Lord, hear the prayer of your people.
interc: For our bishops, priests and deacons, that they may be faithful to the call of God and gentle with the weak.
For vocations to the priesthood and the religious life in our eparchies and parishes.
For those who serve in the sacristy and at the altar, for the choir and the servers, that their service may be offered with love.
For parishes without a priest of their own, and for priests who are sick, lonely or discouraged.
For all of us, that our prayer may rise like incense and our lives may be a pleasing offering.
pm.close: Father, you called Aaron from among his people and in your Son you gave us a High Priest who has no sin. Keep your priests close to your heart, keep your people faithful in prayer, and gather us all around your altar. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

term: High Priest (പ്രധാനാചാര്യൻ, Greek archiereus)

The Hebrew title is kohen gadol, “the great priest”, and the Letter to the Hebrews uses the Greek word archiereus. It means the chief of the priests, who alone entered the holy of holies once a year; the Letter shows that Jesus Christ is the one true High Priest.
kidsaint: Aaron's staff that blossomed

Some people in the camp of Israel complained and asked who had really been chosen to be priest. God told Moses to take twelve wooden staffs, one for each tribe, and to place them in the tent before the Lord overnight. In the morning the staff with Aaron's name had sprouted! It had buds and flowers and even ripe almonds. Now everyone knew whom God had chosen. Lesson: God is the one who calls, and he gives his helpers what they need to serve.

quick: The churches of Macedonia, in great affliction and poverty, gave beyond their means and begged for the privilege of giving.
Above all they gave themselves first to the Lord; Christ became poor for our sake so that we might become rich.
Jesus answers the stones with his works: “If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me.”
2027-07-02.action: Do one hidden act of generosity today and offer it to the Heart of Jesus on this First Friday.
2027-07-02.question: Have I given myself to the Lord first, or only what I have?

family.explain: St Paul tells the people of Corinth about some very poor Christians in Macedonia. They did not have much, but they were so happy in Jesus that they gave to others more than they could really afford, and they begged Paul to let them help. And the best thing they gave was themselves: first they gave themselves to the Lord. Jesus did the same for us. He was rich as God, and he became poor for our sake, and on a Friday he gave everything on the Cross. That is why we remember his Heart on every First Friday.
family.intention: We pray for families who are poor, and that our family may be glad to give.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can give away this week, with joy?”
