A tea-shop owner in a small town near Kuttanad opened his shutter at four every morning, an hour before anyone came. Asked why, he said that he used the hour to sit on his stool and say the morning prayer and the rosary before the first fisherman came to the door. “By the time the first customer comes,” he said, “my heart has had its tea.” The fishermen and the early bus drivers who stopped there said that the shop had a calm that no other tea stall had, and a few of them, who did not even go to church, began to leave their nets on the bench for a moment and say a prayer of their own.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you rose at daybreak to pray. Keep us awake and sober, children of light and of the day. Amen.
share: The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2). How does this make me feel, afraid or ready?
You are all children of light (1 Thessalonians 5:5). Where do I let my light shine?
I must proclaim the good news to the other cities also (Luke 4:43). Where am I sent today?
pm.resp: Lord, keep us awake in you.
interc: For the Church, that she may keep awake and sober and be faithful to the mission she was sent on.
For those who work at night and early in the morning, that the Lord may protect them.
For those who are tempted to give up hope, that they may hear the words: you are children of the day.
For the sick and the dying, that they may live with the Lord whether awake or asleep.
For ourselves, that we may begin each day with prayer, as the Lord did.
pm.close: Father, you have destined us for salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us. Keep us awake and sober, children of the day, and send us in the strength of prayer to proclaim your kingdom wherever you wish. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul says: whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God, and be imitators of me as I am of Christ.
Jesus asks the crowds to count the cost of following him, like a builder planning a tower and a king going to war.
St Ignatius of Loyola, a wounded soldier, became a saint and founded the Society of Jesus for the greater glory of God.
2027-07-31.action: Say a short prayer before a meal and a task today: To the greater glory of God.
2027-07-31.question: For whose glory do I do the ordinary things of my day?

family.explain: St Paul says that we can do everything for the glory of God, even eating and drinking and doing our homework. Today we remember St Ignatius, who was a soldier. When he was hurt, he read about Jesus and the saints, and he decided to serve God with his whole life. He started a group of priests and brothers called the Jesuits, who started schools all over the world, even in Kerala. Before we start something we can say, “For the glory of God.”
family.intention: We pray for teachers, students and all the people in schools and colleges.
family.ask: Ask: “What can I offer to God today, even if it is small?”

illus: An illustration

An old mason near Muvattupuzha was known in his district for never having left a house unfinished. Asked how, he said that before laying a single brick he would sit on the empty plot with a cup of tea and walk through the house in his mind, from the gate to the roof, counting every bag of cement and every wage. “The foundation is not the hard part,” he said. “The hard part is the hundredth day.” Young masons who worked under him said that he never started a job on a Monday without a short prayer at the corner stone. A priest who heard about it said that the old man had understood the Gospel of the tower better than most preachers.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call us to follow you. Teach us to count the cost, to carry the cross, and to do everything for the glory of God. Amen.
share: Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Which part of my ordinary day could I offer to him?
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:27). What is my cross at this time?
Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost (Luke 14:28)? What am I building, and have I counted its cost?
pm.resp: Lord, to your greater glory.
interc: For the Church, that she may do everything for the glory of God and carry the cross of Christ with courage.
For the Jesuits and for all who teach in schools and colleges, that they may form young people in wisdom and faith.
For those who are searching for the meaning of their lives, that they may find the Lord as Ignatius did.
For those who are recovering from illness or injury, that their weakness may become a time of grace.
For all of us, that we may be imitators of Christ in every state of life.
pm.close: Father, you raised up St Ignatius to serve your greater glory. Grant that, following his example, we may do everything for your glory, count the cost with courage, and carry the cross after your Son. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

term: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam (A.M.D.G.)

The Latin motto of the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, meaning “to the greater glory of God.” St Ignatius took it from the spirit of 1 Corinthians 10:31, and the word “greater” (magis) means always asking what serves God's glory more fully.
kidsaint: The soldier who read about Jesus

Íñigo was a soldier who loved adventure and wanted to be famous. One day a cannonball hurt his leg, and he had to lie in bed for many weeks. He was bored, so he asked for some adventure books, but the only books in the castle were about Jesus and the saints. He read them, and he noticed that when he thought about being famous he felt empty, but when he thought about doing great things for Jesus he felt happy for a long time. So he decided to give his life to God. He became St Ignatius, and the priests he started, the Jesuits, built schools all over the world. Lesson: do great things, but do them for God, and your heart will be full.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we celebrate our father in faith, St Thomas. We often call him “doubting Thomas,” but the Gospel shows more. When Jesus decided to go to Judea, where they wanted to stone him, it was Thomas who said: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” He was brave and honest.

On Easter evening he was absent. He would not simply accept the others' word: “Unless I see the mark of the nails… I will not believe.” A week later Jesus came and said: “Put your finger here and see my hands… Do not doubt but believe.” And Thomas fell down: “My Lord and my God!” No one in the Gospels says it more clearly: Jesus is not only teacher or prophet; he is Lord and God.

Jesus said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” That is us. Our ancestors in Kerala did not see Jesus, but they believed the word of Thomas, who had seen and touched. And according to our tradition, Thomas sealed that word with his blood at Mylapore.

So today let us thank God for the faith we received. Let us not be ashamed of it in our schools, offices and on social media. And when doubt comes, do not run away from Jesus; bring it to him, as Thomas did. At this Qurbono, when the Holy Mysteries are raised, say in your heart with Thomas: “My Lord and my God.” Amen.
kids: Children, St Thomas was one of Jesus' twelve apostles. He said he would not believe Jesus was alive unless he could touch his wounds!
Then Jesus came and showed him. Thomas said: “My Lord and my God!”
Later, Thomas travelled all the way to India to tell people about Jesus. That's why we are Christians today! Let's say with Thomas: “My Lord and my God!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, when Jesus drove out demons, his enemies said he was working with Satan. Jesus answered: “If a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.” The devil's work is division: between husband and wife, parents and children, neighbours, parishes, even Churches. The Spirit's work is communion.

Then Jesus warns about the sin against the Holy Spirit, which can never be forgiven. People sometimes fear they have committed it. But the Church teaches: God's mercy has no limits. This sin is to refuse that mercy to the end, to call the Spirit's work evil and close the door. If you are worried that you have committed it, that very worry shows you have not. And Jesus adds: “by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Our tongues can build or destroy.

St Paul says: Christ “is our peace; he has broken down the dividing wall of hostility.” Through his blood those who were far off have been brought near. We who were strangers are now members of God's household, built on the apostles with Christ as the cornerstone.

When the first Christians were threatened, they did not divide; they prayed together, and the place was shaken, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit. Let us do the same. This week take one step to heal a division: a phone call, an apology, a visit. Guard your words. And pray for the unity of all the children of St Thomas. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: a house where everyone fights cannot stand. It falls down!
Jesus wants our families to be strong, with people who forgive each other and help each other.
Is there someone you quarrelled with? Can you say sorry this week? Let's pray: “Jesus, make our family one!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Letter to the Hebrews says: “The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword.” When the Gospel is read in the Holy Qurbono, it is not a story from long ago. Christ himself speaks to us now. That is why we stand, why the candles and the incense honour the Book.

In Mark's Gospel Jesus begins his parable with one word: “Listen!” and ends with another: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” In between is the sower. The same seed falls on the path, on rock, among thorns, and on good soil. Good soil is the heart that hears the word, accepts it, and lets it bear fruit, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

At the burning bush God told Moses his name: “I AM WHO I AM.” The living God speaks. Jeremiah says that God asked only one thing of Israel: “Obey my voice.” To obey means to listen deeply. Much of our trouble comes from not listening: to God, to one another.

And if we are afraid that the Word will judge us, Hebrews adds: we have a high priest who understands our weakness, who was tested in every way as we are, yet without sin. “Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy.” This week give ten minutes each day to the Gospel. Listen. And let the word bear fruit. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus once began a story with one word: “Listen!” Can you say it? Listen!
A farmer threw seeds. Some fell on the path, some on rocks, some in thorns, and some in good soil. The good soil gave lots and lots of fruit!
God's word is the seed, and your heart is the soil. Let's listen to Jesus every day and be good soil!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Letter to the Hebrews tells us: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.” Today our Church remembers her father, Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who went to God on 15 July 1953.

He was a scholar and teacher, but above all a man of prayer. He founded Bethany, the communities of the Imitation of Christ. And he carried a great longing: that the ancient Malankara Church be one with the Church of Peter. On 20 September 1930, with Mar Theophilos and a few others, he entered full communion with the Catholic Church, keeping the beautiful liturgy of our fathers.

It cost him a great deal. He left behind churches, properties and friendships. He began again in small chapels and sheds. But he trusted the promise God made to Moses: “I will be with you.” Like the faithful servant in the parable, he did not bury his talents. Today our Church, spread across India and the world, is the harvest of that sacrifice.

So let us imitate his faith: love for prayer, love for the liturgy, love for the unity of the Church. Let us pray for our Major Archbishop and bishops, for all Christians of Kerala to be one, and, if it is God's will, for the glorification of his servant Mar Ivanios. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember Mar Ivanios, the father of our Malankara Catholic Church.
He loved Jesus and wanted all Christians to be one family with the Pope. He gave up big churches and a lot of money to do this!
Let's thank God for him and pray: “Jesus, make all Christians one family!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, Jesus is at a dinner and notices the guests rushing for the best seats. He says: Sit in the lowest place, and let the host call you higher. “For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” In families, parishes and offices there is often a quiet competition for the best seat. Jesus offers us freedom: let God decide your place.

In the evening Gospel a farmer's enemy sows weeds among his wheat. The servants want to pull them out at once. The master says: no, you will pull out the wheat too; let them grow together until the harvest. We are often impatient servants. We want to separate the good and the bad in the Church and in our families right now. But God is patient. Many who look like weeds today will become wheat tomorrow. Judgment belongs to him.

Then Jesus speaks of the tiny mustard seed that becomes a tree, and of the yeast hidden in flour. God's kingdom grows quietly: a mother's prayer, a catechism class on Sunday morning, a young person's honest word. Do not despise small beginnings.

St Paul reminds the Corinthians: “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.” Remember who you are. And remember: on 1 August the Fifteen Days' Fast begins, in honour of our Mother's Assumption. Let us prepare our hearts with humility. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: when you go to a party, don't run for the best chair! Sit in a simple place, and the host may say, “Come up here, friend!”
He also told a story about a tiny mustard seed that grew into a big tree where birds could build nests.
Small kind acts can grow big too! This week, let someone else go first.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the disciples asked Jesus: “Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” Jesus did not answer with a name. He called a child and stood the child among them: “Unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” A child trusts, receives, asks, and is not ashamed of needing help. That is how we must stand before God.

Then Jesus speaks very strongly: whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better off with a millstone around his neck in the depths of the sea. Their angels always see the Father's face. Children are precious to God. Every family and every parish must protect them, form them, and never give them scandal by our lives.

St Paul tells us what we must teach them: “if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” That is the work of our Sunday School teachers, who give their Sunday mornings to teach our children the faith. Let us thank them and pray for them today.

At Marah the water was bitter; God showed Moses a piece of wood, and the water became sweet. The Fathers saw there the Cross, which makes the bitterness of life sweet. Let us teach our children to love the Cross and the Lord who heals. And next Sunday, 1 August, we begin the Fifteen Days' Fast in honour of our Mother's Assumption. Amen.
kids: Children, today Jesus says something wonderful about you! The disciples asked who is the greatest, and Jesus put a child in the middle and said: “Be like this child!”
You trust God like you trust your mum and dad. That makes Jesus very happy.
Today, say thank you to your Sunday School teacher! And let's pray: “Jesus, I believe you are Lord!”

homily: Dear friends, today is the first day of July, and the Panchangam begins the month by remembering Aaron the High Priest, the brother of Moses. The Letter to the Hebrews says that no one takes the honour of the priesthood for himself: one takes it only when called by God, just as Aaron was (Hebrews 5:4). God brought Aaron near and gave him vestments with the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart, so that he would never forget the people he served.

Aaron was not perfect. The Epistle says that a high priest is subject to weakness and must offer sacrifice for his own sins as well as for those of the people (Hebrews 5:2–3). Aaron made the golden calf. Yet when the plague came he took his censer and ran into the middle of the assembly, and he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped (Numbers 16:48). God works through weak people who stand for the others.

Jesus Christ is the great High Priest who was tested as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). He offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27). Every priest who serves at our altar serves in his name. In the Gospel Zechariah, a priest of Aaron's line, offers incense, and the whole assembly of the people is praying outside (Luke 1:10). The priest and the people pray together.
So today let us pray for our bishops, priests and deacons by name, and let us pray with them at every Holy Qurbono, so that our prayer rises like incense. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what a priest is? A priest is a person whom God chooses to be a special helper for his people. A long time ago Aaron, the brother of Moses, was the first High Priest. He wore a beautiful breastpiece with twelve stones, and on every stone there was a name, so that he carried all the families of Israel on his heart. Today our priests also carry us on their hearts. Say a little prayer for your parish priest today, and when you see him, say thank you!

homily: Dear friends, today is the First Friday, and we look to the Heart of Jesus, the Heart that gave everything. St Paul tells the Corinthians about the churches of Macedonia. They were poor and in affliction, and yet their abundant joy and their extreme poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2). They gave according to their means, and even beyond their means, and they begged for the privilege of giving (2 Corinthians 8:3–4).

What was best of all is that they gave themselves first to the Lord (2 Corinthians 8:5). That is where all true giving begins. And Paul reminds us why: Jesus Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He gave himself first.

In the Gospel Jesus is threatened with stones, and he answers calmly: I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of these are you going to stone me? (John 10:32). He asks that people believe the works, so that they may know and understand that the Father is in him and he is in the Father (John 10:38). We too are to be known by our works. Many who do not read the Scriptures read our lives.
So today let us offer ourselves to the Lord first, and then let us give, with joy, even beyond our means, something that costs us. It will be a work that points to the Father. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know that today is the First Friday? We remember that Jesus loves us so much that he gave everything for us, even his life on the Cross. St Paul tells about some people who were very poor, but so happy in Jesus that they shared what little they had. And best of all, they gave themselves to the Lord. Today, do one kind thing without telling anyone: give a toy, help at home, or say a prayer for someone who is sad. That is how we show the Heart of Jesus to others.

homily: Dear friends, today the Panchangam remembers the Seventy-two Heralds. St Luke tells that the Lord appointed others, seventy or seventy-two in number, and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go (Luke 10:1). They are not the Twelve. They stand for all who are sent to announce that the Lord is coming, and the number reminds us of all the nations of the earth.

The first instruction is to pray: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Luke 10:2). Then they are sent as lambs among wolves, with no purse, no bag and no sandals, and in pairs, so that no one goes alone. They are to say first: Peace to this house! (Luke 10:5). They are to eat what is set before them, to cure the sick, and to say: The kingdom of God has come near to you (Luke 10:9).

St Paul tells the Corinthians that the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power (2 Corinthians 10:4). The Lord's heralds do not fight with force but with peace, with the word, with prayer and with the care of the sick. The authority given to them is for building up and not for tearing down (2 Corinthians 10:8).

Every baptized person is a herald. So let us pray for laborers for the harvest, let us greet our homes with a blessing of peace, and let us go, in pairs if we can, to someone who needs to hear that the kingdom of God is near. Amen.
kids: Children, once Jesus sent seventy-two of his friends to go ahead of him to the villages. They went in pairs, so nobody was alone. Do you know the first thing they said when they came to a house? “Peace to this house!” That is a beautiful greeting, isn't it? You can do the same: when you come home, say a happy hello and wish peace to your family. And you can ask a friend to go with you when you visit a grandparent or a neighbour who is sick. Then you will be a herald of Jesus, just like those seventy-two!

homily: Dear friends, today the Panchangam keeps in bold the memory of Pulikkottil Joseph Ramban, a monk-priest, and it also remembers St Maria Goretti. The Epistle gives us a rule for such days: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). And it adds at once: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8). People pass away, but he does not.

We have an altar, says the Letter (Hebrews 13:10). At the Holy Qurbono we are fed with the Body and Blood of the Lord, and we remember those who have gone before us, among them the priests and monks who once served at the altar. The Letter also says that Jesus suffered outside the city gate, and that we are to go to him outside the camp (Hebrews 13:12–13), for here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come (Hebrews 13:14).

St Maria Goretti did this at the age of eleven. She refused what was wrong, and when she was dying she forgave the one who had hurt her. She prayed, in her own way, what Jesus had prayed: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). The Gospel tells us to be like the faithful and wise servant, whom the master will find at work when he comes (Matthew 24:46).
So let us remember with thanks those who taught us the faith, let us offer God a sacrifice of praise, let us forgive anyone who has hurt us, and let us be ready. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know who taught you to pray? Perhaps your mother or grandmother or a priest. Today we say thank you to God for them. We also remember Maria Goretti, a girl who was only eleven years old. She was very brave. She said no to something that was wrong, and she forgave a person who had hurt her. Jesus is the same today as he was long ago, and he helps us to be brave and kind too. This evening, say a little prayer of thanks for someone who taught you about Jesus, and forgive anyone who has been unkind to you.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Epistle St Paul speaks of a divine jealousy. He has betrothed the Corinthians to one husband, to present them as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). He is afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, their thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3). Another Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel: people accept such things readily enough (2 Corinthians 11:4). In our own days many voices speak about Jesus; we must test them against the Gospel and the Creed, and keep our own devotion simple.

In the Gospel Jesus says, Let us go to Judea again (John 11:7). The disciples are afraid, since people there had lately tried to stone Jesus. Jesus says that there are twelve hours of daylight, and those who walk by day do not stumble because they see the light of this world (John 11:9). Whoever walks with Jesus walks by day. He adds: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to awaken him (John 11:11). For Christians death is a sleep from which the Lord awakens us.

And then Thomas speaks: Let us also go, that we may die with him (John 11:16). It is the bravest sentence the disciples say in this chapter. On Saturday we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, and today we see him follow his Lord, without understanding everything, to Judea and to the tomb.
Let us ask the Lord for a pure devotion and for the courage of Thomas, so that whenever he goes before us we may say, Let us also go. Amen.
kids: Children, do you remember the Apostle Thomas, whose feast we kept last Saturday? Today we hear about a brave thing he did. Jesus said that he was going to a place where some people wanted to hurt him. The other friends were afraid, but Thomas said: “Let us also go!” He did not want to leave Jesus alone. We can be like Thomas. When a friend is sad, when someone is sick, or when it is hard to do the right thing, we can say, “Let us also go; Jesus is with us.” Let us ask Jesus to make us brave friends.

homily: Dear friends, the short Letter to Philemon asks a hard thing in a gentle way. Onesimus, who had been a slave in the house of Philemon, is coming back, and Paul says: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me (Philemon 17). Then he says: If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it (Philemon 18–19). This is a picture of Christ, who took our debt on his own account and paid it with his own hand on the Cross. In the verse just before this reading Paul says that Onesimus now comes back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

Paul adds: Confident of your obedience, I am writing to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. And he asks: prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping through your prayers to be restored to you (Philemon 21–22). A welcome, a guest room and a prayer: this is how the Gospel enters a home.

In the Gospel the disciples are crossing the lake, and they have forgotten to bring bread. Jesus warns them of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, but they think of their empty baskets. He says: You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? (Matthew 16:8–9). The cure for worry is to remember what the Lord has done. And the yeast he warns of is the teaching of pride and hypocrisy, which a little spreads through the whole dough.
So let us welcome someone whom we find hard to welcome, let us forgive a debt, and let us count again the gifts of God, so that the yeast of his kingdom may work in us. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago a man named Onesimus had gone away from his master's house, and then he became a friend of Jesus. St Paul wrote a letter to the master, Philemon, and asked him to welcome Onesimus back as a brother. Paul even said that he would pay whatever Onesimus owed! That is just what Jesus does for us when we say sorry. In the Gospel the friends of Jesus forgot to take bread and began to worry. Jesus reminded them how he had fed thousands with a few loaves. When you worry, remember how good God has been. And this week, welcome somebody who is new or alone: sit with them and play with them.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul comes to the end of a long argument, and he ends it with a song: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Romans 11:33). He has been thinking about the people of Israel, about the Gentiles, and about the way God's plan moves through history. And at the end he does not say: now I understand it all. He says: now I can only praise.

He tells us what he has learned: God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all (Romans 11:32). Nobody can stand before God and say, I deserve this. We all live by mercy: those who came first and those who came later, Jew and Gentile, bishop and child. And the Church reminds us, with Paul, that the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). So no Christian may ever speak of the Jewish people with contempt or pride.

Then the Gospel gives us a picture to examine our own hearts. Jesus is hungry; he sees a fig tree in leaf and goes to it, but finds nothing but leaves (Mark 11:13). A tree that looks full of life and gives no fruit: that can be a person, a home, a parish. Fine words, fine feasts, fine decorations, and no prayer, no justice, no mercy. Jesus is not asking for more show. He is asking for fruit.

So let us ask ourselves where our leaves are, and with God's grace let us begin to bear fruit. And let us do what Paul does: let us thank God from whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things. To him be the glory for ever. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever gone to the mango tree hoping for a mango, and found only leaves? Jesus once did that with a fig tree! He was hungry, and the tree had lots of beautiful green leaves, but no figs. Jesus wants us to be like a tree full of fruit: not only looking nice, but being kind, sharing, praying and helping. And St Paul tells us to thank God for everything, because everything comes from him. This week, thank God for your food before you eat it, and do one kind thing that is like a fruit: share a sweet, help at home, or visit a lonely neighbour.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul asks today: have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! (Romans 11:11). He is speaking of his own people, whom he never stops loving. And he gives us a picture to hold on to: if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy (Romans 11:16). We are branches that have been grafted on, and the root is the faith of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Scriptures of Israel, the psalms we sing at every Qurbono. So there is no room for pride, and no room for contempt, but only gratitude.

The Gospel brings us down from the mountain into the valley. A father cries out of the crowd: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child (Luke 9:38). His son is thrown to the ground again and again. The disciples tried and could not. And Jesus says, with a sigh: Bring your son here (Luke 9:41). Then he rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father (Luke 9:42).

Do you see how much love there is in those words, gave him back to his father? Jesus does not heal the child and keep him; he returns him to his father's arms. There is not a single sorrow of a parent that he does not see. And when we ourselves have stumbled, when we feel that we have fallen for good, it is the same Lord who takes our hand: though we stumble, we shall not fall headlong, for the Lord holds us by the hand (Psalm 37:24).

So today let us bring someone to Jesus: a sick relative, a troubled friend, or ourselves. Let us say with the father in Mark's Gospel: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). And let us thank God for the root that bears us. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever fallen down while running and thought you could never get up? Then someone gave you a hand and you were up again. Today's Gospel is about a father whose little boy was very sick. The father brought his boy to Jesus, and Jesus made him well and gave him back to his father, safe and sound. Jesus always takes our hand when we fall. Also, St Paul tells us we are like branches of a big tree, and the roots of the tree are the people of the Bible, Abraham and Moses and David. We say thank you to them in our hearts. This week, when you fall or make a mistake, say: Jesus, hold my hand. And ask Jesus to help a child who is sick.

homily: Dear friends, the Gospel today takes us to the shore of the lake. Jesus is walking, and he sees two brothers casting a net, and he says: Follow me, and I will make you fish for people (Matthew 4:19). They were not scholars or leaders. They were working people. And the Gospel says: Immediately they left their nets and followed him (Matthew 4:20). Then it happens again with James and John, who were mending their nets in the boat with their father.

Think of what they left: the boat, the nets, the income, the father who needed them. They could not see where this would lead. They only knew who was calling. And that is the heart of every vocation: not a clear plan, but a clear voice. Jesus calls each of us in the middle of our ordinary work. The question is what we are ready to leave behind: a habit, a grudge, a fear, the love of money.

In the Epistle, St Paul shows us what it is to follow Jesus to the end. He worked with his own hands and asked nothing from the Corinthians so that nobody could say he preached for gain (2 Corinthians 11:9). He serves, he does not take. But he warns us as well: Even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). Not everything that shines is of God. The Lord gives us a simple test: you will know them by their fruits (Matthew 7:16): humility, love and service.

Yesterday the Panchangam remembered St Benedict, who began his Rule with the word Listen. Let us listen today to the voice that says: Follow me. Let us leave one net at his feet, and let us serve without asking for a reward. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what Jesus said to the fishermen? He said, Follow me! And they left their nets and boats right away, and went with him. They did not know everything about where they were going, but they loved Jesus and trusted him. Jesus calls you too. He does not call you to leave your family; he calls you to be kind, to pray, to help others and to listen to him. And St Paul tells us to serve people without asking for anything back, just like a good fisherman who shares his fish. This week, do one kind thing for someone without telling anyone, and say: Jesus, I want to follow you.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul gives us in a few words the whole of the Christian life: We do not live to ourselves, and we do not die to ourselves. If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's (Romans 14:7–8). Everything that follows grows from this belonging. If we are the Lord's, then so is our brother, and so is our sister. That is why he asks: Why do you pass judgment on your brother or sister? (Romans 14:10).

The Gospel shows how the Lord looks at people. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). And then he says to his disciples: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Matthew 9:37–38). Notice: he does not first say, go; he says, pray. And those who pray are then the ones he sends.

Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Sheelas, St Silas. He was one of those laborers. The Church at Jerusalem sent him to Antioch with a letter of peace, and he strengthened the believers there. Then he went with Paul, was beaten and put in prison at Philippi, and at midnight he was singing hymns to God (Acts 16:25). Later he served Peter too. He carried the Church's peace and he sang in prison. We pray today also for Most Rev. Antony Mar Silvanos on his name day.
So let us live this day as the Lord's. Let us not judge. Let us pray for laborers for the harvest, and let us ask what work he is asking of us. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember St Silas, who was a helper of St Paul. Once Silas and Paul were put in prison for talking about Jesus. At midnight, in the dark, they did not cry; they sang hymns to God! And the other prisoners listened. Then the doors of the prison opened and the jailer and his family became Christians. Jesus says that many people are waiting to hear about him, and he needs helpers. We can be his helpers too, by being kind, by praying, and by singing and speaking about Jesus. This week, sing a song of praise at home, and ask Jesus to send more helpers to his work.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul speaks to a divided community: some said, I belong to Paul, and others, I belong to Apollos. And Paul answers with a picture from the field: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). In these weeks of rain, our fields are being planted. We know that no farmer makes the seed grow. He prepares the soil, he plants, he waters, and then he waits for God.

Paul adds: you are God's field, God's building (1 Corinthians 3:9). A field needs care in every season; a building rises stone by stone. The faith we have received was planted and watered by many hands that we never saw: the Apostle Thomas, the first Christians of our land, parents and grandparents, priests who kept the Qurbono alive. Tomorrow the Church remembers Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. He worked and prayed for the unity of the Church and for the Malankara tradition, and he began in poverty. What he planted has grown, and the growth is God's.

In the Gospel, two blind men follow Jesus, crying, Have mercy on us, Son of David! (Matthew 9:27). They could not see the road, but they saw who he was. Jesus asks them: Do you believe that I am able to do this? Yes, Lord, they say. And he touches their eyes: According to your faith let it be done to you (Matthew 9:29). Faith is an open hand that receives. And when they were healed, they could not keep silent about him.

So tonight, let us thank someone who planted our faith. Let us do our part in the field faithfully, and give the glory to the Lord who gives the growth. And let us say, with the blind men, Lord, have mercy on us. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever planted a seed and watered it every day? You cannot make the seed grow yourself; only God does that. But you plant it and you water it, and God does the rest. St Paul says that we are all workers in God's garden: some plant, some water, and God makes it grow. Somebody planted our faith: our grandparents, our parents, the priests, the catechism teachers. Tomorrow we remember Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who planted something very important in our Church. In the Gospel two men who were blind cried, Jesus, have mercy on us! And Jesus opened their eyes. This week, plant something small, a seed or a flower, and water it, and say a thank-you prayer for the people who planted your faith.

homily: Dear friends, today we remember Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and the Gospel gives us a scene full of warmth. A woman in the crowd calls out, Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you! (Luke 11:27). She is praising Jesus' mother. And Jesus answers: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it! (Luke 11:28). He does not take away Mary's blessing; he shows us its secret. Who heard the word of God like Mary? Let it be with me according to your word (Luke 1:38). She kept all these things in her heart (Luke 2:19).

In the Epistle, St Paul tells us what her yes made possible: God sent his Son, born of a woman, so that we might receive adoption as children (Galatians 4:4–5). The Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary; that is why the Church calls her Mother of God, and in our own Syriac language, Yoldath Aloho. And because he came, we are no longer slaves but children, and we cry Abba, Father. Everything in the Gospel begins with her yes.

Mount Carmel is a mountain by the sea. There the prophet Elijah bowed down and prayed after three years of drought. His servant looked at the sea seven times, and the seventh time he saw a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand (1 Kings 18:44). Soon there was a heavy rain. Many believers have seen in that little cloud a sign of Mary, small and humble, from whom came the Son who is the rain of grace. The Carmelites took her as their patroness and gave us the scapular, a sign of belonging to her and of the wish to follow her. The sign is not a charm; it points to the Son.

So in these days of rain, let us ask Our Lady of Mount Carmel to obtain for us the blessedness her Son spoke of: to hear the word of God and to obey it. Let us choose one word of the Gospel to keep this week. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Carmel is a green mountain by the sea where the prophet Elijah once prayed for rain. His servant looked at the sky seven times, and the last time he saw a little cloud, as small as your hand. And soon the rain came! Mary is like that little cloud, small and humble, and she brought us Jesus, who brings God's love like rain. Jesus tells us that people are happy when they hear God's word and do it, and Mary always did. Some people wear a little brown cloth called the scapular to remember to follow Mary. This week, choose one thing Jesus asks, like being kind or telling the truth, and do it all week. And say a Hail Mary every day.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul says something beautiful: thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumph, and through us spreads in every place the fragrance that comes from knowing him (2 Corinthians 2:14). The picture is of a procession in which incense is carried, so that its scent reaches people before they even see the one who is passing. Paul is not the victor; Christ is. But Paul and all of us who belong to Christ carry his fragrance.

In these monsoon days, many of our homes use a little incense to drive away the damp smell. The smell stays in our clothes and hair for hours. Paul says it is like this with the gospel: those who have been with Christ carry something of him wherever they go. He adds: we are not peddlers of God's word like so many, but in Christ we speak as persons of sincerity, as persons sent from God and standing in his presence (2 Corinthians 2:17). Let us not water down the gospel to please people.

In the Gospel, Jesus stands up in the synagogue of Nazareth and reads from Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). The Anointed One is anointed for the poor, the captive, the blind and the oppressed. That is the fragrance we are to spread. Today the Church remembers St Alexius of Rome, who, according to the old story, left his riches to live among the poor, and she prays for Thomas Mar Koorilos on the anniversary of his episcopal ordination and for Yoohanon Mar Alexios on his name day.
Let us ask the Lord to make us people who carry the fragrance of Christ: in our kindness to the poor, in our honesty, in the way we pray and the way we speak. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever smelled incense in the church, or a sweet flower in the garden? You can smell it even if you cannot see it! St Paul says that people who stay close to Jesus carry something sweet with them, the love of Jesus. When you are kind to your friends, when you share with someone poor, when you say sorry, people can tell that you belong to Jesus. Today, try to carry the sweet smell of Jesus to everyone you meet.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel the Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign from heaven, to test him. And Mark tells us that Jesus sighed deeply in his spirit and said: Why does this generation ask for a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation (Mark 8:12). Then he left them. He had fed four thousand people with seven loaves only a few verses before. The signs were there. The problem was not a lack of signs but a lack of love for the truth.

That is also the warning in the Epistle. Paul says that the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, with false signs and wonders and deceptions for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved (2 Thessalonians 2:10). He does not tell us to fear. The Lord Jesus will destroy the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). What the Lord wants from us is a heart that loves what is true.

Today the Church remembers Morth Makrina, the sister of St Basil and St Gregory of Nyssa. Gregory wrote her Life, and he calls her his teacher. She turned her family's home into a place of prayer, psalms and charity, and she never asked for a sign. Her whole life was a sign. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).
Let us ask the Lord for a heart like hers: honest, quiet and faithful. And let us not look for wonders when the Lord has already given us the Gospel and the Holy Qurbono. Amen.
kids: Children, imagine your friend says, I will only believe you love me if you do something amazing. That would make you sad, wouldn't it? That is how Jesus felt when some people asked him for a special sign. He had already done so many good things! Today we remember Morth Makrina. She showed Jesus to her brothers just by praying, teaching and sharing. You can also show Jesus to your family, just by being kind and honest every day.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel the disciples are coming down the mountain after seeing Jesus shining, with Moses and Elijah beside him. They ask: Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? Jesus answers: Elijah is indeed coming first to restore all things. But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased (Mark 9:12–13). He means John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

Who was Elijah? A prophet who stood alone for the living God. On Mount Carmel he asked the people: How long will you go limping with two different opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him (1 Kings 18:21). He prayed fervently, and after a long drought he saw a little cloud no bigger than a person's hand rising out of the sea (1 Kings 18:44). In these monsoon days we know what that cloud means. St James says that Elijah was a human being like us (James 5:17). He also became tired and sad, and God sent him bread and water with the words: Get up and eat, otherwise the journey will be too much for you (1 Kings 19:7).

St Paul tells the Colossians that festivals, new moons and sabbaths are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:17). The prophets, too, are lights thrown ahead by the one who is coming. When the disciples looked up on the mountain, they saw no one with them any more, but only Jesus (Mark 9:8). We honour Elijah, but we follow Jesus, the head of the body.
Let us ask the Lord for Elijah's courage to choose, his persistence in prayer and his humility to eat the bread God gives. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what Elijah did when the land was dry and there was no rain? He prayed and prayed, and he sent his servant to look at the sea. Seven times! At last the servant saw a tiny cloud, as small as a hand. And soon there was a big rain, just as in our monsoon! Elijah teaches us to keep praying and not to give up. And when Elijah was tired, an angel gave him bread and said, Get up and eat. God gives us strength for our journey, too.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel Jesus gives two short parables. The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches (Matthew 13:31–32). And it is like yeast that a woman mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened (Matthew 13:33). God's kingdom begins small and hidden, and it grows.

Matthew says that Jesus spoke in parables to fulfil what had been spoken through the prophet: I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world (Matthew 13:35). Today the Church remembers the prophet Daniel, who blessed the God who reveals deep and hidden things (Daniel 2:22). Daniel saw a stone cut out, not by human hands, which became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:35). The Fathers saw in that stone Christ himself.

Daniel lived as a believer in a great empire. Three times a day he knelt to pray with the windows of his room open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). He prayed for his people: we have sinned and done wrong (Daniel 9:5). That is what St Paul means when he says today: We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves (Romans 15:1). And the scriptures were written so that by steadfastness and by their encouragement we might have hope (Romans 15:4).
Let us trust the small seeds of God in our lives, a little prayer, a little kindness, and let us pray together with one voice, so that his kingdom may grow in us. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know how tiny a mustard seed is? Smaller than a pin's head! But when it is planted it grows into a big plant where little birds come to rest. Jesus says God's kingdom is like that. Today we remember Daniel, who prayed three times every day even when it was dangerous, and God took care of him. When you say a little prayer, or do a little kindness, it is like a tiny seed. God makes it grow.

homily: Dear friends, today we remember St Mary Magdalene. The Gospels tell us that she was a woman from Magdala whom Jesus had delivered, that she stood near his cross, and that she came to the tomb early on the first day of the week while it was still dark (John 20:1). She is not the sinful woman of Luke chapter 7; the Gospel does not say so, and we read her as the Gospel gives her. She was a faithful friend.

Peter and the other disciple saw the empty tomb and went home. But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb (John 20:11). She stayed and kept looking. Two angels asked her why she was weeping, and then Jesus himself asked her, and she thought he was the gardener. Then Jesus said her name: Mary! She turned and said, Rabbouni! (John 20:16). The Lord knows his own sheep by name.

Jesus said: Do not hold on to me, but go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. And Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, I have seen the Lord (John 20:17–18). She was the first to announce the resurrection, and so the Church calls her the apostle of the apostles. St Paul says: God has given us the ministry of reconciliation, and we are ambassadors for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18, 20).
Let us ask St Mary Magdalene to teach us to stay and seek the Lord with love, to listen as he calls us by name, and to go and tell others, with joy, that we have seen the Lord. Amen.
kids: Children, imagine you are very sad because you cannot find someone you love. Mary Magdalene was like that on the first Easter morning. She went to the tomb while it was still dark, and she cried. Then someone said, Mary! And she knew at once it was Jesus, because he said her name in his special way. He was alive! Jesus knows your name, too. And like Mary, we can run to tell our friends: Jesus is alive, I have seen the Lord!

homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel the disciples ask Jesus on the Mount of Olives: when will this be, and what will be the sign of your coming? Jesus gives no timetable. He says: Beware that no one leads you astray. You will hear of wars and rumors of wars; see that you are not alarmed (Matthew 24:4, 6). All this is but the beginning of the birth pangs, the pains that lead to a birth. Many will fall away, and because of the increase of lawlessness, the love of many will grow cold. But the one who endures to the end will be saved (Matthew 24:12–13).

Today the Church remembers Ezekiel, a prophet for hard times. He was a priest among the exiles by the river Chebar in Babylon, and there the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God (Ezekiel 1:1). The Lord was not left behind in Jerusalem; he came to his people in exile. God made him a sentinel for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:17), and promised: A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). At the end of the book Ezekiel sees a river flowing from the temple, and everything will live where the river goes (Ezekiel 47:9).

St Paul tells us why we can endure: God has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins (Colossians 1:13–14). Our endurance rests on what Christ has done for us. And the good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the world, as a testimony to all the nations (Matthew 24:14).
Let us ask for the heart of flesh, for the watchfulness of the sentinel, and for the love that does not grow cold. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what a watchman does? He stands high on a wall and looks out, and if he sees danger coming, he shouts so that everyone is safe. God made Ezekiel a watchman for his people. Jesus also asks us to stay awake and not to be afraid when we hear scary news. And God promised a new heart, a soft one that can love. You can ask Jesus every day: Please give me a soft and loving heart.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul tells us that there is a veil over our hearts that only Christ can lift: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (2 Corinthians 3:16). Moses covered his shining face with a veil; but we, with unveiled faces, see the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, and we are changed into his image. We become like what we look at, so what are we looking at?

The Panchangam remembers St Sharbel, a Maronite monk of Lebanon. He left home at twenty-three, became a monk, then a priest, and for twenty-three years lived as a hermit above the monastery of Annaya, in poverty, fasting and prayer. He was stricken while celebrating the Holy Qurbono and died on Christmas Eve 1898. Pope Paul VI canonised him in 1977. His Church belongs, like ours, to the West Syriac family.

In the Gospel Jesus asks for a following that does not turn back. The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). Few are called to a hermitage, but everyone is called to keep the Lord first.
So let us turn to the Lord every morning, give him a quiet half hour in the week, and finish what we have begun in his name. Let us not look back. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever walked in the wet rain with your umbrella and looked at the puddles? You see your own face in the water as in a mirror. St Paul says that when we look at Jesus, it is like looking into a mirror that makes us look more and more like him. St Sharbel loved to look at Jesus in prayer, so much that his whole life shone. Every day, say a little prayer and look at the cross. Jesus will make your heart shine too.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells the Corinthians that there are two kinds of sorrow. Worldly grief produces death; godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret (2 Corinthians 7:10). When I have done wrong, worldly grief makes me hide, blame and sink into shame. Godly grief makes me stand up and go to the Lord, who is waiting.

Think of Peter and Judas. Peter wept bitterly, and the Lord took him back; Judas looked at his sin and not at his Master, and despair finished the work of sin. The Sacrament of Reconciliation is the road of Peter: we confess, and we are lifted up and made lighter.

In the Gospel Jesus is warned that Herod wants to kill him, and he is not afraid. He goes on towards Jerusalem on his Father's timetable. And then he weeps over the city: How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Luke 13:34). The Church teaches that the guilt of his Passion belongs to no people but to all of us as sinners.
So today let us stop being unwilling. Let us run under his wings, as chicks run to the hen in the monsoon rain. Let us go to him with our sorrow and receive his mercy. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever seen a mother hen when the rain comes? She calls her chicks, and they run quickly under her wings, and soon you cannot see them at all! Jesus says that is how much he loves us. When we do something wrong, he wants us to run to him, not away from him. Say, “Sorry, Lord,” and he will keep you warm and safe. And remember to say sorry to the person you hurt too.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells us that we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Think of crossing a flooded field at night with a small lamp. You see only the next step, and you walk because you trust that the ground is there. Faith is that walk. And Paul gives life a single aim: whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him (2 Corinthians 5:9).

He adds a sober reminder: all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But the judge is the Christ who loved us and gave himself for us. The question is not how to escape him but how to be ready to meet him.

The Gospel gives a picture: a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years. The owner says, Cut it down. The gardener says, Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it (Luke 13:8). Jesus is that gardener. He gives us time, and he digs and feeds us with his grace. Even the refuse of our lives he turns into nourishment.

So let us not waste the year he asks for us. Now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Let us take one step by faith today, and let us bear one fruit of the Spirit. Amen.
kids: Children, do you have a tree at home, a mango or a jackfruit or a coconut? Think how long it takes for a tree to give fruit! A man in Jesus' story had a fig tree that gave no fruit for three years. He wanted to cut it down, but the gardener said, “Give it one more year. I will take care of it.” Jesus is like that gardener. He is patient with us, he helps us grow, and he wants us to bear good fruit: kindness, sharing and love. What good fruit will you grow this week?

homily: Dear friends, St Paul says something astonishing: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:20). He has not lost himself; he has found the true centre. The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. Notice the word me: Christ died for each of us by name.

In the Gospel Jesus says that unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). In these monsoon days our farmers know this: the seed disappears into the mud, and then the green shoots come. Jesus is that seed, and he calls us to follow him: whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.

Today the Panchangam remembers Morth Alphonsa. She was born in 1910 at Kudamaloor, lost her mother as a baby, entered the convent at Bharananganam, and spent long years in illness, in prayer and in patience, dying at thirty-five in 1946. Pope Benedict XVI canonised her in 2008. She gave her pain to the Lord with a smile, and her hidden life has borne a great harvest.
So let us learn from her to give our small pains and our whole lives to the Lord, to visit and serve the sick, and to let Christ live in us. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever planted a seed? You put it into the soil and cover it, and for some days you see nothing. But then a tiny green shoot comes up! Jesus says that he is like that seed. He died and rose again and now gives life to everyone. St Alphonsa was a sister who was often sick, but she gave all her pain to Jesus and kept smiling, and now many people pray at her tomb. When something hurts you this week, say, “Jesus, this is for you,” and give a smile.

homily: Dear friends, the Letter to the Hebrews tells us: Let mutual love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:1–2). Abraham ran out to three travellers at noon, and found that they were messengers of God. A home where love is steady and the stranger is welcome is a small Church.

In the Gospel a woman named Martha welcomed Jesus into her home. Let us not be unfair to her. She was the host. Her trouble was that she was worried and distracted by many things, while her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet and listened. Jesus called her name twice, with great love: Martha, Martha. There is need of only one thing, and Mary has chosen the better part (Luke 10:41–42).

John tells us that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. When Lazarus died, Martha ran to meet the Lord and made her great confession: I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God (John 11:27). Mary fell at his feet; Jesus wept; Lazarus came out of the tomb. Martha serves, Mary anoints: the two are halves of one discipleship. Mary of Bethany is not Mary Magdalene.
So let us open our homes, and then sit at his feet. Let the day begin with five minutes of listening, and let our service be done without grumbling. At the Holy Qurbono he serves us himself. Amen.
kids: Children, do you like it when your friends come to your house? Jesus had friends called Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and he loved to visit them. Martha cooked, and Mary sat beside Jesus to listen to him. Jesus loved them both, but he wanted Martha to know that listening to him is the most important thing. Today, when someone comes to your home, say hello with a happy face. And before you do your homework, sit quietly for a moment and tell Jesus, “Welcome, Lord. I am listening.”

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2). But he does not frighten them. You are not in darkness; you are all children of light and children of the day (1 Thessalonians 5:4–5). A thief surprises the sleeping, not those who are awake.

So the instruction is simple: let us not fall asleep as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober (1 Thessalonians 5:6). To keep awake is not to live in fear. It is to be alert in the Lord, the opposite of the sleep of routine, and to keep a clear head. And the reason for our confidence is that God has destined us not for wrath but for salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep we may live with him (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10).

In the Gospel, the first one awake is Jesus himself. At daybreak he went to a deserted place to pray. The crowds wanted to keep him, but he said, I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose (Luke 4:43). His mission comes out of prayer.
So let us rise a little earlier, give the first minutes to the Lord, and then go where we are sent. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know who is awake in the early morning? The farmers, the fishermen, the bakers, the milk sellers, and the birds! Jesus also got up very early in the morning, before everyone else, and went to a quiet place to talk to his Father. Then he went to the next town to tell the people about God. St Paul says that we are children of the light and of the day. So tomorrow morning, when you wake up, say hello to Jesus before you say hello to anyone else. Say, “Good morning, Lord!”

homily: Dear friends, St Paul gives us a sentence that can fill every day: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Nothing is too small, the meal, the work, the journey. And he adds: not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved; be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:33–11:1).

In the Gospel Jesus speaks to large crowds, and he is not gentle. Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:27). He asks us to count the cost, like a builder and a king. He wants the crowd to choose with open eyes. The strong word about hating father and mother means that no love may stand before Christ; elsewhere he says that whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him.

Today the Panchangam remembers St Ignatius of Loyola. He was a soldier, wounded at Pamplona in 1521. In bed he read about Jesus and the saints, and he gave his life to God. He wrote the Spiritual Exercises, gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier, and founded the Society of Jesus in 1540. He died in 1556. His motto is Ad maiorem Dei gloriam: to the greater glory of God. Xavier brought the Gospel to the coast of India.
So let us begin each task with the words, To the greater glory of God. Let us count the cost of our promises, and let us carry the cross after the Lord. Amen.
kids: Children, do you remember how to say your prayer before you eat? St Paul says that even eating and drinking can be done for the glory of God. St Ignatius, whom we remember today, was a soldier who got hurt and read about Jesus while he was in bed. He promised to do everything for the greater glory of God. Before you start your homework or your game, say very quietly, “For you, Jesus.” Every little thing becomes a gift.

intro: Theme: “My Lord and my God!”
We keep the Dukrono of St Thomas, our Father in Faith. The apostle who first doubted made the fullest confession of faith in the Gospels and carried it to India. We are the fruit of his mission.

points.h: From doubt to the fullest confession
sub: Job longed to find God; Thomas wanted to touch the wounds.
Jesus comes back for one disciple and offers his wounds.
Thomas confesses: “My Lord and my God!” The risen Jesus is truly God.
q: Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his dwelling!
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
points.apply: At the elevation in the Holy Qurbono, say silently: “My Lord and my God.”

points.h: The Way, the Truth and the Life
sub: Thomas asked: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
His honest question drew from Jesus one of the greatest sayings of the Gospel.
The path of those who follow Christ grows brighter like the dawn.
q: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
points.apply: Bring your honest questions about faith to the Lord in prayer, and to a priest or catechist.

sub: Isaiah praised the feet of the messenger of peace.
As the Father sent the Son, Christ sends his apostles; tradition holds that Thomas came to India and was martyred at Mylapore.
The St Thomas Christians received his faith; we are called to hand it on.
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.”
Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you.”
points.apply: Teach a child in your family the confession “My Lord and my God.”

concl: Thomas shows that honest doubt can become deep faith when it meets the wounds of Christ.
Let us confess him as Lord and God and carry the faith of our fathers forward.
2027-07-03.resolve: Pray for the Church in India and for missionaries from Kerala serving abroad.

intro: Theme: “He is our peace.”

Jesus warns that a house divided against itself cannot stand. Paul proclaims that Christ has broken down the dividing wall. The Spirit who shook the place where the apostles prayed gives us boldness and unity.

sub: Satan divides; Christ gathers.
Division in hearts, families and parishes weakens our witness.
God promises peace to those far off and those near, and healing.
q: Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal them.
If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.
points.apply: Take the first step to heal one division in your family or neighbourhood.

points.h: Christ breaks down the dividing wall
sub: The Day of Atonement prefigured the cleansing Christ would bring.
By his cross Christ has made Jew and Gentile one, broken down the wall of hostility.
We pray and work for the unity of all Christians, as our Church has done from the reunion of 1930.
q: For on this day atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before the LORD.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Pray this week for Christian unity, especially among the Churches of Kerala.

points.h: Our words and the Holy Spirit
sub: Jesus warns against blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: not a sin too great for mercy, but the refusal of mercy itself (CCC 1864).
Every careless word will be accounted for; words can give life or destroy.
Filled with the Spirit, the apostles spoke God's word with boldness.
q: Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits.
I tell you, on the day of judgment you will have to give an account for every careless word you utter; for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
points.apply: Fast from gossip and harsh words for one week.

concl: Christ unites what sin divides; the Spirit gives words that build up.
Let us be peacemakers in our homes and bold witnesses in the world.
2027-07-04.resolve: Pray Psalm 133 as a family each evening this week.

intro: Theme: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen.”
Jesus tells the parable of the sower. The Letter to the Hebrews calls God's word living and active. The God who revealed his name to Moses speaks to us, and calls us his own priestly people.

sub: God's word never returns empty; the problem is never the seed.
The path, the rocky ground and the thorns are hearts closed by hardness, shallowness or worry.
Good soil hears, accepts and bears fruit with patience.
q: So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and succeed in the thing for which I sent it.
And these are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
points.apply: Ask yourself honestly which soil your heart is this week, and remove one “thorn”.

points.h: The word is living and active
sub: God asks above all: “Obey my voice.”
His word judges the thoughts of the heart; it is a sword that heals.
In the Holy Qurbono, when the Gospel is proclaimed, Christ himself speaks (Second Vatican Council, Sacrosanctum Concilium 7).
q: But this command I gave them, “Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk only in the way that I command you, so that it may be well with you.”

Indeed, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing until it divides soul from spirit, joints from marrow; it is able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
points.apply: Read the Sunday Gospel again at home and keep one verse in your heart.

points.h: A people who belong to “I AM”
sub: God revealed his name to Moses: “I AM WHO I AM.”
Through baptism we become a chosen race, a royal priesthood.
This common priesthood of the faithful is lived by offering our lives with Christ, and is served by the ministerial priesthood.
q: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” He said further, “Thus you shall say to the Israelites, ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people, in order that you may proclaim the mighty acts of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
points.apply: Offer your daily work to God each morning as your spiritual sacrifice.

concl: The Sower is generous; the word is powerful; the harvest depends on our listening.
Let us be good soil and a priestly people.
2027-07-11.resolve: Give ten minutes each day this week to reading the Gospel of Mark.

intro: Theme: “Remember your leaders; imitate their faith.”

Today we remember Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios (died 15 July 1953), founder of the Bethany Ashram and Bethany Sisters, who led the reunion of 1930 and became the first Metropolitan Archbishop of our Church. His cause for canonisation is in progress; we honour him as Servant of God.

sub: God promised Moses: “I will be with you.” He keeps that promise to those he calls to lead.
Mar Ivanios sought the truth of the Church in prayer and study, and followed it at great cost.
We remember him not with nostalgia but by imitating his faith in Christ, who is the same forever.
q: He said, “I will be with you; and this shall be the sign for you that it is I who sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall worship God on this mountain.”
Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
points.apply: Read a short account of the reunion of 1930 with your family.

sub: The master entrusts talents to servants and asks for fruit.
Mar Ivanios used his gifts for prayer, education and the unity of the Church.
Every gift we have is entrusted to us for the Lord's work.
q: With all your soul fear the Lord, and revere his priests.
His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master.’
points.apply: Name one talent God has given you and use it this week for the Church.

sub: God promised shepherds after his own heart.
Paul urged the elders to keep watch over the flock bought by Christ's blood.
We pray for our bishops and priests, and for vocations to the Bethany communities and our seminaries.
q: I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son.
points.apply: Pray today for the cause of Mar Ivanios, leaving the judgement to the Church.

concl: Mar Ivanios teaches that faithfulness to truth and love of unity can shape a whole Church.
Let us remember, imitate and pray.
2027-07-15.resolve: If possible, visit or pray for the tomb at St Mary's Cathedral, Pattom.

intro: Theme: “The lowest place and the hidden seed.”

At a dinner Jesus teaches humility; in the parables he shows how God's kingdom grows quietly, patiently, from small beginnings. In two weeks the Fifteen Days' Fast in honour of the Mother of God begins.

sub: Guests rush for places of honour; Jesus tells them to sit at the lowest.
Humility is not thinking little of ourselves but seeing ourselves truly before God.
The greater one's position, the greater the need for humility.
q: The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself; so you will find favor in the sight of the Lord.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
points.apply: This week let someone else have the honour, the credit or the last word.

points.h: Wheat and weeds: the patience of God
sub: Good and evil grow together in the world and even in the Church until the harvest.
God is patient, giving time for repentance; judgement belongs to him.
Our task is not to uproot others but to be wheat.
q: Through such works you have taught your people that the righteous must be kind, and you have filled your children with good hope, because you give repentance for sins.
Let both of them grow together until the harvest; and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, Collect the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.
points.apply: Replace one judgemental thought about someone with a prayer for them.

sub: The kingdom begins small and grows great; it works quietly like yeast.
Keeping God's law faithfully is Israel's wisdom before the nations; our faithful lives are a witness too.
Mary, the humble handmaid, is the perfect example of this hidden growth.
q: You must observe them diligently, for this will show your wisdom and discernment to the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!”

The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field; it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.
points.apply: Begin now to plan how your family will keep the Fifteen Days' Fast from 1 August.

concl: God's kingdom grows through the humble, the patient and the faithful in small things.
Let us take the lowest place, trust God's patience, and be yeast in the world.
2027-07-18.resolve: Pray the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) each evening this week.

intro: Theme: “Unless you become like children.”

Jesus places a child in the midst of his disciples and teaches that the humble are the greatest. In the 2025–26 lectionary this Sunday was Sunday School Day: a day to thank catechists and renew our duty to hand on the faith.

sub: The disciples ask who is the greatest; Jesus answers with a child.
Childlike faith trusts, depends on the Father, and receives everything as gift.
Like a child quiet at its mother's side, the soul rests in God.
q: But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; my soul is like the weaned child that is with me.
Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes humble like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
points.apply: Spend five minutes in silent, trusting prayer each night before sleep.

points.h: Do not lose one of these little ones
sub: Moses commanded parents to teach God's words at home, on the road, at rest and at rising.
The Father does not want even one little one to be lost.
Parents are the first catechists; Sunday school helps but cannot replace the home (CCC 2223–2226).
q: Keep these words that I am commanding you today in your heart. Recite them to your children and talk about them when you are at home and when you are away, when you lie down and when you rise.
So it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.
points.apply: Thank your children's catechists, and pray with your children every evening.

points.h: Confess with your lips, be healed
sub: God revealed himself as the Lord who heals.
Faith must be confessed openly: Jesus is Lord.
Children learn to confess Christ by seeing adults do it without shame.
